Thus they were listed by him, as the LORD commanded Moses.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 details how the holy things are to be carried when the camp moves. The Kohathites bear the sacred vessels, the Gershonites the curtains, the Merarites the framework — but the most striking note is the danger. The Kohathites must not touch or even look upon the holy things uncovered, lest they die.

Here is a theology of reverence. The God of grace is also the God of holiness, and his nearness is both Israel’s glory and Israel’s peril. The priests must cover the holy things before the Levites may carry them; mediation stands between the people and the lethal glory of God.

Wenham notes the careful gradation: only the priests handle the uncovered vessels, only the Kohathites carry the covered ones, and each task is assigned, named, and counted. The God of order leaves nothing to improvisation when it comes to his own worship.

For us, the chapter both humbles and exalts. It humbles, reminding us that we cannot approach God carelessly. It exalts, for the One who covers the holy things and brings us near is Christ, our High Priest, who alone could handle the glory of God and who clothes us so that we may draw near and live.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Kohathites and the Holy Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Kohathites carry the most sacred vessels, but only after the priests have covered them; to touch or look upon the holy things means death.
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness is perilous; the glory of God must be mediated and covered, lest sinful men be consumed.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the ark carried under coverings, untouched. Now: we approach the holy God only through Christ, who clothes us to draw near.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "Take a census of the sons of Kohath from among the sons of Levi, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, all who can come on duty, to do the work in the tent of meeting. This is the service of the sons of Kohath in the tent of meeting: the most holy things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third census, and a third set of criteria. Chapter 1 counted men from twenty upward who could fight. Chapter 3 counted Levites from a month old, because they were owned. This one counts from thirty years old up to fifty years old, all who can come on duty — the working years, the men strong enough to carry a tabernacle across a desert and mature enough to be trusted with it.

God does not use one measure for everything. A man is claimed as an infant, listed for service in his prime, and released at fifty; and each of those facts is true of the same man at a different point in his life. There is such a thing in Scripture as a season for heavy work and a season for laying it down, and the God who assigns both is not thereby valuing the man differently.

And the Kohathites are given the heaviest charge in Israel: the most holy things — the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars. The highest privilege in the camp, and the next sixteen verses are almost entirely about how dangerous it is.

verseByVerse.quote: When the camp is to set out, Aaron and his sons shall go in and take down the veil of the screen and cover the ark of the testimony with it. Then they shall put on it a covering of goatskin and spread on top of that a cloth all of blue, and shall put in its poles. And over the table of the bread of the Presence they shall spread a cloth of blue and put on it the plates, the dishes for incense, the bowls, and the flagons for the drink offering; the regular showbread also shall be on it. Then they shall spread over them a cloth of scarlet and cover the same with a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles. And they shall take a cloth of blue and cover the lampstand for the light, with its lamps, its tongs, its trays, and all the vessels for oil with which it is supplied. And they shall put it with all its utensils in a covering of goatskin and put it on the carrying frame. And over the golden altar they shall spread a cloth of blue and cover it with a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles. And they shall take all the vessels of the service that are used in the sanctuary and put them in a cloth of blue and cover them with a covering of goatskin and put them on the carrying frame. And they shall take away the ashes from the altar and spread a purple cloth over it. And they shall put on it all the utensils of the altar, which are used for the service there, the fire pans, the forks, the shovels, and the basins, all the utensils of the altar; and they shall spread on it a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single Kohathite touches anything, the priests have work to do. Aaron and his sons shall go in and take down the veil of the screen and cover the ark of the testimony with it. Then goatskin. Then a cloth of blue. Then the poles are put in, so the thing can be lifted without a hand ever coming near it. The same procedure follows for the table, the lampstand, the golden altar and the bronze altar — each wrapped, layer by layer, by priestly hands, before any Levite arrives.

Note who does the covering. Not the men who will carry it. The priests go in first, alone, and make the holy things safe to be near. The Kohathites arrive to find every vessel already shrouded, and lift poles.

The coverings work in both directions, and that is the point. They protect the vessels from the eyes and hands of men who are not permitted, and they protect the men from the glory inside. It is not that the ark was fragile. It is that they were.

Everything in this arrangement says the same thing: nobody comes to the holy God on his own initiative, and nobody handles what is holy except by a way that has been prepared for him by a priest. Israel could carry the ark across a wilderness because Aaron had gone in first. The church comes to God at all because Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf (Heb. 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And when Aaron and his sons have finished covering the sanctuary and all the furnishings of the sanctuary, as the camp sets out, after that the sons of Kohath shall come to carry these, but they must not touch the holy things, lest they die. These are the things of the tent of meeting that the sons of Kohath are to carry. "And Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest shall have charge of the oil for the light, the fragrant incense, the regular grain offering, and the anointing oil, with the oversight of the whole tabernacle and all that is in it, of the sanctuary and its vessels." The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "Let not the tribe of the clans of the Kohathites be destroyed from among the Levites, but deal thus with them, that they may live and not die when they come near to the most holy things: Aaron and his sons shall go in and appoint them each to his task and to his burden, but they shall not go in to look on the holy things even for a moment, lest they die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sentence the chapter has been building to: after that the sons of Kohath shall come to carry these, but they must not touch the holy things, lest they die.

These are the men appointed to the job. They are Levites, from the right clan, at the right age, on the right day, doing exactly what God told them to do — and if a hand slips onto the ark itself they die. Four hundred years later a man named Uzzah found that out on a bad road when the oxen stumbled and he put out his hand to steady the ark, and God struck him down there for his error, and he died there beside the ark of God (2 Sam. 6:7). He was trying to help. It was still death.

Modern readers find that intolerable, and the honest response is not to explain it away but to notice what is actually being said. Holiness is not a mood or a moral quality; the Bible treats it as something like a live current, real enough to kill, and the whole apparatus of poles and coverings exists so that sinful men can work all day within a few feet of it and go home.

Which is exactly how God himself explains it. Read verse 19 and see the motive stated in his own words: deal thus with them, that they may live and not die when they come near to the most holy things. Every prohibition in the chapter is there for their survival. God is not looking for an excuse to strike a Kohathite. He is going to enormous trouble to arrange matters so that men who cannot survive his presence unprotected can spend their working lives carrying his furniture — and he specifies each man’s task and his burden by name so that nobody blunders into what was never his to handle.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Gershonites carry the curtains and coverings; the Merarites bear the framework; each is assigned and supervised.
verseByVerse.theology: Every servant has an appointed task; the body of God’s servants is ordered and complete.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: every clan with its assigned burden. Now: every believer gifted and placed in the body of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take a census of the sons of Gershon also, by their fathers' houses and by their clans. From thirty years old up to fifty years old, you shall list them, all who can come to do duty, to do service in the tent of meeting. This is the service of the clans of the Gershonites, in serving and bearing burdens: they shall carry the curtains of the tabernacle and the tent of meeting with its covering and the covering of goatskin that is on top of it and the screen for the entrance of the tent of meeting and the hangings of the court and the screen for the entrance of the gate of the court that is around the tabernacle and the altar, and their cords and all the equipment for their service. And they shall do all that needs to be done with regard to them. All the service of the sons of the Gershonites shall be at the command of Aaron and his sons, in all that they are to carry and in all that they have to do. And you shall assign to their charge all that they are to carry. This is the service of the clans of the sons of the Gershonites in the tent of meeting, and their guard duty is to be under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest. "As for the sons of Merari, you shall list them by their clans and their fathers' houses. From thirty years old up to fifty years old, you shall list them, everyone who can come on duty, to do the service of the tent of meeting. And this is what they are charged to carry, as the whole of their service in the tent of meeting: the frames of the tabernacle, with its bars, pillars, and bases, and the pillars around the court with their bases, pegs, and cords, with all their equipment and all their accessories. And you shall list by name the objects that they are required to carry. This is the service of the clans of the sons of Merari, the whole of their service in the tent of meeting, under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The other two clans are assigned in the same detail. Gershon takes the curtains of the tabernacle… its covering… the screen for the entrance… the hangings of the court… the cords — the fabric of the dwelling. Merari takes the frames of the tabernacle, with its bars, pillars, and bases, and the pillars around the court with their bases, pegs, and cords — the skeleton. And both work under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest.

Then a phrase that should be lifted out and framed: the Merarites’ loads are to be assigned by name, item by item, down to the pegs. Somewhere in that camp was a man whose entire commission from Almighty God was a bundle of tent pegs, and his name was on a list beside them.

Consider the shape of that. The tabernacle could not stand without the frames, the frames could not stand without the bases, and the whole structure would come down in a night wind without the pegs and cords. The Kohathite carrying the ark had the more glorious burden. He did not have the more necessary one, and nobody in Israel got to choose which he had.

Every congregation contains Merarites — the people carrying the load-bearing timber that nobody looks at, whose absence would be noticed within a week and whose presence is noticed by nobody. God assigned that work himself, by name, and wrote it into Scripture. The parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable (1 Cor. 12:22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–49 — The Levites Numbered for Service
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites are counted for active service; the total of working Levites is 8,580.
verseByVerse.theology: The obedient ordering of God’s servants is sealed once more: all is done as the LORD commanded.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a counted host of servants ready for the march. Now: a church equipped and deployed for the work of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses and Aaron and the chiefs of the congregation listed the sons of the Kohathites, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come on duty, for service in the tent of meeting; and those listed by clans were 2,750. This was the list of the clans of the Kohathites, all who served in the tent of meeting, whom Moses and Aaron listed according to the commandment of the LORD by Moses. Those listed of the sons of Gershon, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come on duty for service in the tent of meeting— those listed by their clans and their fathers' houses were 2,630. This was the list of the clans of the sons of Gershon, all who served in the tent of meeting, whom Moses and Aaron listed according to the commandment of the LORD. Those listed of the clans of the sons of Merari, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come on duty, for service in the tent of meeting— those listed by clans were 3,200. This was the list of the clans of the sons of Merari, whom Moses and Aaron listed according to the commandment of the LORD by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The working Levites are counted clan by clan: Kohathites 2,750, Gershonites 2,630, Merarites 3,200. Three tallies, three clans, each listed separately and each set down with the same care.

Notice how small these numbers are beside the six hundred thousand of chapter 1. The men who actually carried the dwelling place of God across a wilderness for forty years were fewer than nine thousand out of a nation of two million. The visible strength of Israel was the army; the thing that made Israel Israel was carried by a fraction of one tribe.

And every one of them is counted. Not estimated — counted, by clan, by name, by task. There is a particular encouragement in that for anyone whose service is unseen. God has never once lost track of who is doing the work. He keeps the register himself, and he has been publishing it for three and a half thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: All those who were listed of the Levites, whom Moses and Aaron and the chiefs of Israel listed, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come to do the service of ministry and the service of bearing burdens in the tent of meeting, those listed were 8,580. According to the commandment of the LORD through Moses they were listed, each one with his task of serving or carrying. Thus they were listed by him, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The total of working Levites is 8,580, and the chapter closes with the seal that has stamped every chapter so far, given twice over: According to the commandment of the LORD through Moses they were listed, each one with his task of serving or carrying. Thus they were listed by him, as the LORD commanded Moses.

Four chapters are now complete, and they have been an exercise in ordering: a nation counted, a camp arranged, a tribe substituted, a workforce assigned. And the last phrase of each is the same. As the LORD commanded. Not a single arrangement in the whole system was somebody’s good idea.

Each one with his task of serving or carrying. That is the summary of the Levites and it is not a bad summary of a life. Some of it is serving and some of it is carrying, and the difference between drudgery and worship is not in the weight of the load but in who assigned it.

And there is a shadow over the whole splendid arrangement, which the rest of the book will make plain. All this careful holiness — the coverings, the poles, the distances, the pegs, the death penalty at the boundary — exists because God had come to live among a people who could not survive him. Every layer of goatskin says the same thing: he is here, and you cannot come. Then one day a man walked into the middle of the camp with no covering over him at all, and lepers touched him and lived, and he took the poles and the veils and the distance and all of it away — for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Eph. 2:18). The Kohathites carried the presence of God across a desert without daring to look at it. We are invited to look at it, and it has a human face.

4.theology:
The Peril and Glory of Holiness. The Kohathites carry the holiest things yet may not touch or look upon them, “lest they die.” God’s holiness is a consuming reality; his nearness is both Israel’s glory and her peril. The coverings are mercy, allowing sinful men to serve and live.

Mediation Before Approach. The priests must cover the holy things before the Levites may carry them. There is no access to the glory of God except through appointed mediation — fulfilled in Christ, who alone handled the glory and who clothes us to draw near.

Every Servant Assigned. Each clan, each man, each peg and cord is named and counted. The God of order assigns to every servant his task and burden. In the body of Christ, every member is gifted, placed, and precious.
4.examples:
Then: The holy things were wrapped in blue and borne on poles, untouched and unseen, “lest they die”; every Levite knew his task, from the ark to the tent pegs, all done as the LORD commanded.

Now: What the Kohathite could not touch and the priest could only cover, you behold in the face of Christ and live. Approach the holy God with reverence, clothed in his righteousness — and take up your appointed burden in his house, for no faithful service is overlooked by the God who counts every servant by name.

5.title: Laws on Uncleanness and Unfaithfulness
5.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead.<sup>3</sup>You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell."<sup>4</sup>And the people of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt,<sup>7</sup>he shall confess his sin that he has committed. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it and giving it to him to whom he did the wrong.<sup>8</sup>But if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement with which atonement is made for him.<sup>9</sup>And every contribution, all the holy donations of the people of Israel, which they bring to the priest, shall be his.<sup>10</sup>Each one shall keep his holy donations: whatever anyone gives to the priest shall be his."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, If any man's wife goes astray and breaks faith with him,<sup>13</sup>if a man lies with her sexually, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she is undetected though she has defiled herself, and there is no witness against her, since she was not taken in the act,<sup>14</sup>and if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife who has defiled herself, or if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife, though she has not defiled herself,<sup>15</sup>then the man shall bring his wife to the priest and bring the offering required of her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He shall pour no oil on it and put no frankincense on it, for it is a grain offering of jealousy, a grain offering of remembrance, bringing iniquity to remembrance.<sup>16</sup>"And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the LORD.<sup>17</sup>And the priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water.<sup>18</sup>And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD and unbind the hair of the woman's head and place in her hands the grain offering of remembrance, which is the grain offering of jealousy. And in his hand the priest shall have the water of bitterness that brings the curse.<sup>19</sup>Then the priest shall make her take an oath, saying, 'If no man has lain with you, and if you have not turned aside to uncleanness while you were under your husband's authority, be free from this water of bitterness that brings the curse.<sup>20</sup>But if you have gone astray, though you are under your husband's authority, and if you have defiled yourself, and some man other than your husband has lain with you,<sup>21</sup>then' (let the priest make the woman take the oath of the curse, and say to the woman) 'the LORD make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the LORD makes your thigh fall away and your body swell.<sup>22</sup>May this water that brings the curse pass into your bowels and make your womb swell and your thigh fall away.' And the woman shall say, 'Amen, Amen.'<sup>23</sup>"Then the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of bitterness.<sup>24</sup>And he shall make the woman drink the water of bitterness that brings the curse, and the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain.<sup>25</sup>And the priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy out of the woman's hand and shall wave the grain offering before the LORD and bring it to the altar.<sup>26</sup>And the priest shall take a handful of the grain offering, as its memorial portion, and burn it on the altar, and afterward shall make the woman drink the water.<sup>27</sup>And when he has made her drink the water, then, if she has defiled herself and has broken faith with her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain, and her womb shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall become a curse among her people.<sup>28</sup>But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children.<sup>29</sup>"This is the law in cases of jealousy, when a wife, though under her husband's authority, goes astray and defiles herself,<sup>30</sup>or when the spirit of jealousy comes over a man and he is jealous of his wife. Then he shall set the woman before the LORD, and the priest shall carry out for her all this law.<sup>31</sup>The man shall be free from iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity."
5.overview:
With the camp ordered and the servants assigned, chapter 5 turns to the purity of the camp itself. Because God dwells in the midst, the camp must be holy; the unclean are put outside, wrongs must be confessed and restored, and unfaithfulness in marriage is addressed by a solemn ordeal.

The governing reason is stated plainly: “in the midst of which I dwell.” The presence of God among his people is the reason for every command about purity. Holiness is not arbitrary fussiness but the necessary response to the nearness of a holy God.

The ordeal of bitter water in the latter half of the chapter is one of Scripture’s strangest passages, yet it reveals a God who defends the wronged, exposes hidden sin, and refuses to let secret unfaithfulness corrode his people. The God who sees in secret will bring every hidden thing to light.

For the Christian, the chapter presses two truths: that sin defiles the community where God dwells, and that there is a way of confession, restitution, and cleansing. And it points to Christ, who bore our uncleanness outside the camp (Heb 13:12), drank the bitter cup we deserved, and brings the defiled back into the dwelling of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Putting the Unclean Outside the Camp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who are ceremonially unclean must be put outside the camp because God dwells in its midst.
verseByVerse.theology: The presence of God demands the purity of his dwelling place; holiness flows from his nearness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the unclean put outside the camp. Now: Christ bore our uncleanness outside the camp to bring us in.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead. You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell." And the people of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three conditions put a man outside the camp: everyone who is leprous or has a discharge, and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead. And the reason is given without any softening: that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell.

Notice what the three have in common. Skin disease, bodily discharge, and contact with a corpse are all forms of the body coming apart — decay, leakage, death. They are not sins; none of them is anybody’s fault, and a man could contract all three doing nothing but living. What they are is the visible marks of a world under the curse, and God had come to live in the middle of this camp. Where the Author of life dwells, the evidences of death are put at a distance.

It was a hard command and the last verse says Israel obeyed it. Families put out their own relatives. The compensation is that these laws were temporary, reversible, and had cleansing built into them; but a man carrying his sick brother’s bedding to the edge of the camp was not consoled by that on the day.

And this is where it lands. Under this law the unclean man was removed from the presence of God, because uncleanness spreads and holiness does not. Then a leper came to Jesus and knelt down, and Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him (Mark 1:41), and the contamination did not travel up his arm — the cleansing travelled down it. For the first time in the history of the world, holiness proved to be the more contagious of the two. The camp had to put its unclean outside. He went outside and brought them in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a person wrongs another and so breaks faith with the LORD, they must confess, make full restitution, and add a fifth.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin against a neighbor is sin against God; true repentance includes confession and concrete restitution.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: full restitution with a fifth added. Now: gospel repentance bears the fruit of confession and restored relationships.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt, he shall confess his sin that he has committed. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it and giving it to him to whom he did the wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law now turns to wrongs between people, and the definition it gives is arresting: When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt… The offence in view is theft or fraud against a neighbour, and God calls it breaking faith with himself.

That is a straight answer to a question people still ask. If I cheat a man in business, that is between him and me; what has God got to do with it? Everything, says this verse. There is no such category as a purely horizontal sin, because every person you deal with belongs to God and every dealing happens in his presence. David understood it exactly, and said the most startling thing in the Psalms about a sin that had ruined two other lives: Against you, you only, have I sinned (Ps. 51:4).

Then the shape of real repentance, in three steps that will not go out of date. He realizes his guilt — the thing is admitted to be a sin, not a mistake or a difficult season. He shall confess his sin that he has committed — named out loud, specifically, not deplored in general. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it — the money goes back, and more than went missing.

Zacchaeus knew this law. When Christ came into his house he stood up and offered four times over (Luke 19:8), which is more than Numbers required — and Jesus did not tell him to sit down. Grace has never made restitution unnecessary. It is what finally makes it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement with which atonement is made for him. And every contribution, all the holy donations of the people of Israel, which they bring to the priest, shall be his. Each one shall keep his holy donations: whatever anyone gives to the priest shall be his."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a case that closes the last door: if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest.

Suppose the man you defrauded is dead and has left nobody. There is no one to repay. The practical conclusion in every human system is that the debt has evaporated — no claimant, no claim. God’s law says the opposite: the money is still owed, and if there is no human creditor left then God receives it himself.

That single provision says something about the universe. There is no such thing as a wrong that has outlived its victim. Time does not discharge a debt and neither does a funeral. The accounts of a man who was cheated forty years ago are still open, and they are held somewhere higher up.

Read that as bad news and it is very bad news, because most of us have wronged people we can no longer find. Read it in the light of the whole Bible and it is the reason the cross was necessary and the reason it is enough. Every debt is real, permanent, and owed ultimately to God — which is precisely why the settlement of it had to be made with God, and was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–31 — The Ordeal of Bitter Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A husband suspecting his wife of unfaithfulness brings her to the priest for a solemn ordeal that exposes guilt or vindicates innocence.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who sees in secret defends the wronged and brings hidden sin to light, refusing to let unfaithfulness corrode his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: bitter water to test hidden unfaithfulness. Now: every hidden thing will be brought to light before the One who judges righteously.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, If any man's wife goes astray and breaks faith with him, if a man lies with her sexually, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she is undetected though she has defiled herself, and there is no witness against her, since she was not taken in the act, and if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife who has defiled herself, or if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife, though she has not defiled herself, then the man shall bring his wife to the priest and bring the offering required of her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He shall pour no oil on it and put no frankincense on it, for it is a grain offering of jealousy, a grain offering of remembrance, bringing iniquity to remembrance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the longest section of the chapter, and the one that troubles modern readers most: what to do when a husband suspects his wife of adultery and cannot prove it.

Read the situation the law is actually addressing. It is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she is undetected… and there is no witness against her, since she was not taken in the act. There is no evidence. And then, twice over, the law describes the state of the man: if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife who has defiled herself, or if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife, though she has not defiled herself.

That double clause is the key to the whole passage, and it is easily rushed past. The law explicitly contemplates that the woman may be entirely innocent and the man simply consumed. It is not written on the assumption that she did it.

Now ask what would happen to such a woman in the ancient world without this statute. A jealous husband with no evidence had no procedure and no restraint — she could be divorced, disgraced, put out, or worse, entirely at his discretion, and nobody would ask him for proof. What this law does is take the matter out of his hands. He may not act. He must bring it to the priest, in public, at the sanctuary, and let God decide. The grain offering of jealousy he brings has no oil and no frankincense on it — none of the marks of a joyful offering. Nobody is meant to enjoy this.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the LORD. And the priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water. And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD and unbind the hair of the woman's head and place in her hands the grain offering of remembrance, which is the grain offering of jealousy. And in his hand the priest shall have the water of bitterness that brings the curse. Then the priest shall make her take an oath, saying, 'If no man has lain with you, and if you have not turned aside to uncleanness while you were under your husband's authority, be free from this water of bitterness that brings the curse. But if you have gone astray, though you are under your husband's authority, and if you have defiled yourself, and some man other than your husband has lain with you, then' (let the priest make the woman take the oath of the curse, and say to the woman) 'the LORD make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the LORD makes your thigh fall away and your body swell. May this water that brings the curse pass into your bowels and make your womb swell and your thigh fall away.' And the woman shall say, 'Amen, Amen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ceremony itself is deliberately strange, and its strangeness is the point. The priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water. Then the curse is written out, and washed off the scroll into the cup, and the woman drinks it.

Look carefully at what is in that cup: clean water, a little dust off a floor, and some dissolved ink. There is nothing in it that could harm anybody. That is not an oversight; it is the entire design. Every other culture in the ancient Near East had trials by ordeal, and they all worked the same way — the accused was thrown into a river or made to grasp hot iron, and the ordeal itself did the damage. Israel’s ordeal has no mechanism at all. If anything whatever happens to this woman, God did it. The verdict is removed from the water, removed from the priest, and removed above all from the husband, and placed with the only one who knows.

And she is not a passive victim of the ceremony. The priest states the oath in both directions — if no man has lain with you… be free from this water — and the woman answers for herself: Amen, Amen. She says it. An innocent woman standing in that court had every reason to say it loudly, because the only power in the cup was the God who knew she had done nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of bitterness. And he shall make the woman drink the water of bitterness that brings the curse, and the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain. And the priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy out of the woman's hand and shall wave the grain offering before the LORD and bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take a handful of the grain offering, as its memorial portion, and burn it on the altar, and afterward shall make the woman drink the water. And when he has made her drink the water, then, if she has defiled herself and has broken faith with her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain, and her womb shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall become a curse among her people. But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children. "This is the law in cases of jealousy, when a wife, though under her husband's authority, goes astray and defiles herself, or when the spirit of jealousy comes over a man and he is jealous of his wife. Then he shall set the woman before the LORD, and the priest shall carry out for her all this law. The man shall be free from iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two outcomes are set out, and the second is the one usually forgotten. If she is guilty, the curse falls. But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children.

She is not merely acquitted. She is blessed, publicly, with the very thing a woman under this suspicion most needed — vindication in front of the whole community and children in her arms. The gossip in that camp ends the day she walks out of the tabernacle cleared by God himself. No husband can reopen it. No neighbour can whisper about it. A jealous man had one route available to him and it was a route that could exonerate his wife beyond any possibility of appeal.

The law is a hard one and it belongs to a world not ours, and we should not pretend otherwise. But we should be clear about the direction it runs. It removes a woman from the power of a man who cannot prove anything; it forbids him to act on his own suspicion; it costs him an offering; it stages the matter before God rather than in the household; and it gives the innocent a public verdict she could get in no other way. In its own world, this statute protects.

And there is a last thing, easily missed. Verse 31 says the husband shall be free from iniquity — he does not sin by bringing a genuine suspicion to God rather than acting on it himself. That is not a small permission. It says a man eaten by a jealousy he cannot resolve has somewhere to take it, and that the taking of it to God is itself the righteous act. Anybody who has lain awake with a suspicion, about a marriage or anything else, knows the two things it wants to do — fester, or explode. Scripture offers a third: casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7). Hand it over to the one who actually knows, and let him be the judge, because he is, and you are not.

5.theology:
Holiness Because God Dwells. The unclean are put outside the camp “in the midst of which I dwell.” Every purity command flows from the presence of the holy God. Where God lives, the marks of sin and death cannot remain.

Repentance That Restores. True repentance confesses the specific sin, makes full restitution with a fifth added, and honors God in mending the wrong. Sin against a neighbor is breaking faith with the LORD; gospel repentance bears concrete fruit.

The God Who Sees in Secret. The ordeal of bitter water reveals a God who exposes hidden sin, defends the innocent, and refuses to let unfaithfulness corrode his people. Every secret thing will be brought to light before the righteous Judge.
5.examples:
Then: The leprous were put outside the camp, wrongs were restored with a fifth added, and the bitter water exposed hidden unfaithfulness — all because the holy God dwelt in Israel’s midst.

Now: Christ went outside the camp bearing your uncleanness, drank the bitter cup of curse you deserved, and brings the defiled home to dwell with God. Walk in the light, confess your sins, make things right with those you have wronged, and rest in the One who knows every secret and yet declares you clean.

6.title: The Nazirite Vow and the Priestly Blessing
6.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD,<sup>3</sup>he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar made from wine or strong drink and shall not drink any juice of grapes or eat grapes, fresh or dried.<sup>4</sup>All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins.<sup>5</sup>"All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. Until the time is completed for which he separates himself to the LORD, he shall be holy. He shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long.<sup>6</sup>"All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body.<sup>7</sup>Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die, shall he make himself unclean, because his separation to God is on his head.<sup>8</sup>All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"And if any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day he shall shave it.<sup>10</sup>On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two pigeons to the priest to the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>11</sup>and the priest shall offer one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body. And he shall consecrate his head that same day<sup>12</sup>and separate himself to the LORD for the days of his separation and bring a male lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled.<sup>13</sup>"And this is the law for the Nazirite, when the time of his separation has been completed: he shall be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>14</sup>and he shall bring his gift to the LORD, one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish as a sin offering, and one ram without blemish as a peace offering,<sup>15</sup>and a basket of unleavened bread, loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and their grain offering and their drink offerings.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall bring them before the LORD and offer his sin offering and his burnt offering,<sup>17</sup>and he shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD, with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall offer also its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>18</sup>And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering.<sup>19</sup>And the priest shall take the shoulder of the ram, when it is boiled, and one unleavened loaf out of the basket and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved the hair of his consecration,<sup>20</sup>and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. They are a holy portion for the priest, together with the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed. And after that the Nazirite may drink wine.<sup>21</sup>"This is the law of the Nazirite. But if he vows an offering to the LORD above his Nazirite vow, as he can afford, in exact accordance with the vow that he takes, then he shall do in addition to the law of the Nazirite."<sup>22</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>23</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them,<sup>24</sup>The LORD bless you and keep you;<sup>25</sup>the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;<sup>26</sup>the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.<sup>27</sup>"So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them."
6.overview:
Chapter 6 gives us two of the most beautiful provisions in all the Law: the Nazirite vow of total consecration, and the priestly benediction by which God puts his name upon his people. Together they answer the question raised by chapter 5 — how can a sinful people dwell with a holy God? By consecration and by blessing.

The Nazirite vow allowed any Israelite, man or woman, to draw near to the intensity of consecration normally reserved for priests. Abstaining from the vine, leaving the hair uncut, avoiding all contact with death, the Nazirite was a living picture of wholehearted devotion to the LORD.

The chapter then rises to its summit in the Aaronic blessing — three lines, each beginning with the covenant name, each ascending in glory: blessing and keeping, shining face and grace, lifted countenance and peace. Wenham notes that this is the priest placing the very name of God upon Israel.

Both consecration and blessing find their fulfillment in Christ. He is the perfectly consecrated One, the true Nazirite of heart, who never touched the death of sin; and he is the great High Priest who, lifting his hands at Bethany (Luke 24:50–51), blessed his people and ascended — the face of God shining upon us forever in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Nazirite Vow of Consecration
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Any Israelite may take a vow of special consecration, abstaining from the vine, leaving the hair uncut, and avoiding all contact with the dead.
verseByVerse.theology: Total devotion to the LORD is open to all his people, not priests alone; consecration touches every part of life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Nazirite set apart by visible signs. Now: every believer called to wholehearted consecration to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar made from wine or strong drink and shall not drink any juice of grapes or eat grapes, fresh or dried. All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD…

Two things in that sentence are remarkable before the vow is even described. The first is the word. Nazirite comes from nazar, to separate or set apart — the same root as the crown on the high priest’s turban. This is not a person who has taken up a discipline; it is a person who has been made, temporarily, into something like a consecrated object.

The second is either a man or a woman. Everything else in Numbers so far has been determined by birth. You were a priest because your father was Aaron, a Levite because your father was Levi, a soldier because you were twenty and male. This is the first arrangement in the book that anybody at all may enter, and the only qualification is wanting to. A woman, a shepherd, a man from the smallest clan in the smallest tribe could stand up one morning and take on a consecration close to a priest’s. Holiness is not rationed to the professionals.

The first sign is abstinence from the vine — and the law goes to almost comic lengths: no vinegar made from wine… not any juice of grapes… no grapes, fresh or dried… nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins. Nothing is said against wine itself; Scripture calls it a gift that gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 104:15). That is precisely why it is chosen. The Nazirite gives up a legitimate joy — not a sin — and gives it up so completely that even a raisin is out. There is a kind of devotion that shows itself not by abandoning what is evil, which any believer must do, but by laying down for a season something that was perfectly permitted.

verseByVerse.quote: "All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. Until the time is completed for which he separates himself to the LORD, he shall be holy. He shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long. "All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body. Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die, shall he make himself unclean, because his separation to God is on his head. All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second sign is public: no razor shall touch his head… he shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long. Everyone in the camp could see a Nazirite coming. He carried his vow on his head, where he could not forget it and neither could anybody else, and the longer it went on the more obvious it became.

The third sign is the hardest thing in the chapter. All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body. Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die.

Read that as a real situation, not a rule. A man is six months into a year-long vow and word comes that his mother has died. He may not go. He may not touch the body, help with the burial, or stand at the grave. Ordinary priests were permitted to bury their parents (Lev. 21:2–3); only the high priest was held to this standard. For the length of his vow, an ordinary Israelite is bound tighter than a priest.

And the reason given is not squeamishness about corpses. It is because his separation to God is on his head. All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD. Death is what has gone wrong with the world, and this man has put himself, for a season, on the side of life. It is a costly, deliberate, visible protest against the ordinary state of things — and one greater than any Nazirite would one day walk right up to a coffin and touch it, and say Young man, I say to you, arise (Luke 7:14). He did not have to keep away from death. Death had to keep away from him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day he shall shave it. On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two pigeons to the priest to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and the priest shall offer one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body. And he shall consecrate his head that same day and separate himself to the LORD for the days of his separation and bring a male lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the case nobody can plan for. If any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head… A stranger drops dead at his side in the street. He did nothing wrong, chose nothing, could not have prevented it, and is defiled.

And the ruling is severe. He must shave his head — the whole visible sign of his vow gone — bring two birds, a sin offering and a burnt offering, and a lamb for a guilt offering, and begin the entire period again from day one. The previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled. Eleven months of a twelve-month vow, wiped.

Two things must be said about this and they pull against each other, which is why both are needed. The first is that defilement is objective. It is not measured by intention, and a man can be genuinely, entirely innocent and genuinely, entirely unclean at the same time. That is uncomfortable to modern ears, which want guilt and blame to line up exactly, and it is the plain teaching of the passage.

The second is that there is a way back, and God provides it in the same breath. He does not say the vow is finished and the man disqualified. He says: here is the sacrifice, here is the day, start again. Nothing about the man’s worst day is used to end him.

Anybody who has ever had a long, careful, good work in their life ruined by something they did not do knows the sick feeling of verse 12. God’s answer to it is not to pretend the damage did not happen. It is a lamb, and a new first day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Completion of the Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the days of separation are fulfilled, the Nazirite brings offerings, shaves his head, and burns the hair on the altar.
verseByVerse.theology: Consecration culminates in joyful sacrifice and offering; the dedicated life is given back to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the completed vow sealed with sacrifice. Now: the consecrated life offered to God as a living sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law for the Nazirite, when the time of his separation has been completed: he shall be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and he shall bring his gift to the LORD, one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish as a sin offering, and one ram without blemish as a peace offering, and a basket of unleavened bread, loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and their grain offering and their drink offerings. And the priest shall bring them before the LORD and offer his sin offering and his burnt offering, and he shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD, with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall offer also its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the days are complete, the Nazirite does not simply walk away. He comes to the door of the tent with a whole procession of offerings: a male lamb for a burnt offering, a ewe lamb for a sin offering, a ram for a peace offering, and baskets of unleavened bread and cakes and wafers with their grain and drink offerings.

Look at the middle item. A sin offering. This is a man at the summit of his devotion, who has kept a rigorous vow to the last day, who has gone without wine for a year and stayed away from his own family’s funerals — and he cannot conclude the thing without bringing an animal to atone for his sin.

That is the most important sentence in the chapter for anybody inclined to take God seriously, because it is the trap that lies in wait for the serious. The more a man gives up for God, the more quietly he begins to think it counts for something. Israel’s law shut the door on that at the exact moment it was most likely to open: the very ceremony that celebrated a completed consecration required the man to confess that he was still a sinner and needed blood. Nothing in the vow had made him acceptable. The vow was something he did because he was already the Lord’s.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering. And the priest shall take the shoulder of the ram, when it is boiled, and one unleavened loaf out of the basket and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved the hair of his consecration, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. They are a holy portion for the priest, together with the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed. And after that the Nazirite may drink wine. "This is the law of the Nazirite. But if he vows an offering to the LORD above his Nazirite vow, as he can afford, in exact accordance with the vow that he takes, then he shall do in addition to the law of the Nazirite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the strangest moment of the ceremony. And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering.

The hair is the vow. It is the visible sign, grown over months or years, the thing everybody in the camp recognised him by. And at the end he cuts it off with his own hand and burns it.

He does not keep it. There is no relic, no memento, nothing to show anybody afterwards. The entire outward evidence of his devotion goes up in smoke on the altar, and he walks home with a shaved head looking like everybody else. That is where genuine consecration ends — not in a trophy but in an offering, and not in the man being visibly holier but in God being given the whole thing back.

And then the vow is over, and he is handed back his ordinary life. After that the Nazirite may drink wine. There is no suggestion that the abstaining life was superior and he has now descended from it. The season of separation was real and it was a season. Most of the Christian life is lived after the hair is burned, in the ordinary run of things, drinking wine — and it is no less consecrated for that.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives Aaron and his sons the words by which they are to bless Israel, putting the divine name upon the people.
verseByVerse.theology: God himself is the source of all blessing; the priest is only the channel of the name and favor of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priest pronouncing God’s name over Israel. Now: the face of God shines upon us forever in Christ, our great High Priest.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chapter turns, and everything the book has been building toward since chapter 1 arrives. The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them…”

Stop before the words themselves and take in what is happening. God has spent five chapters ordering this camp — counting it, arranging it, cleansing it, consecrating it. Now he gathers all of that up and gives his people a blessing, and he does not leave the wording to the priest. He dictates it.

Aaron does not compose a benediction out of his own goodwill. He is handed a script. What the people hear at the end of every service is not their priest’s hope for them but God’s declaration over them, in God’s own words, delivered through a man’s mouth.

That is why a benediction at the end of a service is not a closing prayer and should never be spoken as one. It is not the minister asking God to be kind to the congregation; it is God telling the congregation what he is. And these particular words have outlived everything around them — a silver amulet dug up in a tomb outside Jerusalem, inscribed with this blessing, is the oldest fragment of biblical text ever found, older than the Dead Sea Scrolls by centuries. Israel wore these lines round her neck into the grave.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD bless you and keep you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD bless you and keep you.

The blessing comes in three lines. Each begins with the covenant name — the LORD, YHWH, the name given at the burning bush — so that the name of God falls on the congregation three times before they leave. And each line is longer than the one before it: in Hebrew, three words, then five, then seven. The blessing swells as it goes.

The first line pairs two verbs that need each other. To bless is to give good — the harvest, the child, the rain, the peace. To keep is to guard what has been given. The Hebrew shamar is the shepherd’s word, the watchman’s word, the word used of a man set over a vineyard at night.

And blessing without keeping is worth nothing, which anyone who has lived long enough knows. Good things are given and then lost — the health, the marriage, the years. To be blessed and not kept is to be handed something you will grieve over later. So the first thing God says over his people is that he gives and then he stands over what he has given.

The Lord Jesus took this word and made it his own on the last night: I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost (John 17:12). The keeping in Numbers 6 was a prayer over a camp in a desert. In his mouth it is a report.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you.

The second line rises from what God gives to what God is toward his people, and it does it with a picture everybody understands without being taught. A shining face is a face that lights up when it sees you. It is what happens to a father’s expression when a child comes into the room, and it is entirely involuntary, which is why it cannot be faked and why we trust it more than words.

The opposite of it is the terror of the Old Testament. How long will you hide your face from me? (Ps. 13:1). Hide not your face from me (Ps. 27:9). A hidden face is not anger; it is worse — it is the absence of regard, the sense that God has turned away and is attending to something else.

And here God commands his priests to tell his people, week after week, that his face is turned toward them and lit up.

Run the test on yourself. Not what you believe about God’s existence, or his power, or even his forgiveness — but this: when God looks at you, what is his face doing? Most people who have any belief at all imagine something between disappointment and patience. This verse says otherwise, and the New Testament says where the light comes from: God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 4:6). If you want to know what the face of God looks like when it is turned toward sinners, there is a face, and it looked at Peter across a courtyard after he had denied it three times.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.

The third line is the longest and it is the summit. Lift up his countenance is a step beyond a shining face; it is the image of someone raising their eyes to look directly at you and hold the look. Not a glance. Attention.

And the last word of the blessing is shalom. English flattens it into the absence of trouble, which is a poor half of it. Shalom is wholeness — everything in its place, everything working, nothing broken, nothing missing. It is what a room looks like when the quarrel is over, and what a body feels like when the illness has gone, and what a life is when the accounts with God are settled.

That is where the whole benediction has been climbing: gifts, then a face, then peace. And it is not a wish. Centuries later Paul writes to a church and gives the same word an address: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1). Aaron lifted his hands over a camp in the wilderness and asked God for shalom on a people who would be in open rebellion within five chapters. He did not know how it would be paid for. The peace was real, and it cost the life of the one who is himself called our peace (Eph. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then God explains what has just happened, in case anybody thought the priest was merely saying something nice. So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them.

Read the whole benediction again and count: the LORD, the LORD, the LORD. Three times the name is spoken over them, and God says that is the transaction. The priest is not describing a blessing; he is placing the name of God on a people, the way a brand is put on a possession or a signature on a deed. Israel walks away from that ceremony carrying the name of the God who owns them.

And notice who does the blessing. Not the priest. And I will bless them. Aaron supplies the mouth; God supplies the blessing. That is a great relief to anybody who has ever sat under a preacher he did not much admire, and a great warning to anybody in the pulpit. The words carry because of whose they are.

The New Testament ends the same way it does here, and it is no accident that the church’s benedictions are built on this pattern. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all (2 Cor. 13:14) — three lines, and the name three times over, and the name is now known to be Father, Son and Spirit. What Aaron placed on Israel in a wilderness, the church places on her people every Sunday. And Christ himself, at the very end, did not preach a last sermon or leave a last instruction: lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:50–51). He went up with his hands in the air over his people, and nothing has happened since to make him put them down.

6.theology:
Consecration for All. The Nazirite vow opened priestly intensity of devotion to any Israelite, man or woman. Holiness is not the preserve of a clerical caste; every believer is called to wholehearted, visible, costly consecration to the LORD, even relinquishing good things to declare that God is better.

God Is the Source of Blessing. The priest only pronounces; God himself blesses. The threefold benediction puts the divine name upon his people, an ascending ladder of grace — blessing and keeping, shining face and grace, lifted countenance and peace — all guaranteed by God’s pledge, “I will bless them.”

Christ the Consecrated High Priest. Jesus is the true Nazirite, wholly the Father’s, who touched our death and conquered it; and he is the great High Priest who, lifting his hands at Bethany, blessed his people. In his face the light of God shines upon us forever, and he is our peace.
6.examples:
Then: Israelites took the Nazirite vow to be wholly the LORD’s, and Aaron lifted his hands to put God’s name upon the people, pronouncing blessing, grace, and peace.

Now: You are called to consecration — to hold even good things loosely for the joy of nearness to God. And you live under a greater benediction: the face of God shines upon you in Christ, your great High Priest, who has put the Father’s name upon you and given you a peace the world cannot take away.

7.title: The Offerings of the Chiefs: God Receives Each One
7.text: <sup>1</sup>On the day when Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle and had anointed and consecrated it with all its furnishings and had anointed and consecrated the altar with all its utensils,<sup>2</sup>the chiefs of Israel, heads of their fathers' houses, who were the chiefs of the tribes, who were over those who were listed, approached<sup>3</sup>and brought their offerings before the LORD, six wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon for every two of the chiefs, and for each one an ox. They brought them before the tabernacle.<sup>4</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses,<sup>5</sup>"Accept these from them, that they may be used in the service of the tent of meeting, and give them to the Levites, to each man according to his service."<sup>6</sup>So Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites.<sup>7</sup>Two wagons and four oxen he gave to the sons of Gershon, according to their service.<sup>8</sup>And four wagons and eight oxen he gave to the sons of Merari, according to their service, under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest.<sup>9</sup>But to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder.<sup>10</sup>And the chiefs offered offerings for the dedication of the altar on the day it was anointed; and the chiefs offered their offering before the altar.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "They shall offer their offerings, one chief each day, for the dedication of the altar."<sup>12</sup>He who offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah.<sup>13</sup>And his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>14</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>15</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>16</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>17</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Nahshon the son of Amminadab.<sup>18</sup>On the second day Nethanel the son of Zuar, the chief of Issachar, made an offering.<sup>19</sup>He offered for his offering one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>20</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>21</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>22</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>23</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old.
