The tabernacle is not at the front where it could be admired and not at the back where it could be forgotten. It is carried in the middle of the people, and every one of them is arranged around it, walking.

That was the whole of Israel’s life for forty years: a column of people with the presence of God moving in the middle of them. It is also a fair description of a church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — Hobab and the Cry of the Ark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses urges Hobab to guide them, then the ark goes before, and Moses cries, “Arise, O LORD!” as it sets out and rests.
verseByVerse.theology: Even as God leads, the cry of faith rises with the ark; the LORD himself goes before his people to scatter their enemies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: “Arise, O LORD!” as the ark led the way. Now: Christ, the true Ark, goes before us, scattering every foe.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Hobab the son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' father-in-law, "We are setting out for the place of which the LORD said, 'I will give it to you.' Come with us, and we will do good to you, for the LORD has promised good to Israel." But he said to him, "I will not go. I will depart to my own land and to my kindred." And he said, "Please do not leave us, for you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you will serve as eyes for us. And if you do go with us, whatever good the LORD will do to us, the same will we do to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a small human scene that readers argue about. Moses turns to his brother-in-law, a Midianite named Hobab, and asks him to come along: Come with us, and we will do good to you, for the LORD has promised good to Israel. Hobab refuses — I will not go. I will depart to my own land and to my kindred — and Moses presses him: Please do not leave us, for you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you will serve as eyes for us.

The obvious question is whether Moses is faltering. He has a pillar of cloud. Why does he need a desert guide? Some readers see a lapse of faith, and the reading is not unreasonable.

But look at what he actually asks for. He does not ask Hobab to choose the route — the cloud does that. He asks for a man who knows the country: where the water is, which wadi floods, where a camp of that size can pitch. God’s guidance settled the destination; it did not tell Israel which side of a valley the wells were on. Divine direction has never made ordinary competence unnecessary, and a man who refuses good advice because he is being led by God has usually confused two different things.

And notice the terms Moses offers: not payment, but partnership. Whatever good the LORD will do to us, the same will we do to you. A Midianite is invited into Israel’s promises on equal terms. Whether he came that day the text does not say — though his descendants, the Kenites, turn up living among Judah generations later (Judg. 1:16), which suggests somebody in that family changed their mind.

verseByVerse.quote: So they set out from the mount of the LORD three days' journey. And the ark of the covenant of the LORD went before them three days' journey, to seek out a resting place for them. And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day, whenever they set out from the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they set out from the mount of the LORD three days’ journey. And the ark of the covenant of the LORD went before them three days’ journey, to seek out a resting place for them. And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day.

Something has changed, and it is worth noticing. Everywhere else in Numbers the ark travels in the middle of the column, carried by the Kohathites with the divisions around it. Here it goes out in front, three days ahead, to seek out a resting place for them.

The image is of God going on ahead to find his people somewhere to stop. Not driving them from behind, not merely accompanying them, but out in front looking for the place where they can lie down. And the phrase — a resting place — is the one that will run through the whole Bible until it arrives at Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28).

Above them the cloud; ahead of them the ark. Shade over their heads and a resting place being chosen before they arrive. The Christian who wants to know whether God has thought about tomorrow can start here: he was three days out in front of Israel, looking for somewhere for them to sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the ark set out, Moses said, "Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before you." And when it rested, he said, "Return, O LORD, to the ten thousand thousands of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then two lines that Israel evidently sang for centuries, one for the setting out and one for the stopping.

Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before you. That is what Moses said whenever the ark went forward. Notice whose enemies they are. Not our enemies — your enemies. Israel understood that the opposition in front of them was not fundamentally opposition to a tribe of former slaves. David sings the same line back a thousand years later at the head of Psalm 68, and the church has been borrowing it ever since.

And then, at the end of the day’s march: Return, O LORD, to the ten thousand thousands of Israel. Come back and settle down among us. It is the prayer of a people who wanted God not merely to fight for them but to come home with them and stay.

Set the two together and you have the shape of the whole Christian hope. He arises and his enemies scatter; he returns and dwells with his people. Both halves are answered in one Man who disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col. 2:15), and of whom it is finally said, Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people (Rev. 21:3).

Sinai is behind them. The cloud is over them, the ark is ahead of them, the trumpets are in the priests’ hands, and Moses is singing. Nothing in the history of the world has ever looked more promising than Israel on the twentieth day of the second month. The next chapter opens with the people complaining.

10.theology:
The Summons of God. The silver trumpets gather, march, war, and rejoice — the audible will of God for his people, sounded by the priests. The church still moves at the clear call of God’s word, and awaits the last trumpet by which Christ will gather all his elect.

God Goes Before and Abides. The ark leads the march “to seek out a resting place” and returns to dwell in the midst. God is both vanguard and center, going before to prepare rest and abiding with his people — fulfilled in Christ, who has gone to prepare a place and dwells with us by the Spirit.

Arise, O LORD! The battles of God’s people are the LORD’s battles; his arising scatters every foe. The cry finds its answer in the risen, ascended Christ, who has scattered sin, death, and the devil, and leads his people in triumph toward the rest of God.
10.examples:
Then: The trumpets called Israel to gather and march, the cloud lifted, and the ark led the host out from Sinai with the cry, “Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered!”

Now: You are a pilgrim, summoned by the gospel trumpet, following the true Ark who goes before you to prepare your rest. When enemies oppress, cry, “Arise, O LORD!” — for the risen Christ has already scattered every foe and will gather you home at the last trumpet. Invite others to come with you, for the Lord has promised good.

11.title: Grumbling and the Seventy Elders
11.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people complained in the hearing of the LORD about their misfortunes, and when the LORD heard it, his anger was kindled, and the fire of the LORD burned among them and consumed some outlying parts of the camp.<sup>2</sup>Then the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down.<sup>3</sup>So the name of that place was called Taberah, because the fire of the LORD burned among them.<sup>4</sup>Now the rabble that was among them had a strong craving. And the people of Israel also wept again and said, "Oh that we had meat to eat!<sup>5</sup>We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic.<sup>6</sup>But now our strength is dried up, and there is nothing at all but this manna to look at."<sup>7</sup>Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium.<sup>8</sup>The people went about and gathered it and ground it in handmills or beat it in mortars and boiled it in pots and made cakes of it. And the taste of it was like the taste of cakes baked with oil.<sup>9</sup>When the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell with it.<sup>10</sup>Moses heard the people weeping throughout their clans, everyone at the door of his tent. And the anger of the LORD blazed hotly, and Moses was displeased.<sup>11</sup>Moses said to the LORD, "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? And why have I not found favor in your sight, that you lay the burden of all this people on me?<sup>12</sup>Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that you should say to me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child,' to the land that you swore to give their fathers?<sup>13</sup>Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? For they weep before me and say, 'Give us meat, that we may eat.'<sup>14</sup>I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me.<sup>15</sup>If you will treat me like this, kill me at once, if I find favor in your sight, that I may not see my wretchedness."<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them to the tent of meeting, and let them take their stand there with you.<sup>17</sup>And I will come down and talk with you there. And I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.<sup>18</sup>And say to the people, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat, for you have wept in the hearing of the LORD, saying, "Who will give us meat to eat? For it was better for us in Egypt." Therefore the LORD will give you meat, and you shall eat.<sup>19</sup>You shall not eat just one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or twenty days,<sup>20</sup>but a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected the LORD who is among you and have wept before him, saying, "Why did we come out of Egypt?"'"<sup>21</sup>But Moses said, "The people among whom I am number six hundred thousand on foot, and you have said, 'I will give them meat, that they may eat a whole month!'<sup>22</sup>Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, and be enough for them?"<sup>23</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Is the LORD's hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not."<sup>24</sup>So Moses went out and told the people the words of the LORD. And he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people and placed them around the tent.<sup>25</sup>Then the LORD came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took some of the Spirit that was on him and put it on the seventy elders. And as soon as the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied. But they did not continue doing it.<sup>26</sup>Now two men remained in the camp, one named Eldad, and the other named Medad, and the Spirit rested on them. They were among those registered, but they had not gone out to the tent, and so they prophesied in the camp.<sup>27</sup>And a young man ran and told Moses, "Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp."<sup>28</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun, the assistant of Moses from his youth, said, "My lord Moses, stop them."<sup>29</sup>But Moses said to him, "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!"<sup>30</sup>And Moses and the elders of Israel returned to the camp.<sup>31</sup>Then a wind from the LORD sprang up, and it brought quail from the sea and let them fall beside the camp, about a day's journey on this side and a day's journey on the other side, around the camp, and about two cubits above the ground.<sup>32</sup>And the people rose all that day and all night and all the next day, and gathered the quail. Those who gathered least gathered ten homers. And they spread them out for themselves all around the camp.<sup>33</sup>While the meat was yet between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD struck down the people with a very great plague.<sup>34</sup>Therefore the name of that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had the craving.<sup>35</sup>From Kibroth-hattaavah the people journeyed to Hazeroth, and they remained at Hazeroth.
11.overview:
Three days out from Sinai, the singing stops and the grumbling begins. Chapter 11 is the hinge of Numbers, where the obedient camp of the early chapters dissolves into discontent. The people complain, fire falls, and then they crave meat, despising the manna — the very bread of heaven.

The tragedy is staggering. God’s presence leads them, his bread feeds them, his promise beckons them, yet they weep for the garlic and fish of slavery. Paul names this in 1 Corinthians 10:6 as a warning written for us: “that we might not desire evil as they did.”

The chapter also reveals the crushing weight of leadership. Moses, overwhelmed, cries out to God in despair, and God graciously distributes the Spirit upon seventy elders to share the burden. Even the mediator needs help; the load of God’s people is too heavy for one man.

God answers the craving with quail — and with judgment. The meat they demanded becomes their grave at Kibroth-hattaavah, “the graves of craving.” The chapter is a sober mirror: discontent with God’s provision is not a small thing but a despising of God himself. And it drives us to Christ, the true Bread from heaven, who satisfies the soul that the manna only foreshadowed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people complain of their misfortunes; the LORD’s fire burns the outskirts of the camp until Moses intercedes.
verseByVerse.theology: Grumbling against God’s providence kindles his anger; complaint is a serious sin against the goodness of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: fire at Taberah for complaining. Now: a warning against the grumbling heart that despises God’s providence.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people complained in the hearing of the LORD about their misfortunes, and when the LORD heard it, his anger was kindled, and the fire of the LORD burned among them and consumed some outlying parts of the camp. Then the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down. So the name of that place was called Taberah, because the fire of the LORD burned among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days out from Sinai. Three days. And the people complained in the hearing of the LORD about their misfortunes, and when the LORD heard it, his anger was kindled.

Notice how little we are told. The text does not say what the grievance was — no famine, no enemy, no specific hardship named. They had been walking for three days and they were unhappy about it, and that is the whole account. The vagueness is the point: this is not a crisis, it is a temperature. A mood had got into the camp.

And look where it happened. Chapter 10 ended with the ark going out three days ahead to find them a resting place and Moses singing over it. This is that same journey. The complaining began inside the very three days God spent looking for somewhere for them to sleep.

Fire falls on the edge of the camp, Moses prays, and it stops. The place is named Taberah, Burning. It is the first of the graves and place-names this book will leave scattered across a desert, each one commemorating a moment when the people of God decided the God who was carrying them was not doing it well enough. Paul says these things were written down for us, and adds the application without softening it: Do all things without grumbling or disputing (Phil. 2:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — Craving Meat and the Weight of Leadership
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people despise the manna and crave meat, weeping for Egypt; Moses, crushed by the burden, cries out to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Discontent with God’s provision despises God himself; the weight of leading God’s people is too heavy for one man alone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: weeping for the food of Egypt. Now: the danger of despising God’s gifts and the need to share heavy burdens.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rabble that was among them had a strong craving. And the people of Israel also wept again and said, "Oh that we had meat to eat! We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic. But now our strength is dried up, and there is nothing at all but this manna to look at."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the craving, and the text is careful about where it starts: Now the rabble that was among them had a strong craving. And the people of Israel also wept again. It begins at the fringe and spreads to the whole nation. Discontent is contagious, and it does not usually start at the centre.

And what comes out of them is one of the most astonishing pieces of self-deception in Scripture: We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic.

Read that menu again. It is specific, sensory, and mouth-watering — a man can almost taste it. And now read what is missing from it. The whips. The quota of bricks. The straw they had to gather themselves. The baby boys thrown into the Nile. An entire nation in forced labour, groaning so loudly that God heard their groaning (Exod. 2:24). None of that survives in the memory. What survives is the garlic.

And the phrase that cost nothing is the finest lie in the sentence. It cost them everything. They were slaves; the fish came with the whip. Memory under the pressure of present discomfort does not merely soften the past — it edits it, and it edits out precisely the thing God rescued them from.

Then the verdict on the present: there is nothing at all but this manna to look at. Bread out of the sky, six mornings a week, for nothing, and it has become nothing at all. Anything God does daily and reliably will eventually stop being seen as a gift, and the surest test of a grumbling season is to ask what has quietly moved from the miracle column to the nothing column.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium. The people went about and gathered it and ground it in handmills or beat it in mortars and boiled it in pots and made cakes of it. And the taste of it was like the taste of cakes baked with oil. When the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the narrator does something remarkable. Right in the middle of the complaint, he interrupts to describe the manna.

Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium. The people went about and gathered it and ground it in handmills or beat it in mortars and boiled it in pots and made cakes of it. And the taste of it was like the taste of cakes baked with oil. When the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell with it.

Three verses of quiet, affectionate detail, and every one of them contradicts the sentence that has just been spoken. Israel said there was nothing to look at; the writer says it looked like bdellium, a pale precious resin. Israel implied monotony; the writer lists four ways of preparing it and says it tasted of cakes baked in oil. Israel said it cost nothing worth having; the writer says it came down with the dew in the night, while they were asleep, without anyone lifting a finger.

It is the gentlest rebuke in the book and one of the most effective. He does not argue with them. He just describes what they have got.

And there is a Man who took this bread and made an astonishing claim about himself with it: I am the bread of life… I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live for ever (John 6:48, 51). The generation that called it worthless was standing in a foreshadowing of Christ every morning and complaining about the taste.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses heard the people weeping throughout their clans, everyone at the door of his tent. And the anger of the LORD blazed hotly, and Moses was displeased. Moses said to the LORD, "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? And why have I not found favor in your sight, that you lay the burden of all this people on me? Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that you should say to me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child,' to the land that you swore to give their fathers? Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? For they weep before me and say, 'Give us meat, that we may eat.' I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me. If you will treat me like this, kill me at once, if I find favor in your sight, that I may not see my wretchedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The complaint reaches Moses and breaks him. What follows is one of the rawest prayers in the Bible, and it should never be tidied up.

Why have you dealt ill with your servant? And why have I not found favour in your sight, that you lay the burden of all this people on me? Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that you should say to me, “Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child”?… I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me. If you will treat me like this, kill me at once, if I find favour in your sight, that I may not see my wretchedness.

The meekest man on earth tells God that he has been badly treated, asks whether the whole arrangement was fair, and requests to be killed. And the image he reaches for is a mother’s: he is being asked to carry a nation the way a nurse carries an infant that will not stop screaming, and he did not give birth to it.

Two things must be said about this prayer, and both matter. The first is that God does not rebuke him for one word of it. Not one. He answers with help. The second is where Moses took it. He was at the absolute end of himself, and he said so to God, not to the elders and not to the congregation. Every syllable of this is prayer.

Anyone in ministry, or caring for a parent, or holding a family together, who has thought things they would not dare say aloud, should read verse 15 and notice that it is in the Bible. God can be told the truth about how it is going. Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7) does not come with a list of anxieties too ugly to bring.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Seventy Elders and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God places his Spirit on seventy elders to share Moses’ burden; Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, and Moses rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology: God graciously distributes the Spirit to share the burden of leadership; Moses longs that all God’s people might be prophets.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Spirit on seventy elders. Now: the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, the longing of Moses fulfilled at Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them to the tent of meeting, and let them take their stand there with you. And I will come down and talk with you there. And I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer to a suicidal prayer is a personnel decision. Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel… And I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.

Notice what God does not do. He does not tell Moses to pray harder, trust more, or find strength in the Lord. He looks at a man crushed by a load and concludes that the load is too big for one man — which is what Moses had just said — and he divides it.

Sit with that, because Christians are often taught that admitting the work is too heavy is a failure of faith. God’s own diagnosis here is structural, not spiritual. Jethro had said the same thing years earlier: You are not able to do it alone (Exod. 18:18). Some burdens are not meant to be carried by one person, and the answer is not more grace for the individual but more shoulders.

And observe how the sharing is done: some of the Spirit that is on you. Not a different spirit, and not a lesser one. The same Spirit, extended. Moses does not lose anything by seventy other men receiving it — there is no arithmetic in which God has less to give because he has given it — and the seventy do not get a discount version. What made Moses able to lead is what will make them able to help.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to the people, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat, for you have wept in the hearing of the LORD, saying, "Who will give us meat to eat? For it was better for us in Egypt." Therefore the LORD will give you meat, and you shall eat. You shall not eat just one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or twenty days, but a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected the LORD who is among you and have wept before him, saying, "Why did we come out of Egypt?"'" But Moses said, "The people among whom I am number six hundred thousand on foot, and you have said, 'I will give them meat, that they may eat a whole month!' Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, and be enough for them?" And the LORD said to Moses, "Is the LORD's hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then God turns to the people, and his answer to their craving is frightening. You shall eat, not one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or twenty days, but a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected the LORD who is among you.

They will get exactly what they asked for, in a quantity that will make them ill, until they cannot bear the sight of it. That is not God losing his temper. It is a specific and terrible form of judgment that the Bible names elsewhere in one line: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15). There are prayers it is a mercy not to have answered.

And notice the diagnosis God gives of the complaint: you have rejected the LORD who is among you. They thought they were complaining about food. He calls it a rejection of himself. Grumbling is never really about the circumstance; it is a verdict passed on the God who arranged it.

Moses, meanwhile, cannot see how it could be done — six hundred thousand men, a month of meat, in a desert — and God’s reply is the sentence to carry out of the chapter: Is the LORD’s hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not. A shortened hand is one that cannot reach far enough. Isaiah picks up the same image and insists the problem has never once been at God’s end: Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save (Isa. 59:1).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses went out and told the people the words of the LORD. And he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people and placed them around the tent. Then the LORD came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took some of the Spirit that was on him and put it on the seventy elders. And as soon as the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied. But they did not continue doing it. Now two men remained in the camp, one named Eldad, and the other named Medad, and the Spirit rested on them. They were among those registered, but they had not gone out to the tent, and so they prophesied in the camp. And a young man ran and told Moses, "Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp." And Joshua the son of Nun, the assistant of Moses from his youth, said, "My lord Moses, stop them." But Moses said to him, "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!" And Moses and the elders of Israel returned to the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy stand round the tent, the Spirit rests on them, and they prophesy. And then a loose end: Now two men remained in the camp, one named Eldad, and the other named Medad, and the Spirit rested on them. They were among those registered, but they had not gone out to the tent, and so they prophesied in the camp.

They were on the list. They simply were not at the meeting. And the Spirit found them where they were, in the middle of the camp, away from the tent, and they began to prophesy in front of everybody.

A young man runs to report it and Joshua reacts exactly as a loyal assistant would: My lord Moses, stop them. Prophecy has broken out in the wrong place, without supervision, outside the authorised venue, and it looks to him like a threat to his master’s standing.

Moses’ answer is the high point of his life. Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!

He is being offered a defence of his own uniqueness and he refuses it — and does not merely refuse it but wishes the opposite as hard as he can wish anything. He wants everybody to have what he has. There is not a trace in him of the instinct that guards its own position, and it is precisely because he had no interest in being irreplaceable that God could trust him with what he was given.

And his wish was granted. Not in his lifetime, and not by degrees. On a morning in Jerusalem fourteen centuries later the Spirit fell on a hundred and twenty ordinary people at once, and Peter stood up and explained it out of Joel: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy (Acts 2:17). Moses said would that all the LORD’s people were prophets. God said yes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–35 — The Quail and the Graves of Craving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends quail in vast quantity, but his anger burns and a plague strikes the greedy; the place is named Kibroth-hattaavah.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin granted is judgment; the craving fulfilled becomes the grave, a solemn warning against despising God’s provision.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the graves of craving. Now: a warning that to desire evil as they did invites the discipline of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a wind from the LORD sprang up, and it brought quail from the sea and let them fall beside the camp, about a day's journey on this side and a day's journey on the other side, around the camp, and about two cubits above the ground. And the people rose all that day and all night and all the next day, and gathered the quail. Those who gathered least gathered ten homers. And they spread them out for themselves all around the camp. While the meat was yet between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD struck down the people with a very great plague. Therefore the name of that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had the craving. From Kibroth-hattaavah the people journeyed to Hazeroth, and they remained at Hazeroth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then God keeps his word about the meat, and the manner of it is dreadful. A wind from the LORD sprang up, and it brought quail from the sea and let them fall beside the camp, about a day’s journey on this side and a day’s journey on the other side, around the camp, and about two cubits above the ground.

Picture the scale. Quail lying and fluttering for a day’s walk in every direction, three feet deep. And the people rose all that day and all night and all the next day, and gathered the quail. Thirty-six hours of frantic collecting without sleeping. The least industrious man in the camp gathered ten homers — something like sixty bushels. They were not hungry any more by then. They were hoarding.

Then: While the meat was yet between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD struck down the people with a very great plague.

The craving and the judgment arrive in the same mouthful. There is no gap between getting what they wanted and discovering what it cost, and the place is named for it — Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of craving. Israel buried its dead at a place whose name means exactly what killed them.

Paul writes this into a letter to a church and does not soften it: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did (1 Cor. 10:6). The word he uses for desire is the same root the Greek Old Testament uses for the name of this place. He is pointing at the graves.

So the chapter that opened three days out from the mountain ends in a burial ground, and the only figure in it who comes out well is the man who wanted everybody else to have what he had. God had given them bread from heaven and they asked for meat; he gave them meat and they died of it. And there is one prayer in the whole episode he answered with unmixed kindness — the prayer of a man at the end of himself who said so.

11.theology:
The Sin of Grumbling. Complaint against God’s providence kindles his anger, for to scorn our circumstances is to accuse the God who ordains them, and to despise the manna is to despise the Giver. Paul names this as a warning written for us (1 Cor 10:6).

The Burden of Leadership and the Gift of the Spirit. Moses buckles under the weight of God’s people, and God shares the burden by distributing his Spirit to seventy elders. The work of leading God’s people is never meant for one man alone; it is borne by Spirit-gifted leaders together.

Sin Granted as Judgment. God answers the craving with quail and with a plague; the graves of craving warn that getting what we sinfully demand can be the severest discipline. Yet Moses’ longing — “would that all the LORD’s people were prophets” — is fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit is poured out on all.
11.examples:
Then: Three days from Sinai, Israel despised the bread of heaven, wept for the food of slavery, and found their graves at Kibroth-hattaavah, while God graciously shared Moses’ burden with seventy Spirit-filled elders.

Now: Beware the grumbling heart that gilds the past and scorns God’s daily provision. Feed on Christ, the true Bread from heaven, who satisfies the soul forever. And if you lead God’s people, do not carry the burden alone or guard it jealously — long, like Moses, for the Spirit to fill all the people of God.

12.title: Miriam and Aaron Oppose Moses
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married, for he had married a Cushite woman.<sup>2</sup>And they said, "Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?" And the LORD heard it.<sup>3</sup>Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.<sup>4</sup>And suddenly the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron and Miriam, "Come out, you three, to the tent of meeting." And the three of them came out.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent and called Aaron and Miriam, and they both came forward.<sup>6</sup>And he said, "Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD make myself known to him in a vision; I speak with him in a dream.<sup>7</sup>Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house.<sup>8</sup>With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the LORD. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?"<sup>9</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and he departed.<sup>10</sup>When the cloud removed from over the tent, behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow. And Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous.<sup>11</sup>And Aaron said to Moses, "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned.<sup>12</sup>Let her not be as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away when he comes out of his mother's womb."<sup>13</sup>And Moses cried to the LORD, "O God, please heal her—please."<sup>14</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again."<sup>15</sup>So Miriam was shut outside the camp seven days, and the people did not set out on the march till Miriam was brought in again.<sup>16</sup>After that the people set out from Hazeroth, and camped in the wilderness of Paran.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 brings the rebellion home — not from the rabble now, but from Moses’ own brother and sister. Miriam and Aaron challenge his unique authority, using his Cushite wife as a pretext but revealing their true grievance: “Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses?”

At the heart of the chapter stands one of Scripture’s most remarkable self-descriptions: “Moses was very meek, more than all people on the face of the earth.” His greatness lay not in self-assertion but in self-forgetfulness. He does not defend himself; God defends him.

God descends in the cloud and vindicates his servant in unforgettable terms — with Moses he speaks “mouth to mouth,” not in riddles. Then Miriam is struck with leprosy, white as snow, a visible judgment on the sin of envy and presumption.

The climax is breathtaking. Moses, the one wronged, cries out for his sister: “O God, please heal her — please.” The meek mediator intercedes for his accuser, a stunning portrait of the heart of Christ, who prayed for those who crucified him. Here is the gospel in miniature: the wronged Mediator pleading for the guilty.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over his Cushite wife, questioning his unique prophetic authority; Moses is exceedingly meek.
verseByVerse.theology: Envy of God-given authority is rebellion against God; true greatness is found in meekness, not self-assertion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses’ siblings challenge his authority. Now: a warning against jealousy of others’ callings and a call to humble meekness.

verseByVerse.quote: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married, for he had married a Cushite woman. And they said, "Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?" And the LORD heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The attack this time comes from inside the family. Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married. His sister and his brother — the woman who watched his basket in the reeds and the man who spoke for him in front of Pharaoh.

The stated grievance is his wife. Cush is the region south of Egypt, and a Cushite woman would have been dark-skinned and foreign. Whether this is Zipporah the Midianite or a second marriage after her death, the text does not say. What it does say, immediately, is that the wife was not what this was about.

Because in the very next breath the real thing comes out: Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?

There it is. The marriage was the presentable objection; the actual complaint is that Moses has a standing they do not. And both of them had a case, humanly speaking — Aaron was the high priest of Israel and Miriam is called a prophetess (Exod. 15:20). They were not nobodies. They were the second and third most important people in the nation, and it was not enough.

Learn to recognise that pattern, because it is how such things almost always present themselves. A grievance is raised on grounds that sound principled, and the energy behind it comes from somewhere else entirely. The test is usually proportion: the reaction is far larger than the stated cause can explain.

And then four words: And the LORD heard it. They said it to each other, privately, in a family. There is no such thing as a private conversation about the servants of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the narrator interrupts his own story with one of the strangest sentences in Scripture. Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.

Readers have long puzzled over Moses writing that about himself, and the honest answer is that it may well be a later editorial note; the same book records his death. But the more important question is why it is here, at this exact point, and that has a clear answer.

It is here because of what Moses does not do in the next verse. He is publicly slandered by his own brother and sister, his marriage is used against him, his call is questioned — and he says nothing. Not a word of self-defence appears in this chapter. The narrator inserts verse 3 so that the reader understands the silence is not weakness or shock. It is character.

And the word does not mean what English suggests. Biblical meekness is not timidity; this is the man who faced down Pharaoh, smashed the tablets, and ground the golden calf to powder. It is strength that has stopped needing to defend itself, because it has handed the defending to somebody else.

There is only one other person in the Bible who describes himself this way. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt. 11:29) — the same word. And when he was accused, he opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7). Moses at the tent door, saying nothing while his family attacks him, is the closest the Old Testament comes to the silence of Christ before Caiaphas.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God summons the three to the tent, descends in the cloud, and declares Moses’ unique standing: he speaks with him mouth to mouth.
verseByVerse.theology: God himself defends his servants and honors the offices he appoints; to speak against his chosen is to provoke his anger.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God vindicates Moses face to face. Now: trust God to defend your honor, and revere the callings he assigns.

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron and Miriam, "Come out, you three, to the tent of meeting." And the three of them came out. And the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent and called Aaron and Miriam, and they both came forward. And he said, "Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD make myself known to him in a vision; I speak with him in a dream.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses said nothing. God does not. And suddenly the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron and Miriam, “Come out, you three, to the tent of meeting.”

Suddenly is the writer’s word and it carries the whole tone of the scene. There is no delay, no investigation, no cooling-off period. The three of them are summoned like children called in from the garden, and then the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent.

Consider the position Aaron and Miriam are now in. They have been talking about their brother behind his back for perhaps an hour, and the Almighty has come down out of the sky in front of the whole camp to speak to them about it, personally, at the door of his own house.

Then he begins with a general principle: If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD make myself known to him in a vision; I speak with him in a dream. That is how God normally deals with prophets, and it is how he had dealt with Miriam and Aaron. Visions and dreams are real revelation and neither of them is being demoted from it.

It is simply not the whole of what God does. And the next verse is going to explain why the comparison they were making was not available to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house. With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the LORD. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and he departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house. With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the LORD. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?

Every phrase raises the ground under Moses higher. Other prophets get visions; he gets God’s mouth. Other prophets get riddles — the strange, sideways, image-laden speech of Ezekiel and Zechariah; he gets it plainly. Other prophets hear; he beholds the form of the LORD. And three times in four verses God calls him my servant, which in Scripture is not a lowly word but nearly a title.

And notice the question God asks. Not why were you not kinder or why were you not fairer, but why were you not afraid. Speaking against a man God had set where he had set Moses was not a family disagreement; it was an act of nerve.

Then the most chilling verse in the chapter: And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and he departed. He goes. No conversation, no chance to answer, no mitigation. The cloud lifts off the tent and the presence withdraws, and only then do they find out what has happened.

One phrase from this speech travelled a long way. Fourteen centuries later a letter to Hebrew Christians quotes it exactly: Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant… but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Heb. 3:5–6). The very sentence God used to establish that nobody in Israel stood where Moses stood is used by the New Testament to say that Moses was, in the end, staff — and there is a Son over the house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Miriam’s Leprosy and Moses’ Intercession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Miriam is struck with leprosy; Aaron pleads, Moses intercedes, and after seven days outside the camp she is restored.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin bears bitter fruit, but the meek mediator intercedes for his accuser — a portrait of the heart of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses prays for the sister who wronged him. Now: Christ intercedes for sinners; we are called to forgive and pray for those who wrong us.

verseByVerse.quote: When the cloud removed from over the tent, behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow. And Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. And Aaron said to Moses, "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned. Let her not be as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away when he comes out of his mother's womb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the cloud removed from over the tent, behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow.

The judgment is visible, immediate, and terrible, and there is a grim aptness in it. She had spoken against a woman for the colour of her skin, and her own has gone white.

Only Miriam is struck. Her name is first in verse 1 and the Hebrew verb there is feminine singular, which marks her as the instigator; Aaron followed her. That does not leave him innocent — God’s anger was kindled against them both — and it may well be that the high priest could not be made ceremonially unclean without paralysing the worship of the whole nation. He is spared the disease and made to watch his sister get it, which is its own punishment.

And Aaron breaks. Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned. Let her not be as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away when he comes out of his mother’s womb.

Two things in that. He calls Moses my lord — the man whose authority he was questioning ten minutes ago — and he says us, not her. He does not attempt to separate himself from her, which is more than many men do when the consequences land on somebody else. And he goes to the brother he wronged, because there is nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses cried to the LORD, "O God, please heal her—please."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Moses cried to the LORD, “O God, please heal her—please.”

Five words in Hebrew. It is the shortest prayer Moses ever prays, and it has please at both ends of it.

Consider who is praying and for whom. This is the man they slandered. He has just been publicly vindicated by God himself in front of the accusers, in the most emphatic terms imaginable, and the vindication could not have been more complete. Any ordinary man would have let it stand for at least a day.

He does not wait an hour. The moment he sees her, he cries out — not a measured intercession, but a broken, doubled, urgent plea for the woman who tried to take his position away from him.

That is what the meekness of verse 3 turns out to consist of. It is not that he could not be provoked; it is that when he was given every right to enjoy the outcome, he wanted her well.

And it is the exact shape of a command that would come much later from a hillside in Galilee: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt. 5:44). Moses had no such command. He had a sister covered in leprosy who deserved it, and he asked God to take it away.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, "If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again." So Miriam was shut outside the camp seven days, and the people did not set out on the march till Miriam was brought in again. After that the people set out from Hazeroth, and camped in the wilderness of Paran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer is answered, and not entirely. If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again.

The image is domestic and humiliating: a father spitting in his daughter’s face, the sharpest public disgrace an ancient household knew, after which she would keep out of sight for a week. God says his displeasure is at least that serious. Miriam is healed and Miriam is disciplined, and the two are not in conflict.

That is a distinction Christians need and often lose. Forgiveness is not the removal of consequences. Miriam did not die and she did not lose her place in Israel; she also spent seven days sitting outside the camp where the whole nation could see her, and the sin was public so the discipline was public. The Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb. 12:6), and the discipline is evidence of the love rather than a qualification of it.

And then the last detail, which is the loveliest thing in the chapter: and the people did not set out on the march till Miriam was brought in again.

Two million people, with a cloud to follow and a land to reach, sat still for a week and waited for one disgraced woman. Nobody moved on without her. Israel had been stalled by rebellion before; this time the nation is stalled by mercy.

Which tells you what kind of God had been offended. He had every right to be finished with her. Instead the whole company of his people stopped where they stood until she could walk back in, and only then did the cloud lift. That is not a footnote. It is a picture of how he treats those he has had to correct, and it is why the next thing anybody hears about Miriam is that she was buried at Kadesh with the whole nation mourning.

12.theology:
Meekness and Self-Forgetfulness. Moses, “very meek, more than all people,” does not defend himself but entrusts his cause to God. True greatness is power surrendered to God — a portrait of Christ, gentle and lowly, who when reviled did not revile in return but entrusted himself to the righteous Judge.

God Vindicates His Servants. God descends to defend Moses, declaring he speaks with him “mouth to mouth.” To attack God’s appointed servant is to provoke God himself. We need not scramble to justify ourselves; the Judge of all the earth will vindicate his own.

The Mediator Intercedes for His Accuser. Moses, the one wronged, cries, “O God, please heal her — please.” The wronged mediator pleads for the guilty — the gospel in miniature, fulfilled when Christ prayed for those who crucified him and ever lives to intercede for sinners.
12.examples:
Then: Miriam and Aaron, envious of Moses’ authority, were rebuked by God himself; Miriam was struck with leprosy, yet the meek Moses interceded for her, and the whole camp waited until she was restored.

Now: Beware envy of others’ God-given callings, and do not grasp for your own vindication — entrust it to God. When others wrong you, follow the Mediator’s example: pray for their healing. And rest in Christ, the wronged Mediator who intercedes for the guilty and brings the penitent home.

13.title: The Twelve Spies: The Sin of Unbelief
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel. From each tribe of their fathers you shall send a man, every one a chief among them."<sup>3</sup>So Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran, according to the command of the LORD, all of them men who were heads of the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur;<sup>5</sup>from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori;<sup>6</sup>from the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh;<sup>7</sup>from the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph;<sup>8</sup>from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun;<sup>9</sup>from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu;<sup>10</sup>from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi;<sup>11</sup>from the tribe of Joseph (that is, from the tribe of Manasseh), Gaddi the son of Susi;<sup>12</sup>from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli;<sup>13</sup>from the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael;<sup>14</sup>from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi;<sup>15</sup>from the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi.<sup>16</sup>These were the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.<sup>17</sup>Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan and said to them, "Go up into the Negeb and go up into the hill country,<sup>18</sup>and see what the land is, and whether the people who dwell in it are strong or weak, whether they are few or many,<sup>19</sup>and whether the land that they dwell in is good or bad, and whether the cities that they dwell in are camps or strongholds,<sup>20</sup>and whether the land is rich or poor, and whether there are trees in it or not. Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land." Now the time was the season of the first ripe grapes.<sup>21</sup>So they went up and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, near Lebo-hamath.<sup>22</sup>They went up into the Negeb and came to Hebron. Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, were there. (Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)<sup>23</sup>And they came to the Valley of Eshcol and cut down from there a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and they carried it on a pole between two of them; they also brought some pomegranates and figs.<sup>24</sup>That place was called the Valley of Eshcol, because of the cluster that the people of Israel cut down from there.<sup>25</sup>At the end of forty days they returned from spying out the land.<sup>26</sup>And they came to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh. They brought back word to them and to all the congregation, and showed them the fruit of the land.<sup>27</sup>And they told him, "We came to the land to which you sent us. It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit.<sup>28</sup>However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. And besides, we saw the descendants of Anak there.<sup>29</sup>The Amalekites dwell in the land of the Negeb. The Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites dwell in the hill country. And the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and along the Jordan."<sup>30</sup>But Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, "Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it."<sup>31</sup>Then the men who had gone up with him said, "We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are."<sup>32</sup>So they brought to the people of Israel a bad report of the land that they had spied out, saying, "The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants, and all the people that we saw in it are of great height.<sup>33</sup>And there we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim), and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them."
13.overview:
Chapter 13 brings Israel to the threshold of the promised land — and to the great crisis of the book. Twelve spies are sent to survey Canaan; all twelve see the same land, the same fruit, the same giants. But ten see through the lens of fear, and two through the lens of faith.

The land is everything God promised — “flowing with milk and honey,” its grapes so heavy they must be carried on a pole between two men. The evidence of God’s goodness is undeniable, borne on their own shoulders. Yet the ten fixate on the obstacles: walled cities, the descendants of Anak, giants.

The pivotal words come from the ten: “we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them.” Here is the anatomy of unbelief — measuring the giants against ourselves rather than against God. Caleb and Joshua measure the same giants against the LORD and conclude, “we are well able.”

The chapter is a mirror for every believer at the edge of obedience. The issue is never the size of the obstacle but the size of our God. Hebrews 3–4 holds this up as the great warning: they failed to enter because of unbelief. And it points to the true and faithful Spy, Joshua/Jesus, who entered the rest and brings his people in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the people’s request, twelve leaders are sent to spy out Canaan; Moses charges them to assess the land and its people.
verseByVerse.theology: God grants the people’s desire to scout the land, setting the stage for a test of faith at the very threshold of promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: twelve spies sent into Canaan. Now: the believer stands at the edge of obedience, called to trust God’s promise.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel. From each tribe of their fathers you shall send a man, every one a chief among them." So Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran, according to the command of the LORD, all of them men who were heads of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel.

Two things need settling before the story starts. The first is whose idea this was. Numbers says God commanded it; Deuteronomy, looking back, says the people came to Moses and said Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us (Deut. 1:22). Both are true, and the combination is familiar from Balaam: the request came from below, and God permitted it. There is a kind of divine yes that is a concession rather than a plan, and it is often the beginning of trouble.

The second is the clause in the middle of God’s own sentence: which I am giving to the people of Israel. Present tense. The land is not a possibility to be assessed; it is a gift already being handed over. So the mission cannot be to find out whether Israel should go. That has been settled since Abraham. The reconnaissance is about how, not whether — and forty days later ten men will come back and answer a question nobody had asked them.

Name that, because it is how a great deal of disobedience gets started among sincere people. God has spoken plainly, and we go away to gather information, and by the time we come back the plain word has quietly become one factor among several.

Which raises a fair question: was it wrong to send the spies at all? Not in itself. Joshua will send two into Jericho with God’s blessing and no rebuke (Josh. 2:1). Prudence is not unbelief, and the man who checks the road before he drives down it is not doubting God. The difference lies in what the information is being gathered for. Joshua’s spies went out to find the way in. These twelve were sent by a people who had not yet decided to go.

verseByVerse.quote: And these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur; from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori; from the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh; from the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph; from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun; from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu; from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi; from the tribe of Joseph (that is, from the tribe of Manasseh), Gaddi the son of Susi; from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli; from the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael; from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi; from the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi. These were the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list that follows is a roll of the finest men in Israel. One from every tribe, and not a junior officer among them — every one is a chief among them. The best men in Israel are sent, which is exactly why what happens next is so devastating. This was not a failure of the second rank.

Two of the names matter. From Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. From Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun.

Then the list ends with a note dropped in almost as an aside: And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.

Hoshea means salvation. Joshua — Yehoshua — means the LORD saves. Moses takes his assistant’s name and puts the name of God into the front of it. It looks like nothing; it is the difference between a word about rescue and a statement about who does the rescuing, and it is being made at the exact moment twelve men are about to go and find out whether they believe it.

Ten of them will come back saying we are not able. The man with the new name will come back saying God is. And that name, carried into Greek, is the name the angel gave a child in Nazareth: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). It was given here, in a list, on the day the spies went out.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan and said to them, "Go up into the Negeb and go up into the hill country, and see what the land is, and whether the people who dwell in it are strong or weak, whether they are few or many, and whether the land that they dwell in is good or bad, and whether the cities that they dwell in are camps or strongholds, and whether the land is rich or poor, and whether there are trees in it or not. Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land." Now the time was the season of the first ripe grapes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ briefing is thoroughly practical: is the land good or bad, are the people strong or weak, few or many, do they live in camps or fortified cities, is the soil rich or poor, is there timber. It is competent military reconnaissance and there is nothing unspiritual about it.

But the last two clauses are of a different order. Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land.

Why say that? He has asked for facts, and facts do not require courage to collect. Moses evidently knew something about the men he was sending, or about human nature, and the sentence reads like a father saying something at a door that he is not sure will be remembered.

And notice what he asks them to carry home. Some of the fruit of the land. Not a map, not a count of the garrisons — fruit. Something they could hold in their hands and taste, a piece of the promise itself brought back into the wilderness. He wanted the nation to see evidence of God’s goodness before it heard anything else.

They did bring it. It made no difference at all, which is the most sobering thing in the chapter. Evidence is not the same as faith, and a man can hold the goodness of God in his own hands and still refuse to trust him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — The Survey of the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The spies traverse the land from south to north, reaching Hebron and the Valley of Eshcol, where they cut a single cluster of grapes.
verseByVerse.theology: The land proves abundantly good, its fruit so heavy it must be carried between two men — the visible evidence of God’s gift.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a cluster of grapes borne on a pole. Now: God gives tangible evidence of his goodness to strengthen our faith.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went up and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, near Lebo-hamath. They went up into the Negeb and came to Hebron. Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, were there. (Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.) And they came to the Valley of Eshcol and cut down from there a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and they carried it on a pole between two of them; they also brought some pomegranates and figs. That place was called the Valley of Eshcol, because of the cluster that the people of Israel cut down from there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They go the whole length of the country, from the wilderness of Zin in the far south to Lebo-hamath in the far north — several hundred miles on foot through hostile territory. It is a thorough job.

At Hebron they see them: Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak. Named individuals, not rumours. The Anakim were a people of famous size, and the spies met three of them by name in a town that the writer pauses to date — Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt — an antiquarian note establishing that this was an old, established, settled civilisation, not a camp.

Then the Valley of Eshcol, which means cluster: they cut down from there a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and they carried it on a pole between two of them; they also brought some pomegranates and figs.

Picture the walk home. Two grown men, a pole across their shoulders, and one bunch of grapes slung between them, all the way back across the desert. It took two of them to carry the fruit of one vine. Nobody in that camp had ever seen anything like it; they had been eating manna for two years.

And these are the two objects that will be set in front of Israel at the same moment: three giants and a cluster of grapes. Both were real. Both were accurately reported. Everything depends on which one a man measures against God.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of forty days they returned from spying out the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of forty days they returned from spying out the land.

Forty days. It is one of Scripture’s heavy numbers — Noah’s rain, Moses on the mountain, Elijah to Horeb, and the Lord Jesus in the wilderness — and it almost always marks a period of testing.

Note that these were forty good days. Nothing went wrong on the journey. No one was caught, no one was killed, God brought all twelve of them safely through several hundred miles of enemy country and home again with the fruit. They had just experienced six weeks of unbroken providential care, in the very land they were about to say could not be taken.

And the sentence that falls in the next chapter will be measured out against this number, one for one: According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years (14:34). A day for a year. Six weeks of looking, and four decades of walking in circles.

There is one other set of forty days in a wilderness, and it is the answer to this one. Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry (Matt. 4:1–2). Israel was tested in a desert for forty days with the fruit of the promise in their hands, and failed. He was tested in a desert for forty days with nothing in his hands at all, and did not. Where the nation looked at what God had given and called it impossible, he looked at what God had not yet given and said Man shall not live by bread alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–33 — The Report: Faith and Fear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All twelve confirm the land is good, but ten magnify the giants while Caleb and Joshua urge faith; the people’s hearts melt in fear.
verseByVerse.theology: The same evidence produces faith in some and fear in others; unbelief measures the obstacles against self, faith against God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the grasshopper report of the ten. Now: the believer must measure every giant against the greatness of God, not self.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh. They brought back word to them and to all the congregation, and showed them the fruit of the land. And they told him, "We came to the land to which you sent us. It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit. However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. And besides, we saw the descendants of Anak there. The Amalekites dwell in the land of the Negeb. The Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites dwell in the hill country. And the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and along the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report begins beautifully and truthfully. We came to the land to which you sent us. It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit.

They use God’s own words. Flowing with milk and honey is the phrase he had used at the burning bush (Exod. 3:8), and here are twelve men confirming it by eyewitness and holding up the evidence. If the report had stopped at the end of verse 27, Israel would have marched that afternoon.

Then one word: However.

Everything turns on it. However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. And besides, we saw the descendants of Anak there.

And here is the thing to see clearly: not one word after the however is false. The people were strong. The cities were fortified. The Anakim were there — Caleb will confirm every detail of it and take Hebron himself forty-five years later (Josh. 14:12–14). This is not a lying report. It is an accurate report arranged in an order that leads to despair.

Unbelief rarely needs to invent anything. It usually just needs to put the facts in a particular sequence, mention God first and briefly, and then spend the rest of the paragraph on the difficulties. By the end of verse 29 the giants and the fortifications and four named nations are filling the whole screen, and the God who had said which I am giving to the people of Israel has not been mentioned once.

verseByVerse.quote: But Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, "Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then one man interrupts. But Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, “Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it.”

Caleb had been on the same journey. He had seen the same walls, met the same three giants at Hebron, and helped carry the same pole. He is not working from better information; he had precisely the information the other ten had.

What he has is a different denominator. The ten measured the giants against Israel and got a true answer: too big. Caleb measured them against God, and the arithmetic came out the other way. Both were doing sums. Only one of them had put the right number at the bottom.

And notice the urgency: let us go up at once. Not let us pray about it, not let us form a committee, not let us wait for a more favourable season. He can see that a delay here is fatal — that a nation which does not move now will talk itself out of it by morning, which is exactly what happens.

Take the measure of the man. He is one voice against ten, in front of a crowd already frightened, and within a day they will be picking up stones to kill him for it. Forty-five years later, an old man of eighty-five walks up to Joshua and asks for the hill country of Hebron — the giants’ own town — with the sentence: I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me… So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day (Josh. 14:11–12). He had been waiting four decades to finish an argument he was right about, and God gave him the ground the giants were standing on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men who had gone up with him said, "We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are." So they brought to the people of Israel a bad report of the land that they had spied out, saying, "The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants, and all the people that we saw in it are of great height. And there we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim), and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ten answer, and their reply is a study in how unbelief talks.

It begins with something true: We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are. Perfectly correct, and entirely beside the point, because the question was never whether Israel was stronger than Canaan.

Then it slides. The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants. That is a straight contradiction of what they said four verses earlier. It was flowing with milk and honey in verse 27; now it eats people. The writer names this for what it is — a bad report, and the Hebrew word means a slander. They have gone from reporting the facts to defaming the gift.

Then it exaggerates: all the people that we saw in it are of great height. And there we saw the Nephilim. All of them. Every single person in Canaan is a giant. That is not observation, it is fear talking, and fear always speaks in totals.

Last comes the sentence that gives the whole thing away: we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them.

Read the two halves. We seemed to ourselves — that is a report on their self-image, and it is honest. And so we seemed to them — that is a report on what was going on inside the heads of men they never spoke to. They have no idea how they appeared to the Canaanites. In fact Rahab will tell us, forty years later, exactly how Israel appeared to Canaan: the fear of you has fallen upon us… our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you (Josh. 2:9, 11). The people the spies thought were laughing at them were terrified of them.

That is the mechanism, and it is a great deal more common than giants. A man decides what he is worth, and then assumes everybody else has reached the same verdict, and lives as though a judgment he passed on himself were a fact about the world. It ruined a nation. The only cure is to stop measuring against the giants and start measuring against God, which is the single difference between Caleb and the ten.

13.theology:
The Anatomy of Unbelief. Ten spies measured the giants against themselves and became grasshoppers; faith measures the giants against God. Unbelief is rarely a denial of facts but a misreading of them — leaving God out of the equation, so that the obstacle eclipses the promise.

The Same Evidence, Two Responses. All twelve saw the same land, fruit, and giants. The difference was not in the eyes but in the heart. God surrounds the call to obedience with tokens of his goodness, yet abundant evidence does not produce faith in an unbelieving heart; faith is a response to the trustworthiness of God.

Joshua, the LORD Saves. Moses renames Hoshea “Joshua” — “the LORD is salvation.” The faithful spy who will lead Israel into the land bears the very name of Jesus, pointing to the One who, unlike that faithless generation, brings his people into the true and eternal rest.
13.examples:
Then: Twelve spies saw the same good land and the same giants; ten shrank in fear like grasshoppers, but Caleb and Joshua, factoring in God, cried, “Let us go up at once, for we are well able.”

Now: At the edge of every hard obedience, the question is never the size of the obstacle but the size of your God. Beware the “however” of unbelief that admits God’s goodness then lets fear overrule it. Measure your giants against the LORD who saves, and go up at once.

14.title: Israel’s Rebellion: The Wilderness Decreed
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night.<sup>2</sup>And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness!<sup>3</sup>Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will become a prey. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?"<sup>4</sup>And they said to one another, "Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt."<sup>5</sup>Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly of the congregation of the people of Israel.<sup>6</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes<sup>7</sup>and said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land.<sup>8</sup>If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land that flows with milk and honey.<sup>9</sup>Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us; do not fear them."<sup>10</sup>Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones. But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will this people despise me?
