And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them?<sup>12</sup>I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they."<sup>13</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Then the Egyptians will hear of it, for you brought up this people in your might from among them,<sup>14</sup>and they will tell the inhabitants of this land. They have heard that you, O LORD, are in the midst of this people. For you, O LORD, are seen face to face, and your cloud stands over them and you go before them, in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night.<sup>15</sup>Now if you kill this people as one man, then the nations who have heard your fame will say,<sup>16</sup>'It is because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land that he swore to give to them that he has killed them in the wilderness.'<sup>17</sup>And now, please let the power of the Lord be great as you have promised, saying,<sup>18</sup>'The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, to the third and the fourth generation.'<sup>19</sup>Please pardon the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your steadfast love, just as you have forgiven this people, from Egypt until now."<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said, "I have pardoned, according to your word.<sup>21</sup>But truly, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD,<sup>22</sup>none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice,<sup>23</sup>shall see the land that I swore to give to their fathers. And none of those who despised me shall see it.<sup>24</sup>But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it.<sup>25</sup>Now, since the Amalekites and the Canaanites dwell in the valleys, turn tomorrow and set out for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea."<sup>26</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>27</sup>"How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against me.<sup>28</sup>Say to them, 'As I live, declares the LORD, what you have said in my hearing I will do to you:<sup>29</sup>your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness, and of all your number, listed in the census from twenty years old and upward, who have grumbled against me,<sup>30</sup>not one shall come into the land where I swore that I would make you dwell, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>31</sup>But your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in, and they shall know the land that you have rejected.<sup>32</sup>But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness.<sup>33</sup>And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness, until the last of your dead bodies lies in the wilderness.<sup>34</sup>According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years, and you shall know my displeasure.'<sup>35</sup>I, the LORD, have spoken. Surely this will I do to all this wicked congregation who are gathered together against me: in this wilderness they shall come to a full end, and there they shall die."<sup>36</sup>And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land—<sup>37</sup>the men who brought up a bad report of the land— died by plague before the LORD.<sup>38</sup>Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive.<sup>39</sup>When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly.<sup>40</sup>And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, "Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned."<sup>41</sup>But Moses said, "Why now are you transgressing the command of the LORD, when that will not succeed?<sup>42</sup>Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you, lest you be struck down before your enemies.<sup>43</sup>For there the Amalekites and the Canaanites are facing you, and you shall fall by the sword. Because you have turned back from following the LORD, the LORD will not be with you."<sup>44</sup>But they presumed to go up to the heights of the hill country, although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp.<sup>45</sup>Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites who lived in that hill country came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is the catastrophe toward which the whole book has been building. The people, swayed by the ten, rebel outright — weeping all night, longing to return to Egypt, even proposing to stone Caleb and Joshua and choose a leader to take them back to slavery. It is the great refusal of grace.

Caleb and Joshua tear their clothes and plead: the land is exceedingly good, the LORD is with us, do not rebel, do not fear. But the congregation reaches for stones. Only the appearing of the glory of the LORD halts the murder.

Then comes Moses’ great intercession — one of the high points of the Old Testament. God threatens to disinherit Israel and make Moses a great nation, and Moses, refusing the offer, pleads not his own glory but God’s name and God’s revealed character: “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity.” He prays God’s own self-revelation back to him.

God pardons — and yet justice falls. The faithless generation will not enter; they will wander forty years, a year for each day, until they die in the wilderness. Only Caleb and Joshua will enter. Hebrews 3–4 makes this the great warning: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief.” And it drives us to the better Mediator, whose intercession secures not a forty-year reprieve but everlasting pardon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Rebellion and the Plea of Caleb and Joshua
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people weep, long for Egypt, and plot to return; Caleb and Joshua plead for faith, but the congregation moves to stone them.
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief hardens into open rebellion and the rejection of God’s gift; faith pleads, but the rebellious heart reaches for stones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel longs to return to Egypt. Now: a warning against the heart that despises grace and shrinks back to bondage.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night. And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness! Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will become a prey. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?" And they said to one another, "Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night.

They cry all night — and then, in the morning, out comes the sentence that has been forming in the dark: Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness!

Mark those words. God is going to take them up, syllable for syllable, in verse 29 and grant them. It is the most terrifying answered prayer in the Bible. They asked to die in the wilderness because they could not think of anything worse to say, and God said: very well.

Then the accusation, and it is the reverse of the truth in every particular. Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will become a prey. The God who split a sea for them is now charged with running an elaborate operation to get them killed, and with using their children as bait. That is what unbelief eventually says out loud about the character of God, and it is worth noticing that it began as a reasonable concern about fortified cities.

Then the bottom of it: Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt. Not a complaint now — a coup and an emigration. They intend to depose Moses, elect a replacement, and march four hundred miles back to the brick pits, where every family in that camp had buried somebody. They would rather have slavery they understand than a promise that requires them to trust somebody. People still make that trade, and they make it for the same reason.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly of the congregation of the people of Israel. And Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes and said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land that flows with milk and honey. Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us; do not fear them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four men respond. Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly, and Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes, which in Israel is what a man does at a funeral or in the face of blasphemy.

And their plea is one of the great speeches in the Old Testament, and every clause of it is faith reasoning out loud. The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land that flows with milk and honey. They do not deny a single fact the ten reported. They start from God’s pleasure in his people rather than from the height of the walls.

Then: Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Bread. The very people the ten described as devouring the land are here reduced to a meal — not because Joshua and Caleb thought Israel was strong, but because they knew who was doing the eating.

And the ground of it: Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us. That is the whole argument in nine words, and it is exactly the calculation the ten refused to do. Literally the Hebrew says their shadow has turned aside — whatever was sheltering Canaan has moved off it, and whatever shelters Israel is standing right in the middle of the camp. If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom. 8:31) is not a new thought. It was shouted at a mob by two men who were about to be stoned for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones. But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones.

That is the answer of the people of God to the two men in the camp who believed him. Not argument — rocks. And it is the whole congregation, not a faction.

Unbelief, when it has run its course, does not merely disagree with faith; it wants faith silenced, because a man who trusts God is unbearable to a room that has decided not to. Stephen made exactly this point to the Sanhedrin, and the sequence of what happened next was the same: Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? (Acts 7:52). They picked up stones for him too.

And then, mid-sentence, God arrives: But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel. The stones never leave their hands. There is a moment here that ought to be seen for what it is — two men standing in front of a crowd with rocks in its fists, entirely defenceless, and the glory of God interposing itself between them and the first throw.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God threatens to disinherit Israel; Moses pleads God’s name and revealed character, and God pardons, though judgment remains.
verseByVerse.theology: The mediator intercedes on the ground of God’s own glory and self-revelation; God pardons for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses pleads God’s character back to him. Now: Christ intercedes on the ground of his own glory, securing our pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them? I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s verdict on the situation is two questions, and they take the whole thing down to the root. How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them?

Two charges, and they are the same charge. To despise is the outward act; not to believe is the inward reality; and God names them in one breath because he sees no gap between them. That is a hard word for a religious culture that has learned to treat unbelief as an intellectual difficulty and contempt as a moral one. In God’s reading of this scene, refusing to trust him after everything he has done is not a failure of evidence. It is an insult.

And note the phrase in spite of all the signs. These are people who watched a sea open. They had eaten bread off the ground that morning and there was a pillar of fire over the tent behind them. More evidence would not have helped, which is the standing answer to anyone who says he would believe if only God did something visible. He did, for two years, in front of this congregation.

Then the offer: I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they. Everything Moses had ever been promised, personally — a great nation from his own line, and no more of these people. It is the same offer God made him at the golden calf, and it is a genuine test as well as a genuine threat.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Then the Egyptians will hear of it, for you brought up this people in your might from among them, and they will tell the inhabitants of this land. They have heard that you, O LORD, are in the midst of this people. For you, O LORD, are seen face to face, and your cloud stands over them and you go before them, in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night. Now if you kill this people as one man, then the nations who have heard your fame will say, 'It is because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land that he swore to give to them that he has killed them in the wilderness.' And now, please let the power of the Lord be great as you have promised, saying, 'The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, to the third and the fourth generation.' Please pardon the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your steadfast love, just as you have forgiven this people, from Egypt until now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ answer is the finest piece of intercession in the Old Testament, and what is most striking is what he does not say.

He does not defend the people. He offers no mitigation and no character witness, because there is none available. He does not accept the offer made to him, though it would have made him a patriarch. He does not appeal to his own long service. Every argument he uses is about God.

First, God’s reputation: the Egyptians will hear of it… and they will tell the inhabitants of this land, and the nations will conclude that the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land that he swore to give to them. Moses’ concern is that God’s name will be dishonoured in the mouths of pagans.

And then, remarkably, he quotes God back to himself. The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty. That is Exodus 34:6–7, God’s own self-description given to Moses on the mountain. He is not telling God what he ought to be like; he is holding up what God said he was like and asking him to be it.

That is the whole method of praying with any confidence, and it has not changed. Not I have been good and not they are worth it, but this is who you have said you are. And notice that Moses quotes the hard half as well as the comfortable half — he will by no means clear the guilty — which is why his prayer is honest and not sentimental. He asks for mercy from a God he has just described as one who does not pretend sin is nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "I have pardoned, according to your word. But truly, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD, none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall see the land that I swore to give to their fathers. And none of those who despised me shall see it. But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it. Now, since the Amalekites and the Canaanites dwell in the valleys, turn tomorrow and set out for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD said, “I have pardoned, according to your word.”

The prayer is answered. The nation is not destroyed, the covenant stands, and Israel exists today because one man stood in a gap.

Yet the same paragraph says: none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall see the land.

Pardoned, and excluded. Both, in five verses, from the same mouth. Any reader who wants to understand the Bible has to be able to hold those two together, because they are not in tension — they are the shape of everything God does with sin. He forgives, fully and for ever, and forgiveness is not the abolition of consequences. David is told the LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die, and in the same breath told what will happen to his household (2 Sam. 12:13–14).

Note also these ten times — God has been counting. It was not one bad afternoon; there is a file, and it goes back to the Red Sea.

And then, against all of it, one exception: But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land. A different spirit. Not better information, not more courage as a temperament, not a stronger constitution. Something else was in him, and God put it there, and it made him the only man of his generation besides Joshua to see the country he had walked through.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–38 — The Sentence of Forty Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God decrees forty years of wandering, a year for each day; the ten faithless spies die by plague, but Caleb and Joshua live.
verseByVerse.theology: The faithless generation forfeits the rest because of unbelief; faith alone enters the inheritance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: forty years in the wilderness for unbelief. Now: Hebrews warns the church not to fail to enter God’s rest through unbelief.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against me. Say to them, 'As I live, declares the LORD, what you have said in my hearing I will do to you: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness, and of all your number, listed in the census from twenty years old and upward, who have grumbled against me, not one shall come into the land where I swore that I would make you dwell, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun. But your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in, and they shall know the land that you have rejected. But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness, until the last of your dead bodies lies in the wilderness. According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years, and you shall know my displeasure.' I, the LORD, have spoken. Surely this will I do to all this wicked congregation who are gathered together against me: in this wilderness they shall come to a full end, and there they shall die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sentence, and its terrible symmetry. God takes the words they shouted in verse 2 and hands them back: what you have said in my hearing I will do to you: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. They said would that we had died in this wilderness. They will.

Then the exact reversal of their own accusation. They had said, our wives and our little ones will become a prey. God says: But your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in, and they shall know the land that you have rejected. The very children they used as the reason for refusing are the ones who will inherit. Their unbelief was dressed up as concern for their families, and God answers by taking better care of their families than they were willing to.

And the arithmetic: According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years. A day for a year. Forty days of looking at the promise, forty years of walking away from it.

Consider what those forty years actually were. Not a punishment inflicted on them from outside so much as their own choice extended and given room. They said they would rather be in the wilderness than in the land; God let them have the wilderness. Hell, in the end, is not somewhere God puts people who wanted him. It is the granting of a preference.

And there is one more phrase, in verse 33, easily missed and unbearable: your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness. The children were not condemned — they inherit — but they carried it. A generation of young Israelites spent their entire youth burying their parents in a desert because of a decision made one night at Kadesh before most of them were born. Nobody sins in a way that stops with themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land— the men who brought up a bad report of the land— died by plague before the LORD. Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land — the men who brought up a bad report of the land — died by plague before the LORD.

The writer says it twice in one sentence, as though he wants to be sure nobody mistakes the grounds. They died for the report.

They were not the only guilty men in the camp; the whole nation had rebelled and the whole nation is under sentence. But these ten die first and die immediately, because they were the ones who put the words into everyone else’s mouth. There is a heavier accounting for those who form what a community believes. Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness (Jas. 3:1) is the same principle, and this is where it comes from.

And in the same breath, the other half: Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive. Twelve went out together, ten die in an afternoon, and the two who had been threatened with stoning the day before are still standing. The crowd had been entirely wrong about who was in danger.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly. And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, "Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned." But Moses said, "Why now are you transgressing the command of the LORD, when that will not succeed? Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you, lest you be struck down before your enemies. For there the Amalekites and the Canaanites are facing you, and you shall fall by the sword. Because you have turned back from following the LORD, the LORD will not be with you." But they presumed to go up to the heights of the hill country, although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp. Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites who lived in that hill country came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly. And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, “Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned.”

It looks like repentance. It even sounds like it — we have sinned is the right sentence. And it is not repentance, and Moses says so.

Look at what has actually changed. Yesterday God said go and they would not; today God says do not go and they will. The direction has reversed and the disposition has not moved an inch. They are still doing what they have decided, and God’s word is still the thing being overridden. That is the definition of the problem, and the fact that their preference now happens to look more obedient makes no difference at all.

Moses names it exactly: Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you… Because you have turned back from following the LORD, the LORD will not be with you. And the detail in verse 44 is devastating: they presumed to go up… although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp. They marched off to fight for the promises of God while the ark of God stayed where it was and watched them go.

They are routed, even to Hormah — a name to keep, because Israel will return to that exact spot in chapter 21, with God, and win.

Hebrews takes this whole chapter and preaches it to Christians without softening a word. And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief… Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion (Heb. 3:18–19; 4:7). The letter’s point is not that Israel was uniquely bad; it is that the same promise is standing in front of its readers and the same refusal is available. And the remedy it offers is the one thing this generation would not do — hear his voice today, while it is still called today, and go in.

14.theology:
Unbelief Forfeits the Inheritance. The faithless generation, refusing to enter the good land, is barred from the rest and dies in the wilderness. Hebrews makes this the great warning to the church: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief.” The promised rest is received by faith alone.

Intercession on the Ground of God’s Glory. Moses refuses his own exaltation and pleads God’s name and revealed character, praying God’s own self-disclosure back to him: “slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love.” This is gospel praying, fulfilled in Christ, who intercedes not on our merit but on the ground of his glory and the Father’s love.

Pardon and Discipline Together. “I have pardoned... but truly... none of these men shall see the land.” God spares the nation yet bars the unbelieving from the rest. Forgiveness does not always remove consequences; mercy and holiness meet in the wise discipline of a faithful God.
14.examples:
Then: Israel wept to return to Egypt and reached for stones against Caleb and Joshua; Moses interceded on the ground of God’s name, and God pardoned the nation yet decreed forty years in the wilderness for the unbelieving generation.

Now: Take heed lest an evil, unbelieving heart lead you to draw back from grace and forfeit God’s rest. Pray boldly as Moses did, pleading not your worthiness but God’s revealed character. And follow Christ, your Joshua, the one who brings his people into the rest that unbelief can never enter.

15.title: Offerings and the Sabbath-Breaker: Grace After Judgment
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you,<sup>3</sup>and you offer to the LORD from the herd or from the flock a food offering or a burnt offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering or at your appointed feasts, to make a pleasing aroma to the LORD,<sup>4</sup>then he who brings his offering shall offer to the LORD a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil;<sup>5</sup>and you shall offer with the burnt offering, or for the sacrifice, a quarter of a hin of wine for the drink offering for each lamb.<sup>6</sup>Or for a ram, you shall offer for a grain offering two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil.<sup>7</sup>And for the drink offering you shall offer a third of a hin of wine, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>8</sup>And when you offer a 15.overview:
After the devastating judgment of chapter 14, chapter 15 opens with the most surprising word: “When you come into the land...” The very generation barred from the land is given laws for life in the land. Grace persists after judgment; the promise stands, though this generation forfeits it.

The chapter gives laws for offerings, for the stranger (one law for native and sojourner alike), and for unintentional sin, which can be atoned for. Then it draws a sharp line between unintentional sin, covered by sacrifice, and the “high-handed” sin of defiant rebellion, which is cut off.

A startling narrative follows: a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned — a vivid case study of high-handed sin, defiance of God’s revealed will. The severity shocks us, but it dramatizes the seriousness of deliberate rebellion against the holy God.

The chapter closes with the command to wear tassels with a cord of blue — visible reminders to obey, lest the heart wander after its own eyes. From offerings to tassels, the message is grace that calls forth holiness. And it all points to Christ, who bore both our unintentional failings and our high-handed rebellion, and who clothes us with reminders of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Offerings in the Land; One Law for All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives laws for grain and drink offerings when Israel enters the land, with one statute for native and sojourner alike.
verseByVerse.theology: Grace persists after judgment; the promise of the land stands, and God’s welcome extends equally to the foreigner.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: laws for offerings in the promised land. Now: the gospel’s welcome to all peoples on equal terms in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you, and you offer to the LORD from the herd or from the flock a food offering or a burnt offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering or at your appointed feasts, to make a pleasing aroma to the LORD, then he who brings his offering shall offer to the LORD a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil; and you shall offer with the burnt offering, or for the sacrifice, a quarter of a hin of wine for the drink offering for each lamb. Or for a ram, you shall offer for a grain offering two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil. And for the drink offering you shall offer a third of a hin of wine, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And when you offer a bull as a burnt offering or sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or for peace offerings to the LORD, then one shall offer with the bull a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with half a hin of oil. And you shall offer for the drink offering half a hin of wine, as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the first sentence of this chapter immediately after the last sentence of the previous one, because the placing is the whole point. Chapter 14 ended with a generation sentenced to die in the sand and a defeated army running from Hormah. Then: When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you…

Not if. God has just told these people that they personally will never see Canaan, and the very next thing out of his mouth is detailed instruction about what to do when they get there — how much flour, how much oil, how much wine goes with a lamb, a ram, a bull.

He is talking to the children. The men listening will die in the wilderness; the boys standing beside them are being given the liturgy of a country they will inherit. And the effect on the fathers must have been extraordinary — they are hearing, in detail, about a life they have forfeited and their sons will have.

That is how God deals with failure. Judgment is real and it is not the end of the sentence. Israel’s worst day is followed at once by legislation for a future she does not deserve, because the promise never depended on the generation it was passing through. If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus it shall be done for each bull or ram, or for each lamb or young goat. As many as you offer, so shall you do with each one, as many as there are. Every native Israelite shall do these things in this way, in offering a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And if a stranger is sojourning with you, or anyone is living permanently among you, and he wishes to offer a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, he shall do as you do. For the assembly, there shall be one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you, a statute forever throughout your generations. You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD. One law and one rule shall be for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the middle of the offering regulations, a principle stated twice in six verses, as though God is determined it will not be missed. One law and one rule shall be for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you… You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD.

The word is ger — the resident foreigner, the outsider living among Israel with no tribe, no land and no ancestry in the covenant. He could not inherit a field. He could inherit everything that mattered: the same offerings, the same access, the same standing at the altar. There was not a second-class rite for him and there was no probationary period.

That is easy to skim past and it was extraordinary in the ancient world, where religion was ethnic by definition and a foreigner worshipped his own gods because they were his own people’s gods. Israel’s law says: if he will come, he comes on identical terms.

Which is why Paul can say what he says to a congregation of Gentiles without any sense of introducing a novelty: you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph. 2:19). The word he uses for strangers is the Greek Old Testament’s word for the ger. He is telling them that the arrangement made for the outsider in Numbers 15 has become their address.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Provision is made for atoning unintentional sin, but the one who sins defiantly, with a high hand, is cut off.
verseByVerse.theology: There is atonement for the sin of weakness and ignorance, but defiant rebellion against God despises his word and finds no sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the line between weakness and defiance. Now: grace covers our failings, but presumptuous rebellion despises the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land to which I bring you and when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall present a contribution to the LORD. Of the first of your dough you shall present a loaf as a contribution; like a contribution from the threshing floor, so shall you present it. Some of the first of your dough you shall give to the LORD as a contribution throughout your generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the law of the first of the dough. Whenever you eat of the bread of the land, you shall present a contribution to the LORD. Of the first of your dough you shall present a loaf as a contribution.

Not the first of the harvest, which is elsewhere — the first of the dough, at the kitchen end of the process. A woman kneading bread in her own house takes a piece off the batch before it is baked and gives it away.

Consider how domestic and how regular that is. The harvest offering happens once a year at the sanctuary with everybody watching. This one happens in an ordinary house, on baking day, several times a month, in front of nobody. It is the smallest possible act of worship and it touches the most ordinary possible object.

God does not confine himself to the ceremonial. He asks for something off the top of the week’s bread, and he asks for it before the loaf goes in the oven — while it still costs something to give, rather than out of what happens to be left over.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you sin unintentionally, and do not observe all these commandments that the LORD has spoken to Moses, all that the LORD has commanded you by Moses, from the day that the LORD gave commandment, and onward throughout your generations, then if it was done unintentionally without the knowledge of the congregation, all the congregation shall offer one bull from the herd for a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD, with its grain offering and its drink offering, according to the rule, and one male goat for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for all the congregation of the people of Israel, and they shall be forgiven, because it was a mistake, and they have brought their offering, a food offering to the LORD, and their sin offering before the LORD for their mistake. And all the congregation of the people of Israel shall be forgiven, and the stranger who sojourns among them, because the whole population was involved in the mistake. "If one person sins unintentionally, he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for the person who makes a mistake, when he sins unintentionally, to make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven. You shall have one law for him who does anything unintentionally, for him who is native among the people of Israel and for the stranger who sojourns among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a long and gracious provision for sin committed unintentionally… without the knowledge of the congregation, and it comes in two forms — the whole nation, and then the single person: if one person sins unintentionally, he shall offer a female goat a year old.

Two things need to be clear. The first is that unintentional sin is still sin. It requires a sacrifice, blood, a priest and atonement. Israel was not permitted the modern assumption that what a man did not mean does not count. A wrong done in ignorance is a real wrong, and the person harmed by it is really harmed.

The second is that God legislated for it in advance, in detail, on both scales, before anybody had committed it — including the case where the entire nation is wrong together and nobody notices. That is a category worth pausing on. A whole community can be sincerely, collectively mistaken about something, and Scripture assumes it will happen.

And note the phrase repeated at the end of each case: and they shall be forgiven… and he shall be forgiven. Not excused. Forgiven — which requires that something was genuinely wrong. The provision is not a technicality; it is the reason a person can live with the knowledge that a great deal of the damage he has done in his life was done without knowing it. Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Ps. 19:12) is a prayer with an answer.

verseByVerse.quote: But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken his commandment, that person shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sharp line is drawn. But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of the LORD… his iniquity shall be on him.

The high hand is a raised fist. It is not sin committed in weakness, or in a moment, or in ignorance; it is sin as defiance — knowing exactly what God has said and doing it anyway, deliberately, as a gesture. And for that one category the whole chapter offers no sacrifice at all. There is no goat listed.

Now this frightens sensitive Christians badly, and it should be handled carefully. The question people ask is whether they have committed it. And the shape of the answer is in the text: the high-handed man reviles and despises. He is not sorry, and it does not cross his mind to be. A person lying awake afraid that he has sinned beyond forgiveness has already given the evidence that he has not, because the high-handed man does not lie awake.

Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, which is about as deliberate as sin gets, and was restored on a beach over breakfast. What is being described here is not the seriousness of a sin but the direction of a life — a settled contempt that has no intention of returning. And the New Testament says the identical thing in the identical way: if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins (Heb. 10:26). Not because the blood of Christ is insufficient. Because a man who has decided to despise it will not come and be washed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–41 — The Sabbath-Breaker and the Tassels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned as a case of high-handed sin; Israel is given tassels with a cord of blue as reminders to obey.
verseByVerse.theology: Defiant sin is deadly serious, but God graciously provides visible reminders to keep his commandments and resist wandering hearts.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: tassels of blue to prompt obedience. Now: the believer needs constant reminders of grace to walk in holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: While the people of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. And those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation. They put him in custody, because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. And the LORD said to Moses, "The man shall be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp." And all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him to death with stones, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, without warning, a story. While the people of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. He is arrested, held in custody, and stoned outside the camp at God’s explicit command.

The severity is shocking and the reader should not be talked out of the shock. But notice where the story has been placed. It comes immediately after the definition of the high-handed sin, and it is there as the case study.

Look at the detail. He was not caught in some ambiguous grey area; he was gathering fuel, in the open, on the Sabbath, in a camp where God’s presence stood over the tabernacle in a pillar of fire — and the Sabbath command had been given at Sinai with the whole mountain shaking, and was the sign of the covenant itself (Exod. 31:13–17). And the reason he was put in custody is stated: because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. Nobody improvised. Moses did not rule; he waited and asked.

What was on trial was not firewood. It was whether the word of God meant anything in that camp at all, at the exact moment a nation under sentence was deciding how seriously to take him. The man had raised his fist, in public, and the whole congregation had to see what that meant.

And remember who was later accused of breaking this same Sabbath, and what he said about it: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27–28). The Lord of the Sabbath took the whole weight of its broken commandment on himself, and was executed outside a city, under the same law, for crimes he had not committed.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the people of Israel, and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a cord of blue on the tassel of each corner. And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them, not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after. So you shall remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, after the stoning, God does something tender. Make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a cord of blue on the tassel of each corner.

A thread of blue, sewn into the hem of every cloak in Israel. Blue was the colour of the tabernacle curtains and the high priest’s robe — the most expensive dye in the ancient world, and now a strand of it on a shepherd’s coat.

The purpose is given exactly: it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them, not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after.

God knows how forgetting works. It is not that a man decides to disobey; it is that his eye falls on something and he follows it, and by the time he thinks about God the thing is done. So God puts something in his line of sight at the very bottom edge of his vision, on the corner of the garment, where a man glances a hundred times a day without meaning to. He cannot look down without seeing blue.

Notice the order in the last verse, too. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. The rescue comes first and the commandments come second. Israel does not obey in order to be brought out; she was brought out, and the tassel is there to remind her whose she already is.

And these are the tassels a desperate woman took hold of in a crowd, twelve years ill and out of money, when she came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment (Matt. 9:20). A thread sewn into a hem to remind Israel of the commandments, and she reached for it, and the power went out of him, and he turned round and called her daughter.

15.theology:
Grace After Judgment. Immediately after decreeing the wilderness wandering, God says, “When you come into the land which I am giving you.” The promise outlasts the failure; God’s covenant is more durable than his people’s unbelief. His discipline never cancels his grace.

Weakness and Defiance. God distinguishes the unintentional sin of weakness, fully atonable, from the high-handed sin of defiant rebellion that despises his word. Grace abounds for the stumbling believer; but presumptuous contempt for God spurns the very provision of mercy — a warning Hebrews presses upon the church.

Reminders of Grace and Holiness. The tassels of blue are God’s tender provision for forgetful hearts, turning wandering eyes back to his commandments, grounded in redemption: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt.” We obey because we have been redeemed.
15.examples:
Then: The generation barred from the land was given laws for life in the land; a defiant Sabbath-breaker was stoned outside the camp; and Israel was clothed with tassels of blue to remember and obey.

Now: Rest in the grace that covers your stumbling, but beware the high-handed heart that despises God’s word. Christ suffered outside the gate, bearing the law-breaker’s curse for you. Surround yourself with reminders of grace — the Word, the table, the saints — that your wandering eyes may turn back to the Lord who redeemed you.

16.title: Korah’s Rebellion: The One Mediator
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and On the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men.<sup>2</sup>And they rose up before Moses, with a number of the people of Israel, 250 chiefs of the congregation, chosen from the assembly, well-known men.<sup>3</sup>They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, "You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"<sup>4</sup>When Moses heard it, he fell on his face,<sup>5</sup>and he said to Korah and all his company, "In the morning the LORD will show who is his, and who is holy, and will bring him near to him. The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him.<sup>6</sup>Do this: take censers, Korah and all his company;<sup>7</sup>put fire in them and put incense on them before the LORD tomorrow, and the man whom the LORD chooses shall be the holy one. You have gone too far, sons of Levi!"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said to Korah, "Hear now, you sons of Levi:<sup>9</sup>is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself, to do service in the tabernacle of the LORD and to stand before the congregation to minister to them,<sup>10</sup>and that he has brought you near him, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you? And would you seek the priesthood also?<sup>11</sup>Therefore it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"<sup>12</sup>And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and they said, "We will not come up.<sup>13</sup>Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also make yourself a prince over us?<sup>14</sup>Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you put out the eyes of these men? We will not come up."<sup>15</sup>And Moses was very angry and said to the LORD, "Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them."<sup>16</sup>And Moses said to Korah, "Be present, you and all your company, before the LORD, you and they, and Aaron, tomorrow.<sup>17</sup>And let every one of you take his censer and put incense on it, and every one of you bring before the LORD his censer, 250 censers; you also, and Aaron, each his censer."<sup>18</sup>So every man took his censer and put fire in them and laid incense on them and stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron.<sup>19</sup>Then Korah assembled all the congregation against them at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>21</sup>"Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment."<sup>22</sup>And they fell on their faces and said, "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?"<sup>23</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>24</sup>"Say to the congregation, Get away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram."<sup>25</sup>Then Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him.<sup>26</sup>And he spoke to the congregation, saying, "Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be swept away with all their sins."<sup>27</sup>So they got away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. And Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the door of their tents, together with their wives, their sons, and their little ones.<sup>28</sup>And Moses said, "Hereby you shall know that the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and that it has not been of my own accord.<sup>29</sup>If these men die as all men die, or if they are visited by the fate of all mankind, then the LORD has not sent me.<sup>30</sup>But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up with all that belongs to them, and they go down alive into Sheol, then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD."<sup>31</sup>And as soon as he had finished speaking all these words, the ground under them split apart.<sup>32</sup>And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households and all the people who belonged to Korah and all their goods.<sup>33</sup>So they and all that belonged to them went down alive into Sheol, and the earth closed over them, and they perished from the midst of the assembly.<sup>34</sup>And all Israel who were around them fled at their cry, for they said, "Lest the earth swallow us up!"<sup>35</sup>And fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men offering the incense.<sup>36</sup>Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>37</sup>"Tell Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers out of the blaze. Then scatter the fire far and wide, for they have become holy.<sup>38</sup>As for the censers of these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, for they offered them before the LORD, and they became holy. Thus they shall be a sign to the people of Israel."<sup>39</sup>So Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers, which those who were burned had offered, and they were hammered out as a covering for the altar,<sup>40</sup>to be a reminder to the people of Israel, so that no outsider, who is not of the descendants of Aaron, should draw near to burn incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his company—as the LORD said to him through Moses.<sup>41</sup>But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, "You have killed the people of the LORD."<sup>42</sup>And when the congregation had assembled against Moses and against Aaron, they turned toward the tent of meeting. And behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared.<sup>43</sup>And Moses and Aaron came to the front of the tent of meeting,<sup>44</sup>and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>45</sup>"Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces.<sup>46</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun."<sup>47</sup>So Aaron took it as Moses said and ran into the midst of the assembly. And behold, the plague had already begun among the people. And he put on the incense and made atonement for the people.<sup>48</sup>And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.<sup>49</sup>Now those who died in the plague were 14,700, besides those who died in the affair of Korah.<sup>50</sup>And Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tent of meeting, when the plague was stopped.
16.overview:
Chapter 16 records the most serious challenge yet to God’s appointed order — Korah, a Levite, with Dathan and Abiram, leading 250 chiefs in revolt against Moses and Aaron. Their slogan sounds almost pious: “all the congregation are holy... why do you exalt yourselves?” But it is rebellion against God’s own appointment of the priesthood.

The issue is the mediator. Korah wants access to God without the appointed priest; he despises the principle that sinful men may approach the holy God only through the one God appoints. It is, at root, the rejection of mediation itself.

God’s judgment is swift and terrible. The earth opens and swallows Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their households; fire consumes the 250. Yet even after this, the people grumble against Moses, and a plague breaks out.

Then comes one of the most breathtaking images in all Scripture: Aaron, with his censer of incense, “stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.” The priest interposes himself, and the wrath is halted. Here is the gospel in a single picture — the mediator standing between the dead and the living, holding back the judgment. It points unmistakably to Christ, our great High Priest, who stands between us and the wrath of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and 250 chiefs challenge Moses and Aaron, claiming all are holy; Moses calls for a test before the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Rebellion against God’s appointed mediation, however pious its rhetoric, is rebellion against God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Korah despises the appointed priesthood. Now: a warning against rejecting the one Mediator God has appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and On the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men. And they rose up before Moses, with a number of the people of Israel, 250 chiefs of the congregation, chosen from the assembly, well-known men. They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, "You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coalition is formidable and carefully assembled. Korah is a Levite of the clan of Kohath — the highest-ranking Levitical family, the men who carried the ark. Dathan, Abiram and On are Reubenites, from the tribe of the demoted firstborn. And with them 250 chiefs of the congregation, chosen from the assembly, well-known men. Two hundred and fifty of the most respected men in Israel, by name.

Then their slogan, and it must be taken seriously because it is almost entirely true. You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?

Is the congregation holy? Yes — God had said so at Sinai: you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exod. 19:6). Is the LORD among them? Yes; the cloud is over the tent as they speak. Every premise is orthodox and quotable.

And the conclusion drawn from them is a lie. From we are all holy Korah infers therefore no one may be set over us — which does not follow, and which conveniently places Korah at the head of the movement to abolish leadership.

That is how the dangerous errors work. They are not built out of falsehoods; they are built out of true statements arranged to reach a desired destination. And the surest tell is personal: watch who ends up better off if the argument wins. Korah wanted the priesthood, and the case for total equality was the vehicle. Diotrephes did the same thing in a New Testament church, and John names the motive without ceremony — he likes to put himself first (3 John 9).

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses heard it, he fell on his face, and he said to Korah and all his company, "In the morning the LORD will show who is his, and who is holy, and will bring him near to him. The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him. Do this: take censers, Korah and all his company; put fire in them and put incense on them before the LORD tomorrow, and the man whom the LORD chooses shall be the holy one. You have gone too far, sons of Levi!" And Moses said to Korah, "Hear now, you sons of Levi: is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself, to do service in the tabernacle of the LORD and to stand before the congregation to minister to them, and that he has brought you near him, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you? And would you seek the priesthood also? Therefore it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Moses heard it, he fell on his face. Again. It is the third time in this book that a direct attack on him has put him flat on the ground rather than on his feet arguing, and it is the single most consistent thing about the man.

Then he answers, and his question goes straight past the theology to the appetite. Is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself… And would you seek the priesthood also?

Korah was a Kohathite. He carried the ark. Of all the hundreds of thousands of men in that camp, he was among the few dozen permitted to touch the poles of the holiest object on earth. And Moses’ diagnosis is that it was not enough for him.

Discontent of this kind almost never afflicts the people with least. It grows in men who already have a great deal and can see one thing more. Korah was not excluded from the presence of God; he was in it every day, and his eye was on the one door still shut. Is it too small a thing is a question worth putting to yourself the next time you are aggrieved about a position, because the honest answer usually exposes how much has stopped counting.

And Moses ends by naming the real defendant: it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him? Aaron did not appoint himself. A man complaining about an appointment God made is not in a dispute with the appointee.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and they said, "We will not come up. Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also make yourself a prince over us? Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you put out the eyes of these men? We will not come up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dathan and Abiram will not even come. We will not come up — the phrase bookends their whole reply, and it is a refusal to be in the same room.

And what they say is one of the most brazen inversions in the Bible. Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness?

Read that again. A land flowing with milk and honey is God’s own phrase for Canaan, used at the burning bush and in every promise since. They have taken it and applied it to Egypt. The place of slavery, infanticide and the lash has become, in this sentence, the promised land — and the God who brought them out is charged with murder.

Then the sneer: you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. Which is true, and it is true because of the verdict in chapter 14, which fell because the nation refused to go in. They are blaming Moses for the consequence of their own rebellion.

And the last line — Will you put out the eyes of these men? — accuses him of trying to blind the people. The meekest man on earth, who had just offered to be blotted out of God’s book for them, stands accused of deception and tyranny by men who have relabelled slavery as paradise. There is no arguing with this. It is not a position; it is a mood that has found words.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s glory appears; the earth opens and swallows the rebels and their households, and fire consumes the 250 offering incense.
verseByVerse.theology: God vindicates his appointed mediation with terrible judgment; to usurp the priesthood is to perish before the holy God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the earth swallows the rebels. Now: the fearful seriousness of rejecting God’s appointed way of approach.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses was very angry and said to the LORD, "Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them." And Moses said to Korah, "Be present, you and all your company, before the LORD, you and they, and Aaron, tomorrow. And let every one of you take his censer and put incense on it, and every one of you bring before the LORD his censer, 250 censers; you also, and Aaron, each his censer." So every man took his censer and put fire in them and laid incense on them and stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron. Then Korah assembled all the congregation against them at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation. And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces and said, "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Say to the congregation, Get away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is finally angry — Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them — and it is the anger of a man defending not his dignity but his integrity, and defending it to God rather than to them.

Then he sets the test, and its design is exact: every one of you take his censer and put incense on it… 250 censers; and you also, Aaron, your censer.

Incense was the one act reserved to the priest alone. Korah claimed there was no such reservation; very well, then let him do it. The test is not artificial — it is simply the disputed claim, acted out. If everyone is holy, then everyone may burn incense before the LORD and nothing will happen. Two hundred and fifty men agreed to find out.

Then a detail that shows what kind of man Moses was even now. God says Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment — and the two brothers fall on their faces and cry O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation? They are pleading for the people who are at that moment gathered against them, and they win a reprieve for everybody except the ringleaders.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him. And he spoke to the congregation, saying, "Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be swept away with all their sins." So they got away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. And Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the door of their tents, together with their wives, their sons, and their little ones. And Moses said, "Hereby you shall know that the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and that it has not been of my own accord. If these men die as all men die, or if they are visited by the fate of all mankind, then the LORD has not sent me. But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up with all that belongs to them, and they go down alive into Sheol, then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD." And as soon as he had finished speaking all these words, the ground under them split apart. And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households and all the people who belonged to Korah and all their goods. So they and all that belonged to them went down alive into Sheol, and the earth closed over them, and they perished from the midst of the assembly. And all Israel who were around them fled at their cry, for they said, "Lest the earth swallow us up!" And fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men offering the incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses puts the whole thing on the record before it happens, which is the mark of a genuine prophet: If these men die as all men die… then the LORD has not sent me. But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up… then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD. He stakes his entire commission on an event he cannot manufacture, announced in advance, in front of everybody.

And as soon as he had finished speaking all these words, the ground under them split apart. Not a pause. The last syllable and the earth opens.

Notice the phrase Moses used: if the LORD creates something new. The verb is bara — the word of Genesis 1:1, used in the Old Testament only of God, only of what he alone can do. And then fire from the LORD consumes the two hundred and fifty men standing there with censers in their hands.

The horror of it should not be smoothed over, and neither should its point. What was being tested was whether a man may approach God on his own terms if he is sincere and well regarded and part of a majority. Two hundred and fifty well-known men said yes. They were not irreligious; they were holding incense, in the act of worship, doing the most spiritual thing available to them, and it killed them. There is a way of coming to God that is worse than not coming at all, and Nadab and Abihu had already demonstrated it on a smaller scale.

Jude looks back at this scene and puts it in a list of three, as one of the standing warnings of Scripture: men who walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion (Jude 11). Korah has become a category — the man who will not have the mediator God appointed, and appoints himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–50 — Aaron Between the Dead and the Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rebels’ censers are made into altar plating as a warning; the people grumble again, a plague breaks out, and Aaron’s incense halts it.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest interposes himself between the wrath of God and the people — the gospel in a single image, fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Aaron stands between the dead and the living. Now: Christ stands between us and the wrath of God, halting our destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Tell Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers out of the blaze. Then scatter the fire far and wide, for they have become holy. As for the censers of these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, for they offered them before the LORD, and they became holy. Thus they shall be a sign to the people of Israel." So Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers, which those who were burned had offered, and they were hammered out as a covering for the altar, to be a reminder to the people of Israel, so that no outsider, who is not of the descendants of Aaron, should draw near to burn incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his company—as the LORD said to him through Moses. But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, "You have killed the people of the LORD." And when the congregation had assembled against Moses and against Aaron, they turned toward the tent of meeting. And behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared. And Moses and Aaron came to the front of the tent of meeting,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The censers of the dead men are hammered flat and used to plate the altar, to be a sign to the people of Israel. The instruments of the rebellion become the visible skin of the place of sacrifice. Every Israelite who came to the altar for the rest of that generation approached over hammered bronze that had been in the hands of men who died claiming they did not need a priest.

And then comes the sentence that shows how little of this had gone in. But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, “You have killed the people of the LORD.”

The next day. One day after the earth opened and fire fell in front of the entire nation, the entire nation concludes that Moses and Aaron are responsible. They watched God do something no man could do, announced in advance, and by morning they had reinterpreted it as a leadership problem.

That is what the heart does with evidence it does not want. It does not deny the event; it re-explains it. And it is why more signs would not have saved this generation, and why the rich man in the parable was told that his brothers will not be convinced even if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31).

verseByVerse.quote: and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces. And Moses said to Aaron, "Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun." So Aaron took it as Moses said and ran into the midst of the assembly. And behold, the plague had already begun among the people. And he put on the incense and made atonement for the people. And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped. Now those who died in the plague were 14,700, besides those who died in the affair of Korah. And Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tent of meeting, when the plague was stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment. The plague begins, and people start dying where they stand.

What follows is the finest scene in the book of Numbers.

And Moses said to Aaron, “Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun.” So Aaron took it as Moses said and ran into the midst of the assembly.

Take in every detail. He takes a censer — the very object two hundred and fifty men had died holding the day before, and the thing the whole rebellion had been about. He takes fire from off the altar, the place of sacrifice, not from anywhere else. And then an old man of eighty-three runs — into a plague, toward the people who had spent the morning accusing him of murder, with nothing in his hands but incense.

And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.

There is the priesthood the rebels said was unnecessary, doing the one thing nobody else in that camp could do. Korah’s argument had been that Israel did not need a mediator. Within forty-eight hours, fourteen thousand seven hundred people were dead and the only thing standing between the rest of them and the same end was one man with a censer, planted in the middle of a dying crowd.

Stand back and look at the figure of him: not on a mountain, not behind a curtain, but out in the open ground with corpses on one side and the living on the other, holding back the wrath of God with his own body and an offering. That is what a priest is for. And when the true Priest came, he did not carry the offering in his hands. He is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2), and he stood between the dead and the living by being the dead, and rose, and the plague was stopped for ever.

16.theology:
Rebellion Against the Mediator Is Rebellion Against God. Korah’s pious-sounding slogan masked a refusal of God’s appointed mediation and a grasping for the priesthood God withheld. “It is against the LORD that you have gathered.” To reject the one Mediator God appoints — supremely Christ — is to perish before the holy God.

The Holiness That Consumes. The earth swallowed the rebels and fire consumed the 250. God alone determines how he may be approached, and to defy his appointed way is lethal. The same glory that blesses can consume; we are spared only because a better Mediator bore the fire in our place.

The Priest Between the Dead and the Living. Aaron ran with his censer and “stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.” Here is the gospel in a single image — the mediator interposing himself to halt the wrath, fulfilled in Christ our High Priest, who stands forever between us and the judgment of God.
16.examples:
Then: Korah grasped for the priesthood and was swallowed by the earth; the people grumbled and a plague broke out; and Aaron ran into the midst of death and stood between the dead and the living until the plague was stopped.

Now: Do not despise the place God has given you or grasp for what he has withheld; rebellion against his order is rebellion against him. And rest in the wonder that Christ, your great High Priest, has run into the midst of your death and stands between you and the wrath of God. Because he stands, the plague is stopped, and you live.

17.title: Aaron’s Staff Buds: Resurrection and the Confirmed Priesthood
17.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, and get from them staffs, one for each fathers' house, from all their chiefs according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. Write each man's name on his staff,<sup>3</sup>and write Aaron's name on the staff of Levi. For there shall be one staff for the head of each fathers' house.<sup>4</sup>Then you shall deposit them in the tent of meeting before the testimony, where I meet with you.<sup>5</sup>And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you."<sup>6</sup>Moses spoke to the people of Israel. And all their chiefs gave him staffs, one for each chief, according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs.
