Two things are wrong with it and both are fatal. The first is the name he calls them. Rebels — a true word, but not the word God had just used. God had given no rebuke at all; he had offered water. Moses steps in front of a God who is being generous and presents him as a God who is furious, and the people watching learn something false about their Maker. The second is the pronoun. Shall we bring water for you out of this rock? Not shall the LORD. Somewhere between the tent and the rock, the mediator has quietly slipped into the middle of the sentence. And then he lifts his hand and strikes the rock, twice — not once, but twice, in temper, doing what he was not told to do and doing it hard.

And here is the thing that should stop the reader cold: and water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their livestock. It worked. Every last person and animal in that camp had their thirst met through a man who was at that moment sinning against God. Do not miss what this says. God’s kindness to his people is not throttled by the state of his servant’s heart. A church can be fed under a preacher who is in the wrong; a family can be blessed through a father who is angry. Which is a mercy for the people, and a trap for the servant, because the water gushing out felt exactly like approval — and it was not.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them." These are the waters of Meribah, where the people of Israel quarreled with the LORD, and through them he showed himself holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verdict falls on both brothers: Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them. Forty years of bearing this nation, and it ends here. Every honest reader feels the same objection, so let us put it plainly: is that not out of all proportion? He hit a rock.

Three things answer it. First, God names the sin himself, and it is not bad temper — it is you did not believe in me. Under the anger was unbelief; Moses did not trust that a spoken word would be enough. Second, the charge is public: in the eyes of the people. Moses was not a private man having a bad morning. He was the one lens through which two million people saw God, and he smeared it. The higher the platform, the less private the failure — which is why James warns that teachers will be judged with greater strictness (Jas. 3:1). Third, and deepest, Paul tells us what the rock was: they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:4). At Horeb the Rock was struck, once, and life poured out. Here he was to be spoken to — because the smitten Rock is never struck twice. Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many (Heb. 9:28), is now approached with words, not blows. Moses took a hammer to that picture in front of the whole nation, and God would not let the picture be defaced.

Then verse 13 closes the account: These are the waters of Meribah… and through them he showed himself holy. He was going to be shown holy at those waters one way or the other. If his servant would not do it, his servant would become the occasion of it. Yet do not close the page thinking Moses was lost. Fourteen centuries later, on another mountain, a man appears in glory inside the land he was refused, and stands there talking with Jesus about his exodus (Luke 9:30–31). Moses was kept out of Canaan. He was never kept out of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses asks Edom — Israel’s kinsmen, the descendants of Esau — for peaceful passage through their land, promising to touch nothing. Edom refuses, and comes out with a strong army. Israel, forbidden to fight their brother nation (Deut 2:4-5), turns away. Even on the edge of the promise, the road is hard and the welcome cold.
verseByVerse.theology: Edom’s refusal of their kinsman Israel (vv.18-21) continues the long, sad estrangement of Esau’s line from Jacob’s (Gen 25-27; cf. Obadiah). God restrains Israel from retaliating against a brother nation (Deut 2:4-5), teaching patience and submission to his timing rather than force. The pilgrim road to the promise is often blocked and unwelcoming, but God’s people press on by his appointed way, not their own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel swallowed the insult and took the long way around, trusting God’s route rather than forcing their own.

Now: the way to our inheritance is often blocked and unwelcoming, even by those who should be kin. We press on God’s appointed path, not repaying hostility with hostility (Rom 12:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom: "Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that we have met: how our fathers went down to Egypt, and we lived in Egypt a long time. And the Egyptians dealt harshly with us and our fathers. And when we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. And here we are in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory. Please let us pass through your land. We will not pass through field or vineyard, or drink water from a well. We will go along the King's Highway. We will not turn aside to the right hand or to the left until we have passed through your territory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message Moses sends to Edom opens with a word chosen with care: Thus says your brother Israel. Edom is Esau; Israel is Jacob (Gen. 36:1). These are twins. Their mother felt them fighting before either of them was born, and four hundred years later their descendants are still on opposite sides of a border, one asking and one refusing. Old family wounds do not heal by being outlived. They get inherited.

What Moses actually says is a summary of the gospel of the exodus told to an outsider: hardship, slavery, harsh treatment — and when we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. That is the testimony, offered without embarrassment to a pagan king. And then the request, and its terms are almost painfully modest. Not a field. Not a vineyard. Not so much as a drink from a well. Only the King’s Highway, the main trade road, walked straight down the middle, not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

It is a request from a nation of well over half a million people who could have taken what they asked for. But God had already told them not to: You shall not contend with them, for I will not give you one foot breadth of their land, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession (Deut. 2:4–5). Esau despised his birthright and God still kept a promise to him. His people are not to be trampled by the people of the promise. The God who chooses is not therefore careless of those he did not choose.

verseByVerse.quote: But Edom said to him, "You shall not pass through, lest I come out with the sword against you." And the people of Israel said to him, "We will go up by the highway, and if we drink of your water, I and my livestock, then I will pay for it. Let me only pass through on foot, nothing more." But he said, "You shall not pass through." And Edom came out against them with a large army and with a strong force. Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his territory, so Israel turned away from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not pass through, lest I come out with the sword against you. Israel tries again, sweetening the offer — we will pay for any water we drink, we will go on foot, nothing more. And Edom answers with three words and an army. Blood counted for nothing. The brother came out with a large force to stop his brother walking down a public road.

Then the sentence that shows what forty years in the wilderness have actually produced: so Israel turned away from him. They had the numbers. They had just watched God split a sea. They had every human reason to force the crossing, and they walked away, because God had said the land was Esau’s. That is obedience with nothing in it for the obedient — the hardest kind there is, and the kind that makes no sense at all unless you believe God is running the map.

And look where that detour goes. Because Edom said no, Israel takes the long road south around Mount Seir — and it is on that very road, in the next chapter, that the people become impatient and God sends the serpents and lifts up the bronze one on a pole. The closed door led to the pole in the wilderness that Jesus would one day claim as a picture of his own cross (John 3:14). Keep that in view when the door in front of you is shut by someone who ought to have opened it. Israel could not see the bronze serpent from Kadesh. The detour was not the loss of the plan. It was the plan.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Mount Hor, Aaron’s life ends. On God’s command, Moses strips Aaron of his priestly garments and puts them on his son Eleazar; then Aaron dies on the mountain. The first high priest passes, but the priesthood continues — the garments pass to the next. A whole generation is dying in the wilderness, and even Aaron, because of Meribah, does not enter the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Aaron dies outside the land, under the same judgment as Moses (v.24), and the priestly garments pass to Eleazar (v.28) — the office outlives the man. The old priesthood was marked by death: “they were prevented by death from continuing in office” (Heb 7:23). This very weakness magnifies Christ, the priest who “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Heb 7:24) — who never dies, never passes his garments to a successor, and “always lives to make intercession” (Heb 7:25).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Aaron’s garments were lifted from his shoulders and laid on his son’s; the high priest died, and the people mourned him thirty days.

Now: our High Priest never dies and never hands off his office. “He always lives to make intercession” (Heb 7:25) — a priest forever, whose ministry for us can never be interrupted by death.

verseByVerse.quote: And they journeyed from Kadesh, and the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came to Mount Hor. And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron at Mount Hor, on the border of the land of Edom, "Let Aaron be gathered to his people, for he shall not enter the land that I have given to the people of Israel, because you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come to Mount Hor, and God speaks to the two brothers about the older one: Let Aaron be gathered to his people, for he shall not enter the land… because you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah. The sentence passed at Meribah is now to be carried out, and Aaron hears it announced over his own head.

But notice the phrase God uses. Not Aaron shall die, though he will. Let Aaron be gathered to his people. That expression runs all through the Pentateuch — Abraham was gathered to his people (Gen. 25:8), and Isaac, and Jacob — and it plainly means more than burial, because Abraham was not buried with his people; he was buried in a cave in a foreign country while his kin lay hundreds of miles away in Ur and Haran. To be gathered is to be brought in to a company that is already assembled somewhere else. The Old Testament says this quietly, without a doctrine attached, the way a family speaks of someone going home.

And look at what Aaron does with the news. Nothing. Not a word of protest is recorded, no plea for a reprieve, no argument that forty years of service had earned a better ending. He is told to climb a mountain he will not come down from, and within two verses he is climbing it. A man can take God’s hardest word and still walk toward him carrying it — and that, not the golden calf, is the last thing Scripture shows us Aaron doing.

So the God who shuts the land against Aaron opens something else in the same breath. He is not permitted a border crossing; he is granted a gathering. That is the exact shape of a Christian funeral, where the loss and the welcome are announced in one sentence, and it is the reason Paul can say that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Cor. 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Take Aaron and Eleazar his son and bring them up to Mount Hor. And strip Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron shall be gathered to his people and shall die there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take Aaron and Eleazar his son and bring them up to Mount Hor. And strip Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. Read that slowly, because it is one of the most affecting scenes in the Torah and it is easy to walk past.

Picture the climb. An old man goes up a mountain in the full dress of the high priest — the blue robe with its bells and pomegranates round the hem, the ephod, the breastpiece with its twelve engraved stones, one for each tribe, worn over the heart, and on the turban the plate of gold that read Holy to the LORD (Exod. 28). He has worn that for forty years. He has carried the names of the tribes over his heart into the presence of God on the Day of Atonement. And at the summit, in front of his son, Moses takes it off him — piece by piece, the turban, the breastpiece, the robe — until the greatest priest Israel has ever had is standing on a bare rock in his undergarment with nothing to show for any of it. Then he dies.

The garments do not die. They go onto Eleazar, and Israel comes down the mountain with a high priest. But the man is gone, and that is precisely the limitation Hebrews puts its finger on: the former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb. 7:23–24). There was another hill, and another set of garments taken off a priest, and soldiers who threw dice for them at the foot of the cross (John 19:23–24). But that priest had no successor and needed none. He came back for his own office. He is wearing it still.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses did as the LORD commanded. And they went up Mount Hor in the sight of all the congregation. And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron died there on the top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar came down from the mountain. And when all the congregation saw that Aaron had perished, all the house of Israel wept for Aaron thirty days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went up Mount Hor in the sight of all the congregation. The whole nation stood at the bottom and watched. Three men went up the mountain and two came down, and the second one was wearing the robes of the first. Israel did not need to be told what had happened; they read it off the shoulders of the man walking back toward them.

Then: all the house of Israel wept for Aaron thirty days. Thirty days — the full mourning, the same the nation would later give Moses (Deut. 34:8). And look at who they were weeping for. This is the man who made the golden calf and then told Moses the most feeble lie in Scripture, that he threw the gold in the fire and there came out this calf (Exod. 32:24). This is the man who stood beside Miriam and spoke against his own brother (Num. 12:1–2). And a whole nation wept for him for a month. God had not merely tolerated Aaron; God had made him the man Israel could not bear to lose. That is what grace does with a failure who is not thrown away.

The chapter has been an inventory of endings. Miriam buried at Kadesh, Moses barred from the land, Aaron stripped on a mountain, a door slammed by a brother. Every leader Israel had is going into the ground, and the people are left at the bottom of a hill weeping. And this is the exact place where Hebrews turns and shows what is different now: because our priest lives forever, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25). Israel came down Mount Hor with a priest still alive. So does the church, and hers will not be stripped, and she will not be gathering at the foot of any mountain to weep for him.

21.title: The Bronze Serpent: Look and Live
21.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he fought against Israel, and took some of them captive.<sup>2</sup>And Israel vowed a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will indeed give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD heeded the voice of Israel and gave over the Canaanites, and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. So the name of the place was called Hormah.<sup>4</sup>From Mount Hor they set out by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. And the people became impatient on the way.<sup>5</sup>And the people spoke against God and against Moses, "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food."<sup>6</sup>Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died.<sup>7</sup>And the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. Pray to the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us." So Moses prayed for the people.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live."<sup>9</sup>So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel set out and camped in Oboth.<sup>11</sup>And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the sunrise.<sup>12</sup>From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered.<sup>13</sup>From there they set out and camped on the other side of the Arnon, which is in the wilderness that extends from the border of the Amorites, for the Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.<sup>14</sup>Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD, "Waheb in Suphah, and the valleys of the Arnon,<sup>15</sup>and the slope of the valleys that extends to the seat of Ar, and leans to the border of Moab."<sup>16</sup>And from there they continued to Beer; that is the well of which the LORD said to Moses, "Gather the people together, so that I may give them water."<sup>17</sup>Then Israel sang this song: "Spring up, O well!—Sing to it!—<sup>18</sup>the well that the princes made, that the nobles of the people dug, with the scepter and with their staffs." And from the wilderness they went on to Mattanah,<sup>19</sup>and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth,<sup>20</sup>and from Bamoth to the valley lying in the region of Moab by the top of Pisgah that looks down on the desert.<sup>21</sup>Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying,<sup>22</sup>"Let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into field or vineyard. We will not drink the water of a well. We will go by the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory."<sup>23</sup>But Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his people together and went out against Israel to the wilderness and came to Jahaz and fought against Israel.<sup>24</sup>And Israel defeated him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as to the Ammonites, for the border of the Ammonites was strong.<sup>25</sup>And Israel took all these cities, and Israel settled in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon, and in all its villages.<sup>26</sup>For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land out of his hand, as far as the Arnon.<sup>27</sup>Therefore the ballad singers say, "Come to Heshbon, let it be built; let the city of Sihon be established.<sup>28</sup>For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar of Moab, and swallowed the heights of the Arnon.<sup>29</sup>Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! He has made his sons fugitives, and his daughters captives, to an Amorite king, Sihon.<sup>30</sup>So we overthrew them; Heshbon, as far as Dibon, perished; and we laid waste as far as Nophah; fire spread as far as Medeba."<sup>31</sup>Thus Israel lived in the land of the Amorites.<sup>32</sup>And Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they captured its villages and dispossessed the Amorites who were there.<sup>33</sup>Then they turned and went up by the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against them, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.<sup>34</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand, and all his people, and his land. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon."<sup>35</sup>So they defeated him and his sons and all his people, until he had no survivor left. And they possessed his land.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 contains the brightest gospel light in the whole book of Numbers, for our Lord himself pointed to it: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). The people grumble yet again — “there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food” (the manna!) — and God sends fiery serpents among them, and many die. The judgment fits the sin: a people who spit venom at God are bitten by venom.

The people repent and cry out, and God gives a remedy so strange and so glorious that it can only be the gospel. He does not remove the serpents. He commands Moses to make a bronze serpent and lift it up on a pole, and “everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” The cure is not in medicine or effort but in a look. The dying are not told to fight the serpents, or to climb the pole, or to be worthy — only to look. Keller observed that this is salvation by faith alone in its purest Old Testament form: not by doing, but by looking away from yourself to the thing God has provided. The simplest, weakest, most desperate look saves.

And what was lifted up? An image of the very thing that was killing them — a serpent, the curse itself, raised on a pole. Ferguson marvels at the depth of this: on the cross, God lifted up his Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom 8:3), made him to be sin and a curse for us (2 Cor 5:21; Gal 3:13). The serpent, the symbol of the curse since Eden, was lifted up so that all who looked might live. So Christ became the curse, lifted up on the pole of the cross, and every sin-bitten, dying sinner who looks to him in faith — not by working, only by looking — shall live. “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isa 45:22). This is the heart of the gospel, hidden in the heart of Numbers.
21.theology:
Look and live. The bronze serpent saves by sight, not effort — the purest Old Testament picture of justification by faith. Christ lifted up saves all who simply look to him (John 3:14–15).

The curse lifted up. The serpent, emblem of the curse, was raised on a pole. So Christ became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), bearing the very judgment that was killing us.

Judgment that fits the sin. Venomous words met venomous serpents. God's judgments hold up a mirror, yet his mercy provides a remedy in the midst of the curse.
21.examples:
Then: God sent fiery serpents for Israel's grumbling, then provided a bronze serpent on a pole, so that everyone bitten who looked at it would live.

Now: You have been bitten by the serpent of sin and are dying. Do not look to yourself, your works, or your worthiness. Look to Christ lifted up on the cross, who became the curse for you, and live. The weakest look of faith saves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens with a small but telling episode. The Canaanite king of Arad attacks Israel and takes captives. Israel vows to the LORD, and God gives them victory; they devote the cities to destruction and name the place Hormah. After years of defeat and delay, here is a first taste of the conquest to come — granted in answer to a vow of dependence on God.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel’s vow and God’s response (vv.2-3) show the pattern of holy war: victory comes not by Israel’s might but by the LORD’s gift, sought in prayer and vow. It is a small firstfruit of the conquest, a sign that the God who disciplines his people has not abandoned his promise to give them the land.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: attacked and taking losses, Israel turned to God with a vow, and he gave the victory.

Now: our battles are won the same way — not by our strength but by casting ourselves on God, who “gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor 15:57).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he fought against Israel, and took some of them captive. And Israel vowed a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will indeed give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction." And the LORD heeded the voice of Israel and gave over the Canaanites, and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. So the name of the place was called Hormah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens with an ambush. The king of Arad hears that Israel is on the move, attacks, and carries off prisoners — the first thing to happen after Aaron’s funeral is a raid. And Israel’s response is the most surprising sentence in the book so far: And Israel vowed a vow to the LORD. Not a complaint. Not a mob at the tent door. A vow. In twenty chapters this is the first time trouble has produced prayer instead of grumbling, and the change is the whole point of the verse.

Then look at the name of the place. So the name of the place was called Hormah. Israel has been to Hormah before. In chapter 14, after the sentence of forty years had fallen, the people decided to invade anyway without God, and the Amalekites and Canaanites came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah (14:45). That was the low-water mark of the nation — a rout on the very ground where they now win.

Same place. Same enemy. Opposite outcome. The one variable is whether God went with them, and it is the only variable that has ever mattered. If there is a piece of ground in your own history where you were badly beaten — a besetting sin, a relationship, a fear you have lost to a hundred times — this verse says the ground is not the reason. Israel did not need a different battlefield. She needed a different way of going up. And the difference between the disaster of chapter 14 and the victory of chapter 21 is a single act of dependence: they asked first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — The Bronze Serpent: Look and Live
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the long detour around Edom, the people grow impatient and speak against God and Moses, despising the manna as “worthless food.” God sends fiery serpents, and many die. When the people confess and Moses prays, God’s remedy is startling: make a bronze serpent, set it on a pole, and everyone who looks at it will live. It is one of the clearest gospel pictures in the Old Testament — and Jesus himself said so.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus makes this the great type of his cross: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14-15). The cure is by looking, not by working — an act of pure faith in God’s strange provision. The bronze serpent, made in the image of the very thing that was killing them, pictures Christ “made... to be sin” (2 Cor 5:21) and “made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13), lifted up so that all who look to him in faith might live.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the dying Israelite had only to turn his eyes to the bronze serpent on the pole, and he lived — no medicine, no effort, just a look of faith.

Now: “Look to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isa 45:22). Salvation is by looking to Christ crucified, not by trying to cure ourselves. Whoever looks, lives (John 3:14-15).

verseByVerse.quote: From Mount Hor they set out by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. And the people became impatient on the way. And the people spoke against God and against Moses, "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Mount Hor they set out by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. Read the map behind that sentence. Canaan is north. They are marching south, away from it, back down toward the sea they crossed forty years ago, because a cousin would not let them use his road. They have just buried Aaron. And the text says the people became impatient on the way — the Hebrew is blunter than that: the soul of the people became short. Shortness of soul. It is the fraying that comes not at the start of a hard thing but three-quarters of the way through, when the end was supposed to be in sight and the road turns the wrong way instead.

Then out comes the complaint, and it contradicts itself inside a single breath: there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food. There is no food, and we cannot stand the food. Grumbling does not have to be coherent. It only has to be loud, and the people making it never notice, because the point was never the food.

But the last phrase should stop us. This worthless food is the manna. It is the bread God rained out of the sky every morning for forty years, gathered before dawn by two million people who did nothing to produce it. The Psalms call it the grain of heaven… the bread of angels (Ps. 78:24–25). And Israel, standing in it, calls it contemptible. This is not a complaint about catering. It is a verdict passed on the goodness of God by people whose mouths are full of his generosity — and it is nearer to us than we would like. Anything given daily and reliably stops registering as a gift. Ask what in your life you have stopped thanking God for, and you will usually find it is whatever he has been most faithful about.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died. And the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. Pray to the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us." So Moses prayed for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died. The judgment is fitted to the crime with terrible precision. A people whose words had turned venomous are answered by venom. What had been coming out of their mouths now comes at them out of the sand. The word rendered fiery is seraphim, burning ones — most likely for the fire the poison put in the wound, though the desert south of Edom is real snake country and the horror was literal enough: swelling, thirst, and hours to live.

Now the second surprise of the chapter. The people come back — and this time they do not bargain, excuse, or blame. We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. That is a straight confession with nothing shaved off it. They name the sin, they name both parties they wronged, and they ask for the one thing they cannot do for themselves: Pray to the LORD.

So Moses prayed for the people. Six words, and they are a marvel. This is the man they had just attacked. This is the man who, one chapter ago, lost the land of promise because his patience with this nation finally snapped. He has every earthly reason to be finished with them. He prays. There is a kind of love that is not exhausted by being rejected by the people it loves, and there is only one place it comes from — and Israel is about to be shown it, hammered out of bronze and hoisted on a pole.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now watch what God does not do. They asked him to take away the serpents from us. He does not take away the serpents. So far as the chapter tells us, the snakes are still in the sand when Israel breaks camp in verse 10. Instead he says: Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live. He leaves the danger in the world and puts a remedy in the middle of it.

Anyone who has begged God to remove something and watched him not remove it should sit with that for a moment. Paul asked three times for a thorn to be taken out and was told instead, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12:8–9). God frequently declines to clear the field and provides instead something that lets his people live in it. That is not a smaller answer than the one requested. It is a costlier one, and it leaves the sufferer with God himself rather than merely with relief.

Then consider what he tells Moses to put on the pole. Not a lamb. Not an angel. Not a symbol of purity. A serpent — an image of the very thing that is killing them, cast in metal, lifted up dead and harmless where every dying man in the camp can see it. And the cure is a look. Not a pilgrimage to the pole, not a touch, not a fee, not a period of improvement first. A man lying in his tent with a swollen leg, too far gone to stand, can still turn his head. God set the price of life at the one thing a dying man is still able to do.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live. Thirteen hundred years later, a rabbi came to Jesus by night with questions about being born again, and Jesus reached past every other text in the Old Testament for this one: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (John 3:14–15). Of all the pictures available to him — the lamb, the ark, the manna, the mercy seat — this is the one the Lord chose to explain his own cross.

See why. The serpent was the emblem of the curse, from Eden onward. To hang the curse on a pole in front of the camp was to display it defeated. And Paul says exactly what happened at Calvary in the same terms: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Gal. 3:13). He did not merely deal with the poison. He became, in the sight of the whole camp, the thing that was killing us — for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21) — and hung there, and drew every dying eye to himself. There is nothing to do but look. Not look and then earn it. Not look after cleaning up. Look, and live, in that order and no other.

One postscript, because Scripture tells it. Seven hundred years later King Hezekiah went through Judah smashing idols, and among the things he broke in pieces was the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (2 Kgs. 18:4). He gave it a contemptuous nickname: Nehushtan, a mere piece of bronze. The very object God had given to save them had been turned into a god. That is a warning worth taking home. Anything God gives you as a window — a church, a translation, a teacher, a way of praying — you are entirely capable of turning into a wall, and the tell is always the same: you begin to love the means more than the Christ it was pointing at.

Break the bronze, then, and keep the Christ. The serpent on the pole was only ever an arrow pointing down forty centuries to a hill outside Jerusalem, where the Son of God hung in the open air with the whole curse of the world on him, and did not come down, and let the dying look at him. He is what the pole was for. Every eye that has ever turned to him has lived, and not one that turned has been refused.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — The Journey and the Song of the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel journeys on, stage by stage, toward Moab. Along the way the people sing a joyful little song over a well God gives them: “Spring up, O well!” After the venom and the grumbling, here is a moment of gladness — God still providing water in the desert, and his people, for once, singing their thanks instead of voicing their complaints.
verseByVerse.theology: The Song of the Well (vv.17-18) is a rare, bright note of grateful worship in a book full of murmuring — God’s provision met, this time, with song rather than complaint. The itinerary (vv.10-20) marks real progress toward the land; the pilgrim people are moving forward under God’s leading, and joy over his gifts is the fitting response of those being brought home.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: instead of grumbling over water, this time Israel sang over it — a people learning, slowly, to meet God’s provision with praise.

Now: the difference between a grumbling life and a grateful one is often the same gift received two ways. “Give thanks in all circumstances” (1 Thess 5:18) — sing over the well.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel set out and camped in Oboth. And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the sunrise. From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered. From there they set out and camped on the other side of the Arnon, which is in the wilderness that extends from the border of the Amorites, for the Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the serpents, the text does something almost startling: it goes quiet. And the people of Israel set out and camped in Oboth. And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim… No drama, no oracle, no rebellion. Set out and camp, set out and camp. Four verses of a nation simply travelling.

That is not filler. Most of the Christian life is these verses rather than the ones before them. There are the days when the serpents come and the pole goes up, and then there are the long stretches of ordinary obedience where nothing happens except that you keep going in the right direction. God records both. The Holy Spirit thought the campsite at Oboth was worth a line in the Bible.

And the geography is quietly hopeful. Zered, then the Arnon — and the Arnon is the northern border of Moab, which means Israel has finally stopped going south. The long detour around Edom is over. They are moving up the eastern side of the Dead Sea, parallel to the land, and every camp from here on is closer to the Jordan than the last.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD, "Waheb in Suphah, and the valleys of the Arnon, and the slope of the valleys that extends to the seat of Ar, and leans to the border of Moab."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the writer quotes a song from a book we do not have: Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD. Nothing else in Scripture mentions it, and no copy has ever been found. It appears to have been a collection of victory poems celebrating what God did for Israel in battle, and Moses cites two lines of it as a geographer might cite a gazetteer, to fix the location of the Arnon crossing.

A reader can be forgiven for finding that unsettling. Does a lost book mean the Bible is missing something? It does not, and the reader should have the answer clearly. Scripture quotes outside sources fairly often — the Book of Jashar in Joshua and 2 Samuel, court annals in Kings, and in the New Testament Paul quotes two pagan Greek poets without embarrassment (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Inspiration has never been the claim that no other book existed, or that every source an inspired writer consulted was itself inspired. It is the claim that what God caused to be written is true, and that what he has given is enough: able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Tim. 3:15).

So the lost book is not a hole in the Bible. It is a footnote in it — evidence that these events happened in a real country with real rivers, that other people were writing them down, and that the man recording this expected his readers to be able to check.

verseByVerse.quote: And from there they continued to Beer; that is the well of which the LORD said to Moses, "Gather the people together, so that I may give them water." Then Israel sang this song: "Spring up, O well!—Sing to it!— the well that the princes made, that the nobles of the people dug, with the scepter and with their staffs." And from the wilderness they went on to Mattanah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And from there they continued to Beer — the name simply means Well — that is the well of which the LORD said to Moses, “Gather the people together, so that I may give them water.” Set that beside the last chapter and the difference is staggering. At Meribah there was no water and a mob formed and a mediator lost his temper and a rock was struck twice. Here God announces the water before anyone has complained. Nobody quarrels. Nobody has to be shouted at. He gathers them, and gives.

And Israel does something she has not done since the far bank of the Red Sea. She sings. Then Israel sang this song: “Spring up, O well!—Sing to it!—the well that the princes made, that the nobles of the people dug, with the scepter and with their staffs.” It is a working song, the kind men chant while they dig, with the leaders down in the pit swinging their staffs at the sand alongside everybody else. God provides the water; the nobles do the digging; the whole camp sings while it happens. Grace and effort in one verse, and neither one crowding out the other.

Nothing in the chapter marks the change in this people more clearly than that song. The same nation that called God’s bread worthless twelve verses ago is now singing at a hole in the ground. Judgment fell, mercy was lifted up on a pole, and the survivors came out of it singing. That is what God is doing in the wilderness, and it has never been anything else: he is making, out of complainers, a people who sing.

verseByVerse.quote: and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, and from Bamoth to the valley lying in the region of Moab by the top of Pisgah that looks down on the desert.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four more camps, and then a view. From Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, and from Bamoth to the valley lying in the region of Moab by the top of Pisgah that looks down on the desert.

These are ordinary place-names and the writer is not preaching from them. But they are Hebrew words, and a Hebrew reader would have heard what they mean, in this order: Mattanah, a gift; Nahaliel, torrent of God; Bamoth, high places. From a gift, to a river, to the heights. It is the shape of the last few verses laid out in the itinerary itself, and even if the names are only geography, the road really did run that way.

And where does it end? At the top of Pisgah — the ridge from which, one book later, Moses will be shown the whole land before he dies (Deut. 34:1) — that looks down on the desert. For thirty-eight years the wilderness was the horizon in every direction. Now they are standing above it, looking down on it. The place that swallowed a generation has become a view from a height. That is not yet the promised land, but it is the first time Israel has been able to see the wilderness from the outside, and every believer who has come out the far side of a long, wasted, disciplined stretch knows exactly what that morning felt like.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–35 — Victory over Sihon and Og
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the tide turns decisively. Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan refuse Israel passage and come out to fight — and Israel defeats them both, taking their lands east of the Jordan. After forty years of wandering and defeat, God begins to give his people the land. These twin victories became a byword in Israel’s memory of what God can do.
verseByVerse.theology: The defeat of Sihon and Og (vv.21-35) is the first great conquest, celebrated for generations as a monument of God’s power (Ps 135:11; 136:19-20). The wilderness generation’s unbelief had delayed the promise, but it could not cancel it: God is faithful, and in his time he gives what he pledged. These victories east of the Jordan are the down payment on the whole inheritance — a reminder that God finishes what he begins (Phil 1:6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the giants Sihon and Og fell before Israel, and the long-promised land began, at last, to be theirs.

Now: the God who kept his word to a wandering, faithless people keeps it still. What he has promised, he will perform; “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Phil 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying, "Let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into field or vineyard. We will not drink the water of a well. We will go by the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory." But Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his people together and went out against Israel to the wilderness and came to Jahaz and fought against Israel. And Israel defeated him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as to the Ammonites, for the border of the Ammonites was strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel sends Sihon king of the Amorites the same message she sent Edom, almost word for word: no field, no vineyard, not a drop from a well, straight down the King’s Highway and out the other side. The courtesy has not changed. What has changed is God’s instruction, and it matters. Edom was protected — I have given Mount Seir to Esau (Deut. 2:5) — and so Israel turned away from an insult without drawing a sword. Sihon is not protected. Of him God had said, Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon… Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle (Deut. 2:24).

And Sihon does not merely refuse. He gathered all his people together and went out against Israel to the wilderness. He marched out into open desert to attack a nation that had asked to use a road. Deuteronomy adds the hardest line in the account: the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate (Deut. 2:30). We should not soften that, and we should not overreach it either. Sihon wanted this war; God did not manufacture an appetite in him that was not already his own. What God did was decline to restrain a man bent on his own violence, and then use it. That is a sovereignty that runs straight underneath human wickedness without ever becoming its author.

The result is the first territory Israel has ever owned: from the Arnon to the Jabbok, a substantial kingdom taken in one afternoon by a people who forty years earlier had been too frightened to cross a border.

verseByVerse.quote: And Israel took all these cities, and Israel settled in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon, and in all its villages. For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land out of his hand, as far as the Arnon. Therefore the ballad singers say, "Come to Heshbon, let it be built; let the city of Sihon be established. For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar of Moab, and swallowed the heights of the Arnon. Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! He has made his sons fugitives, and his daughters captives, to an Amorite king, Sihon. So we overthrew them; Heshbon, as far as Dibon, perished; and we laid waste as far as Nophah; fire spread as far as Medeba."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the chapter does something wonderfully sly. Heshbon had not been Amorite for very long; Sihon had taken it from Moab in an earlier war, and the Amorite poets had written a victory ballad about it. That is the song quoted here — Come to Heshbon, let it be built… For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar of Moab. It is the conqueror’s taunt, in the conqueror’s own words, gloating over Moab’s ruin.

And Israel sings it over the rubble of Heshbon. The taunt-song of the winner is now being chanted at the winner’s funeral. Every empire composes its ballad; the ballad outlives the empire and ends up being sung by somebody else standing on the ruins. That is not cynicism, it is history, and Scripture keeps a copy of the lyrics to prove it.

Notice one line in particular: You are undone, O people of Chemosh! He has made his sons fugitives, and his daughters captives. Chemosh was the national god of Moab, the one they sacrificed to and named their children after. And the song about him says he turned his own worshippers into refugees. That is the plain difference between an idol and God. An idol takes everything you have and then cannot hold the ground you gave it for. Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases. Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands (Ps. 115:3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Israel lived in the land of the Amorites. And Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they captured its villages and dispossessed the Amorites who were there. Then they turned and went up by the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against them, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. But the LORD said to Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand, and all his people, and his land. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon." So they defeated him and his sons and all his people, until he had no survivor left. And they possessed his land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One more kingdom stands between Israel and the Jordan, and it is the worst one. Then they turned and went up by the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against them. Og was a giant, the last of the Rephaim, and Deuteronomy preserves the detail that anyone who has heard the story never forgets — his iron bed was over thirteen feet long, and you could go and look at it in Rabbah (Deut. 3:11).

Now remember chapter 13. Ten men came back from Canaan and said, there we saw the Nephilim… and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (13:33), and a whole generation died in the sand rather than face them. Here is that same terror, wearing a crown, coming down the road at Edrei with an army behind him. And God says to Moses, Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand. The new generation goes out and fights the giant their parents ran from, and wins, and takes his land. The wilderness has done its work. The fear that killed the fathers no longer holds the sons.

Israel never forgot that day. Sihon and Og are still being sung about centuries later, in a psalm where every second line is the same refrain: to him who struck down great kings, for his steadfast love endures forever… Sihon, king of the Amorites… and Og, king of Bashan, for his steadfast love endures forever (Ps. 136:17–20). That is how Israel learned to read her own military history — not as a record of her courage, but as an inventory of his mercy. The God who hung a serpent on a pole for a camp of dying grumblers is the God who walks in front of them against giants. He does not save halfway. He deals with the venom, and then he clears the road.

22.title: Balak and Balaam: The Sovereign God over a Pagan Prophet
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the people of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>2</sup>And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites.<sup>3</sup>And Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many. Moab was overcome with fear of the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And Moab said to the elders of Midian, "This horde will now lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field." So Balak the son of Zippor, who was king of Moab at that time,<sup>5</sup>sent messengers to Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor, which is near the River in the land of the people of Amaw, to call him, saying, "Behold, a people has come out of Egypt. They cover the face of the earth, and they are dwelling opposite me.<sup>6</sup>Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I shall be able to defeat them and drive them from the land, for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed."<sup>7</sup>So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand. And they came to Balaam and gave him Balak's message.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, "Lodge here tonight, and I will bring back word to you, as the LORD speaks to me." So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.<sup>9</sup>And God came to Balaam and said, "Who are these men with you?"<sup>10</sup>And Balaam said to God, "Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent to me, saying,<sup>11</sup>'Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and it covers the face of the earth. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I shall be able to fight against them and drive them out.'"<sup>12</sup>God said to Balaam, "You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed."<sup>13</sup>So Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your own land, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you."<sup>14</sup>So the princes of Moab rose and went to Balak and said, "Balaam refuses to come with us."<sup>15</sup>Once again Balak sent princes, more in number and more honorable than these.<sup>16</sup>And they came to Balaam and said to him, "Thus says Balak the son of Zippor: 'Let nothing hinder you from coming to me,<sup>17</sup>for I will surely do you great honor, and whatever you say to me I will do. Come, curse this people for me.'"<sup>18</sup>But Balaam answered and said to the servants of Balak, "Though Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more.<sup>19</sup>So you, too, please stay here tonight, that I may know what more the LORD will say to me."<sup>20</sup>And God came to Balaam at night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you."<sup>21</sup>So Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab.<sup>22</sup>But God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the LORD took his stand in the way as his adversary. Now he was riding on the donkey, and his two servants were with him.<sup>23</sup>And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand. And the donkey turned aside out of the road and went into the field. And Balaam struck the donkey, to turn her into the road.<sup>24</sup>Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow path between the vineyards, with a wall on either side.<sup>25</sup>And when the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she pushed against the wall and pressed Balaam's foot against the wall. So he struck her again.<sup>26</sup>Then the angel of the LORD went ahead and stood in a narrow place, where there was no way to turn either to the right or to the left.<sup>27</sup>When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam. And Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff.<sup>28</sup>Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, "What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?"<sup>29</sup>And Balaam said to the donkey, "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you."<sup>30</sup>And the donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your donkey, on which you have ridden all your life long to this day? Is it my habit to treat you this way?" And he said, "No."<sup>31</sup>Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, with his drawn sword in his hand. And he bowed down and fell on his face.<sup>32</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why have you struck your donkey these three times? Behold, I have come out to oppose you because your way is perverse before me.<sup>33</sup>The donkey saw me and turned aside before me these three times. If she had not turned aside from me, surely just now I would have killed you and let her live."<sup>34</sup>Then Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, "I have sinned, for I did not know that you stood in the road against me. Now therefore, if it is evil in your sight, I will turn back."<sup>35</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Balaam, "Go with the men, but speak only the word that I tell you." So Balaam went on with the princes of Balak.<sup>36</sup>When Balak heard that Balaam had come, he went out to meet him at the city of Moab, on the border formed by the Arnon, at the extremity of the border.<sup>37</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not send to you to call you? Why did you not come to me? Am I not able to honor you?"<sup>38</sup>Balaam said to Balak, "Behold, I have come to you! Have I now any power of my own to speak anything? The word that God puts in my mouth, that must I speak."<sup>39</sup>Then Balaam went with Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth.<sup>40</sup>And Balak sacrificed oxen and sheep, and sent for Balaam and for the princes who were with him.<sup>41</sup>And in the morning Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal, and from there he saw a fraction of the people.
22.overview:
With chapters 22–24 the narrative pulls back to show us something Israel could not see: while they camp on the plains of Moab, unaware, a spiritual battle is being waged over their destiny. Balak king of Moab, terrified of Israel, hires the renowned pagan seer Balaam to curse them. The drama that unfolds is one of the most remarkable demonstrations of God's sovereignty in all of Scripture, for God will so overrule this hireling prophet that Balaam cannot speak anything but blessing over the people God has blessed.

The famous episode of the talking donkey is not comic relief but theology in story form. Balaam, the celebrated seer who claims to see what others cannot, is blind to the angel of the LORD standing in his path with a drawn sword — while his donkey sees plainly. The prophet who boasts of open eyes is more blind than his beast. Calvin and others note the biting irony: God humbles the proud seer by speaking through a donkey and by giving sight to an animal that he withholds from the man. The God who can open a donkey's mouth can open or shut any mouth he pleases.

Here is the deep comfort of the chapter: the people of God are surrounded by enemies who plot their ruin, and they do not even know it — yet God is in complete control of the plot. “No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed” (Isa 54:17). Ferguson notes that Balaam is the picture of every enemy of the church: God holds even the curses of the wicked in his hand and turns them to blessing. Romans 8 stands over this chapter: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” The God who would not let Balaam curse his people is the God who works all things, even the schemes of his enemies, for the good of those he has blessed in Christ.
22.theology:
Sovereignty over enemies. God so controls the pagan Balaam that he cannot curse the people God has blessed. No weapon fashioned against God's people shall prosper.

The security of the blessed. They are blessed, and the blessing of God cannot be reversed by any curse. If God is for us, who can be against us (Rom 8:31)?

God humbles the proud. The seer is blinder than his donkey; all true sight is God's gift. The Lord can open a beast's mouth and shut a prophet's, as he pleases.
22.examples:
Then: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but God forbade the curse, opened a donkey's mouth to rebuke the blind seer, and decreed that only blessing would fall.

Now: You are surrounded by enemies you cannot see, who plot against you — yet God holds their curses in his hand and turns them to blessing. Those whom God has blessed in Christ cannot be cursed. Rest in the sovereign Lord who is for you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel camps on the plains of Moab, and Balak king of Moab is terrified — this vast people has swallowed the Amorites, and now they are at his door. Unable to fight them, Balak sends for Balaam, a famous pagan diviner, to come and curse Israel, for “he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed.” The enemy of God’s people, unable to defeat them by the sword, reaches for a curse.
verseByVerse.theology: Balak’s strategy assumes what the pagan world believed — that a skilled diviner could manipulate the spiritual realm and bend a deity’s power to curse. The whole narrative will dismantle that lie: no curse can touch those the LORD has blessed (Rom 8:31, 33). Balak’s fear (v.3) is the fear of a world that senses God’s people are protected by a power it cannot overcome, and so resorts to darker means.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: unable to conquer Israel in open battle, Moab reached for sorcery, hiring a curse against the people God had blessed.

Now: the enemy still cannot defeat God’s people head-on, and still resorts to schemes. But “if God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom 8:31). No curse prospers against those the LORD has blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho. And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites. And Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many. Moab was overcome with fear of the people of Israel. And Moab said to the elders of Midian, "This horde will now lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field." So Balak the son of Zippor, who was king of Moab at that time,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the people of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho. After forty years, that is where they stop. Not in the wilderness. On the flat ground on the east bank, with the river in front of them and the walls of Jericho visible across it. Everything from here to the end of the book happens in this one camp, within sight of the land.

And the first thing that happens is that somebody looks at them and is terrified. Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites. He had watched Sihon and Og disappear in a fortnight. Now this enormous nation is camped on his border, and Moab is overcome with fear. His own image for it is the best line in the chapter: This horde will now lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field. Not a battle — a grazing. An animal with its head down, working steadily across a meadow, indifferent and unhurried, and when it lifts its head the field is gone.

What Balak cannot see is that God had expressly forbidden Israel to touch him: Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession (Deut. 2:9). Moab was in no danger whatever. The king is lying awake at night planning against a nation that has been ordered to leave him alone — and the plan he makes will end up destroying his people in a way Israel’s army never would have. That is what fear does when it will not consult God. It manufactures the disaster it was trying to avoid.

verseByVerse.quote: sent messengers to Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor, which is near the River in the land of the people of Amaw, to call him, saying, "Behold, a people has come out of Egypt. They cover the face of the earth, and they are dwelling opposite me. Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I shall be able to defeat them and drive them from the land, for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Balak sends for a specialist. Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor, which is near the River — the River is the Euphrates, which puts Pethor somewhere in upper Mesopotamia, roughly four hundred miles away. Think about the effort involved. A delegation of Moabite and Midianite elders travels the best part of a month, each way, across the whole fertile crescent, because Balak has heard of a man whose word works. Fear is expensive, and it will pay for anything.

And what does Balak want for his money? Not an army. Not an alliance. Come now, curse this people for me. He believes what most of the ancient world believed: that words spoken by the right man with the right ritual have force in themselves, and that a people can be weakened before a sword is ever drawn. His reason for choosing Balaam is stated plainly: for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed.

Read that sentence again and notice what is missing from it. There is no God in it. Balak imagines that blessing and cursing are a technique available for hire, resident in a man, purchasable at a price. And that is why the next three chapters are not really about Balaam at all. They are about what happens when the machinery of pagan religion is aimed at a people whom the living God has already spoken over. Balak will spend a fortune, build twenty-one altars, kill forty-two animals and climb three mountains, and every single time he opens his hired mouth, out will come a blessing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balak’s messengers come with fees for divination. God tells Balaam plainly, “You shall not go with them... for [Israel] is blessed.” Balaam refuses — for now. But Balak sends a second, grander delegation with greater promises, and Balaam, though he mouths pious words about not going beyond the LORD’s command, clearly wants to go. God lets him go — but on a short leash: “only do what I tell you.” The diviner’s heart is being exposed.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s first word is unmistakable: Israel “is blessed” and cannot be cursed (v.12). Balaam’s second inquiry, after God has already answered, reveals a heart that wants the reward and is looking for a loophole (cf. 2 Pet 2:15, “the way of Balaam... who loved gain from wrongdoing”). God’s permission to go (v.20) is not approval but the giving-over of a man to the desire he will not surrender — while God remains absolutely sovereign over what Balaam may say.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God had already said no, but Balaam, hungry for the reward, kept the door open — asking again, hoping for a different answer.

Now: when we already know God’s will but keep asking, hoping he will bless what our hearts have set on, we walk “the way of Balaam.” Beware the prayer that is really a search for permission (2 Pet 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand. And they came to Balaam and gave him Balak's message. And he said to them, "Lodge here tonight, and I will bring back word to you, as the LORD speaks to me." So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand. The Hebrew word is the ordinary one for the fee paid to a professional diviner, and it tells us plainly what Balaam is. He is not a prophet of Israel. He is a freelance seer in the international market, of the kind archaeologists have since found mentioned by name in a plaster inscription at Deir Alla, a few miles from this very camp — Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods. A real man, with a reputation across the region, in the business of blessing and cursing for money.

And then he opens his mouth and says something startling: I will bring back word to you, as the LORD speaks to me. The LORD — Yahweh, the covenant name, the name revealed at the burning bush. This pagan diviner uses it, and in the next verse God actually answers him. That combination unsettles readers, and it should be faced rather than tidied away.

Here is the plain answer. God is not restricted to speaking through good men. He spoke through Caiaphas, who was at that moment arranging the death of his Son, and John notes that Caiaphas did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied (John 11:49–51). He spoke through Saul after the Spirit had left him (1 Sam. 19:23–24). The gift is not the proof of the man. Balaam’s own end will make the verdict clear enough — the New Testament calls him a man who loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15) — but for now the point stands: God will use a hireling’s mouth rather than let one word be spoken against his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And God came to Balaam and said, "Who are these men with you?" And Balaam said to God, "Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent to me, saying, 'Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and it covers the face of the earth. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I shall be able to fight against them and drive them out.'" God said to Balaam, "You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God came to Balaam and said, “Who are these men with you?” God is not gathering information. It is the question he asked in Eden — Where are you? — and he asks it for the same reason: to make a man say out loud what he is doing. Balaam answers, and his summary is accurate as far as it goes, though he leaves out the fee.

Then the answer comes, and there is nothing ambiguous in it. Three sentences, and each one shuts a door: You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed. No negotiation, no conditions, no room. And the last four words are the foundation of everything that follows in chapters 23 and 24. Not they are good. Not they deserve it. God has just spent twenty-one chapters recording their grumbling, their idolatry, their rebellion, and their funerals. They are blessed — because he blessed them, and for no other reason on earth.

That is the security of the people of God, stated in a sentence, and stated to an enemy. The blessing does not rest on Israel’s conduct, so Israel’s conduct cannot cancel it. It rests on a promise made to Abraham long before any of these people were born, and the God who made it does not take it back. Which is why Paul, arguing the same case for the church, can pile up every enemy he can think of and then ask, almost with a laugh, Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Rom. 8:33). There stood a professional curser with a purse of gold in the next room, and heaven had already ruled. He was too late by four hundred years.

verseByVerse.quote: So Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your own land, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you." So the princes of Moab rose and went to Balak and said, "Balaam refuses to come with us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam sends the delegation home, and at first glance he looks obedient. Then compare what God said with what he reports. God said: You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed. Balaam says: Go to your own land, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you.

The whole heart of the man is in that edit. He passes on the travel restriction and suppresses the reason. He does not tell Balak that the people are blessed and the project is impossible; he tells him that permission has been withheld. One of those closes the matter forever. The other is an invitation to try again — and the messengers hear it exactly that way, reporting back with a shrug that Balaam refuses to come with us, as though the man himself were the obstacle.

This is how a divided heart talks. It says nothing technically untrue and leaves the door ajar. Every one of us knows the manoeuvre: the answer that is accurate in every particular and dishonest in its whole effect, given so that the thing we still want remains available. The test is simple and uncomfortable. When you decline something you would rather have accepted, do you shut the door, or do you leave it looking as though a better offer might open it?

verseByVerse.quote: Once again Balak sent princes, more in number and more honorable than these. And they came to Balaam and said to him, "Thus says Balak the son of Zippor: 'Let nothing hinder you from coming to me, for I will surely do you great honor, and whatever you say to me I will do. Come, curse this people for me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak reads the gap exactly as it was left for him. Once again Balak sent princes, more in number and more honorable than these. A bigger delegation, higher-ranking men, and the offer improved in both currencies at once: I will surely do you great honor, and whatever you say to me I will do. Money and status, and a blank cheque on top.

Notice how precisely the temptation is targeted. Balak does not offer Balaam an argument. He does not try to persuade him that cursing Israel is right. He simply raises the price, because he has correctly judged that this is a man who has a price. The second embassy is a verdict on the first refusal: nobody sends a better offer to someone who has genuinely said no.

And this is the point at which the reader should stop being a spectator. There are things we have refused once, cleanly, and would refuse again at that price — and the honest question is not whether we refused, but what would have to be added to the offer. A little more money. A little more standing. The one person whose good opinion still governs us. Satan is a patient negotiator, and he keeps the file open. When the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time (Luke 4:13).

verseByVerse.quote: But Balaam answered and said to the servants of Balak, "Though Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more. So you, too, please stay here tonight, that I may know what more the LORD will say to me." And God came to Balaam at night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam’s reply is magnificent, and every reader should keep it in mind, because it will be quoted against him for ever after: Though Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more. Theologically it is flawless. It is also, in his mouth, a lie — not in what it asserts but in what it conceals, because the very next sentence is please stay here tonight, that I may know what more the LORD will say to me.

What more? God had already said it, plainly, twice over. There is nothing more to know. A man who says he cannot be bought and then asks the buyer to wait overnight while he checks again has told you everything about himself. He wants the money and he wants God to authorise it, and he is prepared to keep asking until the answer improves. Peter names the disease with brutal economy: he loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15). The lips are orthodox; the appetite is for hire.

And so God gives him what he keeps asking for. If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you. Every reader stumbles here, and the question deserves a straight answer: has God changed his mind? He has not. This is permission, and permission is not approval. Scripture knows this dreadful mercy well — Israel demanded a king until God gave them one, and it ruined them (1 Sam. 8:7–9); of an earlier generation the psalm says, he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15). There is a stage at which the most frightening thing God can do to a man who will not stop asking is to say yes. Balaam got his trip. Verse 22 will tell us what God thought of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–35 — The Donkey and the Angel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road, God’s anger burns against Balaam, and the angel of the LORD stands in the way with a drawn sword — unseen by the prophet, but seen by his donkey. Three times the donkey swerves to save Balaam’s life, and three times he beats her. Then God opens the donkey’s mouth, and she rebukes him; and God opens Balaam’s eyes to see the angel. The famous seer is blinder than his beast. It is at once absurd and profound: God will use even a donkey to humble a proud prophet.
verseByVerse.theology: The talking donkey is God’s gentle mockery of a “seer” who cannot see (vv.23-31): the animal perceives the angel that the prophet misses. It exposes Balaam’s spiritual blindness and God’s absolute control — if God can make a donkey speak his word, he can certainly put his words in Balaam’s mouth. The episode humbles human pretension: God “catches the wise in their craftiness” (1 Cor 3:19) and can use the lowliest instrument to accomplish and reveal his will.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the renowned seer, riding blindly toward danger, was saved by a donkey who saw what he could not, and rebuked by the beast he despised.

Now: God still humbles our pride with the unlikeliest instruments, and “chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise” (1 Cor 1:27). Beware being so sure of your own sight that a donkey sees more than you.

verseByVerse.quote: So Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab. But God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the LORD took his stand in the way as his adversary. Now he was riding on the donkey, and his two servants were with him. And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand. And the donkey turned aside out of the road and went into the field. And Balaam struck the donkey, to turn her into the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab. But God’s anger was kindled because he went. The two sentences sit side by side without a word of explanation, and the reader is meant to feel the jolt. He had permission. He went. God was angry. Permission had never been the same thing as pleasure, and Balaam knew the difference perfectly well — he had spent two nights trying to convert one into the other.

So the angel of the LORD took his stand in the way as his adversary. The Hebrew word for adversary here is satan — in its ordinary sense, one who stands in the road to oppose. Heaven has come out onto the highway with a drawn sword to stop a man from going where heaven has just told him he may go. That is not a contradiction. It is God placing an obstacle in the path of a servant he does not intend to lose, which is a kindness that looks, from the saddle, exactly like an obstruction.

And now the joke that runs through the rest of the chapter begins. The donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand. The donkey saw.
