Then Eleazar the priest said to the men in the army who had gone to battle: "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded Moses: only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead, everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire, and it shall be clean. Nevertheless, it shall also be purified with the water for impurity. And whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water. You must wash your clothes on the seventh day, and you shall be clean. And afterward you may come into the camp."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What comes next is easy to miss and morally enormous. The army has just carried out a God-commanded judgment, and God does not send them home as heroes. He sends them outside the camp. Encamp outside the camp seven days. Whoever of you has killed any person and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves and your captives on the third day and on the seventh day.

Seven days of exclusion, and the cleansing agent is the water made from the ashes of the red heifer in chapter 19 — the provision for defilement by death. Israel’s soldiers came back from obeying God and were unclean. Not guilty; unclean. There is no garland here, no parade, no suggestion that killing at God’s command left a man untouched by it. He had handled death, and death defiles whoever handles it, and he had to be washed before he could worship.

That single provision is one of the most humane things in the Old Testament, and it should be set against every triumphalist use this chapter has ever been put to. A religion that sends its soldiers home to a week outside the camp and a sprinkling of water is not a religion that glories in blood.

Eleazar adds the rule for the plunder: everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire… and whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water. Gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, lead — through the flame; everything else through the water. Nothing comes into the camp of God unpurified, and the test applied is the material’s own capacity to survive. Paul reaches for exactly this image for the day when every Christian’s work is examined: each one’s work will become manifest… because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done (1 Cor. 3:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plunder of the war is carefully divided — half to the soldiers, half to the congregation — and from each a tribute is set apart for the LORD and the Levites. Then the officers, having found not one man missing from their ranks, bring a freewill offering of gold to the LORD in gratitude. Even the spoils of war are consecrated; even victory is met with worship and thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.theology: A portion of everything is set apart “as a contribution to the LORD” (vv.28-29) — even the spoils of war belong first to God, who gave the victory (cf. 1 Chr 29:14). The officers’ freewill offering after finding no soldier lost (vv.48-50) is thanksgiving for God’s protecting hand. Victory is received as grace and returned in worship; the God who wins the battle is given the glory and the firstfruits of its reward.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: not a single Israelite soldier had fallen, and the grateful officers brought their gold to the LORD in thanks for his protection.

Now: every victory, every safe deliverance, calls for worship and thanksgiving. What we receive from God’s hand we return to him in gratitude, for “from you comes all things, and of your own have we given you” (1 Chr 29:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take the count of the plunder that was taken, both of man and of beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation, and divide the plunder into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation. And levy for the LORD a tribute from the men of war who went out to battle, one out of five hundred, of the people and of the oxen and of the donkeys and of the flocks. Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as a contribution to the LORD. And from the people of Israel's half you shall take one drawn out of every fifty, of the people, of the oxen, of the donkeys, and of the flocks, of all the cattle, and give them to the Levites who keep guard over the tabernacle of the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The division of the spoil is governed by two principles, and both of them are fairer than anybody would have arranged on their own.

First, the plunder is split into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation. Twelve thousand men did the fighting; half the proceeds go to the other five hundred and ninety thousand who stayed at home. That is a startling concession, and it is exactly the ruling David will make centuries later when his soldiers want to cut out the men who guarded the baggage: as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage; they shall share alike (1 Sam. 30:24). The people of God share the outcome of a work that only some of them were able to do.

Second, the tribute to God is levied unequally, and in the direction nobody would expect. The men who fought give one out of five hundred; the congregation who stayed home gives one drawn out of every fifty — ten times as much. The ones who bore the risk are taxed at a tenth of the rate of the ones who did not. God’s arithmetic takes account of what a thing cost the giver, which is precisely the principle Jesus applies while watching a widow put in two small coins: they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had (Mark 12:44).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the plunder remaining of the spoil that the army took was 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 persons in all, women who had not known man by lying with him. And the half, the portion of those who had gone out in the army, numbered 337,500 sheep, and the LORD's tribute of sheep was 675. The cattle were 36,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 72. The donkeys were 30,500, of which the LORD's tribute was 61. The persons were 16,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 32 persons. And Moses gave the tribute, which was the contribution for the LORD, to Eleazar the priest, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the accounts, in full: 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 captives, halved down the middle and the LORD’s tribute worked out to the animal — 675 sheep, 72 cattle, 61 donkeys, 32 persons.

Modern readers skim it. Consider instead who is doing the counting: you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the congregation. The lawgiver, the high priest and the tribal heads together, in public, with the figures written down to the last head of livestock. No single man handles it and nothing is taken on trust.

That is not incidental to the story of a religious community. It is exactly the standard Paul held himself to when carrying the church’s money: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Cor. 8:20–21). Wherever God’s people handle wealth, the books are to be open. A ledger is a spiritual document.

verseByVerse.quote: From the people of Israel's half, which Moses separated from that of the men who had served in the army— now the congregation's half was 337,500 sheep, 36,000 cattle, and 30,500 donkeys, and 16,000 persons— from the people of Israel's half Moses took one of every 50, both of persons and of beasts, and gave them to the Levites who kept guard over the tabernacle of the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The congregation’s half is listed again with the same precision — 337,500 sheep, 36,000 cattle, 30,500 donkeys, 16,000 persons — and out of it Moses takes one in fifty and gave them to the Levites who kept guard over the tabernacle of the LORD.

The Levites did not fight, did not travel, and own no land anywhere in Israel; and out of a war they took no part in, they are given a portion. That is the pattern the whole book has been laying down. The tribe with no inheritance is provided for by the inheritance of everyone else, so that men can stand at the tabernacle full time and Israel can be a worshipping nation.

And notice the rate. The soldiers hand over one in five hundred; the congregation, one in fifty; and out of the congregation’s share the Levites are paid. The tribe that carried no weapon, took no risk and owned no ground comes out of this battle with a portion, because the arrangement of chapter 18 does not lapse just because the nation happens to be at war. God’s provision for the men who serve at his tent is not suspended by circumstances, and it is not funded out of what is left over. It is a line item.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officers who were over the thousands of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, came near to Moses and said to Moses, "Your servants have counted the men of war who are under our command, and there is not a man missing from us. And we have brought the LORD's offering, what each man found, articles of gold, armlets and bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and beads, to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest received from them the gold, all crafted articles. And all the gold of the contribution that they presented to the LORD, from the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, was 16,750 shekels. (The men in the army had each taken plunder for himself.) And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and brought it into the tent of meeting, as a memorial for the people of Israel before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers come to Moses with a report and an offering, and both are remarkable.

The report first: Your servants have counted the men of war who are under our command, and there is not a man missing from us. Twelve thousand men went out against five kings and twelve thousand came back. They had counted, which is what commanders do after a battle, and the number matched. In an ancient war that is not luck and they did not think it was.

Then the offering, and it is the surprising part. Men who have won a total victory without a single casualty do not usually respond like this: we have brought the LORD’s offering, what each man found, articles of gold, armlets and bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and beads, to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD. Atonement. Not thanksgiving — atonement. They had lost nobody, and their instinct was that they needed covering.

These are the men who had spent a week outside the camp being sprinkled with the water for impurity, and they had understood what it meant. Coming home alive is not a verdict on your worthiness. Twenty-four thousand of their countrymen had died at Peor and these twelve thousand had not, and the difference was mercy and nothing else. So they emptied their pockets of the gold they had picked up on the battlefield and gave it away.

Sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels of it, brought into the tent of meeting, as a memorial for the people of Israel before the LORD. Not melted down, not spent, not made into anything — laid up in God’s house as a reminder. So the last act of the last war Moses ever ordered was a pile of enemy jewellery in the tabernacle, put there by soldiers who came home whole and could think of nothing to say about it except that they had been spared and had not earned it. There are worse epitaphs for a campaign, and there is no better posture for anybody who has come through something they did not deserve to come through.

32.title: The Tribes East of Jordan: The Danger of Settling for Less
32.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Gad and the people of Reuben came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the chiefs of the congregation,<sup>3</sup>"Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon,<sup>4</sup>the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel, is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock."<sup>5</sup>And they said, "If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for a possession. Do not take us across the Jordan."<sup>6</sup>But Moses said to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben, "Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here?<sup>7</sup>Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land that the LORD has given them?<sup>8</sup>Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land.<sup>9</sup>For when they went up to the Valley of Eshcol and saw the land, they discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land that the LORD had given them.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled on that day, and he swore, saying,<sup>11</sup>'Surely none of the men who came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, because they have not wholly followed me,<sup>12</sup>none except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun, for they have wholly followed the LORD.'<sup>13</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone.<sup>14</sup>And behold, you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel!<sup>15</sup>For if you turn away from following him, he will again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people."<sup>16</sup>Then they came near to him and said, "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones,<sup>17</sup>but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel, until we have brought them to their place. And our little ones shall live in the fortified cities because of the inhabitants of the land.<sup>18</sup>We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance.<sup>19</sup>For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan to the east."<sup>20</sup>So Moses said to them, "If you will do this, if you will take up arms to go before the LORD for the war,<sup>21</sup>and every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the LORD, until he has driven out his enemies from before him<sup>22</sup>and the land is subdued before the LORD; then after that you shall return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel, and this land shall be your possession before the LORD.<sup>23</sup>But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out.<sup>24</sup>Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep, and do what you have promised."<sup>25</sup>And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben said to Moses, "Your servants will do as my lord commands.<sup>26</sup>Our little ones, our wives, our livestock, and all our cattle shall remain there in the cities of Gilead,<sup>27</sup>but your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before the LORD to battle, as my lord orders."<sup>28</sup>So Moses gave command concerning them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel.<sup>29</sup>And Moses said to them, "If the people of Gad and the people of Reuben, every man who is armed to battle before the LORD, will pass with you over the Jordan and the land shall be subdued before you, then you shall give them the land of Gilead for a possession.<sup>30</sup>However, if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan."<sup>31</sup>And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben answered, "What the LORD has said to your servants, we will do.<sup>32</sup>We will pass over armed before the LORD into the land of Canaan, and the possession of our inheritance shall remain with us beyond the Jordan."<sup>33</sup>And Moses gave to them, to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben and to the half-tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph, the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, the land and its cities with their territories, the cities of the land throughout the country.<sup>34</sup>And the people of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer,<sup>35</sup>Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah,<sup>36</sup>Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran, fortified cities, and folds for sheep.<sup>37</sup>And the people of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim,<sup>38</sup>Nebo, and Baal-meon (their names were changed), and Sibmah. And they gave other names to the cities that they built.<sup>39</sup>And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and dispossessed the Amorites who were in it.<sup>40</sup>And Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh, and he settled in it.<sup>41</sup>And Jair the son of Manasseh went and captured their villages, and called them Havvoth-jair.<sup>42</sup>And Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages, and called it Nobah, after his own name.
32.overview:
As Israel stands at the edge of the Promised Land, the tribes of Reuben and Gad, who own great herds of livestock, look at the rich grazing lands east of the Jordan and ask to settle there — short of Canaan, short of the inheritance God had promised across the river. “Do not take us across the Jordan,” they say. It is a request that troubles Moses deeply, for it echoes the very sin that doomed the previous generation: a reluctance to enter the land God had given, a settling for less than the fullness of the promise.

Moses' rebuke is sharp: “Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here? Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land?” He fears a repeat of Kadesh-barnea, where unbelief spread like a contagion and a whole generation forfeited the inheritance. Keller often warned of this temptation — to settle on the near side of the river, to take the good pasture in hand rather than press on into the fuller blessing God has promised. The danger is not always open rebellion; sometimes it is the quiet contentment with a lesser good that keeps us from the greater one God intends.

Yet the chapter resolves not in condemnation but in a covenant of responsibility. Reuben and Gad agree that their fighting men will cross the Jordan and fight alongside their brothers until the whole land is subdued, only then returning to their eastern holdings. The settlement is granted on the condition that they not abandon their brothers in the battle. Wenham notes the principle of solidarity: the people of God advance together, and no tribe may enjoy its rest while its brothers still fight. And the warning rings out as one of the most memorable lines in Scripture: “Be sure your sin will find you out” (v. 23). Ferguson notes the abiding truth — sin is never finally hidden; what is done in the dark comes to light before God. The chapter calls us both to press on to the full inheritance Christ has promised and never to settle on the near bank, and to keep faith with our brothers and sisters until the whole work is done.
32.theology:
The danger of settling for less. Reuben and Gad nearly settle short of the inheritance. We are tempted to be content with a lesser good rather than press into the fullness God promises in Christ.

Solidarity in the battle. No tribe may enjoy rest while the brothers still fight. The people of God advance together, keeping faith with one another until the whole work is done.

Your sin will find you out. Sin is never finally hidden; what is done in the dark comes to light before God. Hidden disobedience is always exposed in the end.
32.examples:
Then: Reuben and Gad sought to settle east of the Jordan but were bound by covenant to fight alongside their brothers until all Israel received its inheritance.

Now: Do not settle on the near bank, content with a lesser good while the full inheritance of Christ lies across the river. Press on, keep faith with your brothers and sisters in the battle, and remember: your sin will find you out, for nothing is hidden from God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Request of Reuben and Gad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tribes of Reuben and Gad, rich in livestock, see the good grazing land east of the Jordan and ask to settle there rather than crossing into Canaan. Moses reacts sharply: is this not exactly what the spies did a generation ago — discouraging their brothers from entering the land, and bringing God’s judgment on the whole nation? He fears their request is a refusal to share in the conquest, a repeat of the old unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ alarm (vv.6-15) is that settling short of the promise, and leaving the brothers to fight alone, would “discourage the heart of the people” as the spies once did (v.7-9). The great sin of the wilderness generation was unbelief that would not enter and that spread its fear to others. The passage warns against contentment with a lesser inheritance and against a self-interest that abandons the family of God to struggle alone (cf. Gal 6:2, “bear one another’s burdens”).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses feared that seeking their own comfort while their brothers fought would repeat the spies’ sin and infect the whole camp with discouragement.

Now: beware settling for less than God’s full purpose, and beware a comfort that leaves your brothers to carry the battle alone. “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock. So the people of Gad and the people of Reuben came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the chiefs of the congregation, "Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon, the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel, is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock." And they said, "If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for a possession. Do not take us across the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch the order of the sentences, because the order is the whole diagnosis. Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock. The possessions come first. Then the looking. Then the wanting. Then the request.

And listen to how they put it to Moses. They name nine towns, they observe that the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel is a land for livestock, and they add — twice — your servants have livestock. There is not one word about the promise to Abraham, nothing about their brothers, nothing about the crossing. The entire case is built out of an inventory.

Then the five words that alarm Moses: Do not take us across the Jordan.

Be fair to them before condemning them. This land was not forbidden; God had given it to Israel in chapter 21, and Moses will in fact grant the request. Their instinct was not wicked and their situation was real — they had enormous herds and here was enormous grass. But something has quietly reversed. They had walked forty years toward a promise, and having found excellent pasture within sight of it, they asked to stop. The danger to a believer is almost never a decision to abandon God. It is the discovery of somewhere comfortable a few miles short, and the slow conversion of a stopping place into a home.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben, "Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here? Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land that the LORD has given them? Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land. For when they went up to the Valley of Eshcol and saw the land, they discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land that the LORD had given them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses answers with a question that has been quoted in every generation since: Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here?

He does not begin with their motives or their livestock. He begins with the other eleven tribes. Whatever Reuben and Gad had thought about, they had not thought about the men who would be crossing the river without them into fortified cities — the same amount of fighting, distributed across fewer shoulders.

And his real fear is in the next verse: Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over? The Hebrew is stronger than discourage; it is to make the heart melt, to dissolve a man’s nerve. Moses is not chiefly worried about two missing regiments. He is worried about what everybody else will conclude when they see that crossing turned out to be optional. Then he names the precedent: Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea. Ten men came back from the Valley of Eshcol and melted the heart of a nation, and it cost forty years and six hundred thousand graves.

That is a sobering thing to weigh. The ten spies did not force anyone to do anything. They simply described their own reluctance out loud, in public, with conviction — and a nation went to pieces. Nobody in the church makes a private decision about how much of God’s call they intend to obey. Somebody is always watching, and taking the measure of what is apparently allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD's anger was kindled on that day, and he swore, saying, 'Surely none of the men who came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, because they have not wholly followed me, none except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun, for they have wholly followed the LORD.' And the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone. And behold, you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel! For if you turn away from following him, he will again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses then tells the whole Kadesh story again — the oath, the exclusion of everyone over twenty, the two exceptions, the forty years, the generation that died — and he tells it to men who were children when it happened and have lived under its sentence their entire lives.

Notice the reason God gave for the sentence, quoted here twice in two verses: because they have not wholly followed me, and of Caleb and Joshua, for they have wholly followed the LORD. The Hebrew phrase means to fill up after him, to follow all the way. The condemned generation had not renounced God. They had followed him partially, and stopped where it got frightening. And Moses is looking at two tribes proposing to follow as far as the river and no further.

Then the sharpest words in the chapter: And behold, you have risen in your fathers’ place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel!… you will destroy all this people. That is not measured diplomacy, and Moses is not a hot-tempered man at this point in his life; he is a man of a hundred and twenty who has buried a generation and cannot bear to watch it begin again.

And his final charge is the one that a modern reader instinctively resists: you will destroy all this people. He holds two tribes responsible for what their choice would do to the other ten. There is no private discipleship in Scripture. If one member suffers, all suffer together (1 Cor. 12:26), and Paul flatly denies that any believer is his own man: none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself (Rom. 14:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reuben and Gad answer Moses’ fear with a pledge: they will build folds for their flocks and towns for their families, but they themselves will arm and go ahead of their brothers into battle, and not return to their inheritance until all Israel has received theirs. Moses accepts, but with a solemn warning: “be sure your sin will find you out.” Their inheritance is granted — on the condition that they keep their word and share the fight.
verseByVerse.theology: The tribes’ pledge to fight alongside their brothers before enjoying their own rest resolves Moses’ concern: they will not abandon the family of God. Moses’ warning, “be sure your sin will find you out” (v.23), is a timeless truth — a broken vow, a shirked duty, will not stay hidden; God sees, and consequences follow (cf. Gal 6:7, “whatever one sows, that will he also reap”). Solidarity with the brothers and integrity of one’s word are the conditions of the blessing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the two tribes promised to fight for their brothers first and rest afterward — and were warned that a broken promise would surely find them out.

Now: “be sure your sin will find you out” (v.23) is as true as ever. God sees the vow we keep and the one we break; “whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Gal 6:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they came near to him and said, "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones, but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel, until we have brought them to their place. And our little ones shall live in the fortified cities because of the inhabitants of the land. We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance. For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan to the east."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their reply is one of the best moments in the book. They do not argue, do not defend themselves against a brood of sinful men, and do not withdraw the request. They come nearer and improve it.

We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones, but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel — and not merely go, but go before them, in the front rank, taking the first of whatever was coming. And then the sentence that settles the matter: We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance.

Take the measure of that promise. They already have their land. Nothing on the far bank will ever belong to them. They are committing themselves and their sons to a war of conquest that will run for years, for the sole purpose of getting other families into fields they will never set foot in, and they will not go home until the last tribe is settled. Joshua records the discharge seven years later: You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God (Josh. 22:3). They kept it to the letter.

That is what a Christian is called into. Not merely securing your own standing with God and then watching from the east bank, but crossing over on behalf of people whose inheritance will never be yours, and staying until they have it. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others (Phil. 2:4).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said to them, "If you will do this, if you will take up arms to go before the LORD for the war, and every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the LORD, until he has driven out his enemies from before him and the land is subdued before the LORD; then after that you shall return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel, and this land shall be your possession before the LORD. But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out. Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep, and do what you have promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses accepts, and spells the terms out with a lawyer’s precision: armed, over the Jordan, before the LORD, until the land is subdued — then after that you shall return and be free of obligation. And then the warning that has passed into the language, and is almost always quoted wrongly: But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out.

It is usually heard as your secret sins will eventually come to light, which is a true thing the Bible says elsewhere (Luke 12:2) but is not what this verse says. Here the sin is pictured as a pursuer. If these men break this promise, the broken promise will hunt them down and catch them. Sin is not a stain waiting to be discovered; it is a creditor on the road behind you, and it knows your name. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal. 6:7).

And then a small, easily missed correction. They had said, we will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones. Moses replies: Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep. He gives them back their own sentence with the order reversed. They had put the animals first; he puts the children first. Not a syllable of rebuke, just the words rearranged — and any man who has ever let his work quietly take precedence over his family knows exactly what has been done to him in that verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben said to Moses, "Your servants will do as my lord commands. Our little ones, our wives, our livestock, and all our cattle shall remain there in the cities of Gilead, but your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before the LORD to battle, as my lord orders." So Moses gave command concerning them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel. And Moses said to them, "If the people of Gad and the people of Reuben, every man who is armed to battle before the LORD, will pass with you over the Jordan and the land shall be subdued before you, then you shall give them the land of Gilead for a possession. However, if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan." And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben answered, "What the LORD has said to your servants, we will do. We will pass over armed before the LORD into the land of Canaan, and the possession of our inheritance shall remain with us beyond the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The agreement is not left as a handshake. Moses gave command concerning them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers’ houses, restates the terms in front of them, and adds the consequence of failure: if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan — that is, they forfeit the east bank altogether and take their chances with everyone else.

So the arrangement is witnessed by the incoming leadership, binding on both parties, enforceable after Moses is dead, and with the penalty defined in advance. Moses is a man with weeks to live, dealing with people who have just made him a fine promise, and he writes it down and hands it to somebody who will still be alive to enforce it.

That is not cynicism about their sincerity. It is realism about human memory. Good intentions expressed in a moment of conviction have a way of thinning out over seven years of war while your family is three hundred miles away. Reuben and Gad were helped enormously by the fact that somebody had put their promise beyond the reach of their own later feelings — which is precisely why God gives his people vows, covenants and public ceremonies rather than leaving everything to the state of the heart on the day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–42 — The Settlement of the Transjordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land east of the Jordan is given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, and they set about building and fortifying their cities. The agreement is sealed and the settlement begins. The eastern tribes have their portion — with the obligation still binding them to cross over and fight for the rest.
verseByVerse.theology: The settlement (vv.33-42) records the fulfillment of the agreement — land granted, cities built, on the understanding that the pledge will be honored. It shows God accommodating the real circumstances of his people while holding them to their commitments. The Transjordan tribes would later be commended for keeping their word (Josh 22:1-4), a reminder that faithfulness to promises made before God is not optional.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the eastern tribes received and built their inheritance — bound still by their promise to fight for their brothers before enjoying it.

Now: God grants us much, and holds us to our commitments. Received blessing does not release us from promised duty; faithfulness follows us into our rest.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses gave to them, to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben and to the half-tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph, the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, the land and its cities with their territories, the cities of the land throughout the country. And the people of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer, Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah, Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran, fortified cities, and folds for sheep. And the people of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim, Nebo, and Baal-meon (their names were changed), and Sibmah. And they gave other names to the cities that they built.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land is granted, and the two and a half tribes set about building. Then a detail that is easy to read past: they rebuild Nebo and Baal-meon, their names being changed, and Sibmah, and they gave other names to the cities that they built.

They renamed the towns because of what the old names meant. Nebo was a Babylonian god. Baal-meon means lord of the dwelling — Baal, in the title deeds of the town they now lived in. These families had watched twenty-four thousand of their countrymen die at Baal of Peor a few weeks earlier, and they were not going to raise their children in a place with that name over the gate. God had said, make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips (Exod. 23:13), and they took him seriously enough to repaint the signposts.

Taking possession of anything for God has always involved that kind of renaming. A believer comes into an inherited situation — a family, a business, a set of habits, a house — and finds somebody else’s name written over the door of it. Leaving the name up because it was there first is how a place quietly stays what it always was.

verseByVerse.quote: And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and dispossessed the Amorites who were in it. And Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh, and he settled in it. And Jair the son of Manasseh went and captured their villages, and called them Havvoth-jair. And Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages, and called it Nobah, after his own name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with three men and their conquests: Machir takes Gilead, Jair takes the villages and calls them Havvoth-jair, Nobah takes Kenath and called it Nobah, after his own name. The land is settled, the fences go up, and the tribes east of the Jordan are home.

Was it a mistake? Scripture does not say so, and we should not say more than Scripture. Moses granted it, God permitted it, and Joshua later commended these men in the warmest terms for keeping every word of the bargain (Josh. 22:2–4). But the later history is sober reading. The eastern tribes were outside the river that protected everybody else, first in the path of every invasion from the east, and when the Assyrian came it was Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh who went into exile first (1 Chr. 5:26). Good grass, and no river in front of it. There is nothing here to condemn and a great deal to think about, and the chapter leaves it exactly there.

What it does not leave in doubt is the promise these men made and kept. They crossed a river they did not need to cross, fought a war they had nothing to gain from, and stayed at it until every last family in Israel was standing on its own ground. Only then did they go home. And that is the shape of something far greater than themselves, because there is a Captain who has already entered his rest and has not stopped working, and who has said plainly what he is doing in the meantime: I go to prepare a place for you… I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also (John 14:2–3). He will not go home until every one of his brothers has his inheritance.

33.title: The Stages of the Journey: Every Step Known to God
33.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the stages of the people of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their companies under the leadership of Moses and Aaron.<sup>2</sup>Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD, and these are their stages according to their starting places.<sup>3</sup>They set out from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the day after the Passover, the people of Israel went out triumphantly in the sight of all the Egyptians,<sup>4</sup>while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck down among them. On their gods also the LORD executed judgments.<sup>5</sup>So the people of Israel set out from Rameses and camped at Succoth.<sup>6</sup>And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, which is on pass over the Jordan into the land of Canaan,<sup>52</sup>then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you and destroy all their figured stones and destroy all their metal images and demolish all their high places.<sup>53</sup>And you shall take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given the land to you to possess it.<sup>54</sup>You shall inherit the land by lot according to your clans. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance. Wherever the lot falls for anyone, that shall be his. According to the tribes of your fathers you shall inherit.<sup>55</sup>But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those of them whom you let remain shall be as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land where you dwell.<sup>56</sup>And I will do to you as I thought to do to them."
33.overview:
Chapter 33 is a travelogue — a careful record of every place Israel camped on the long journey from Egypt to the plains of Moab, forty-two stages in all. To the casual reader it is a dry list of unpronounceable place names. But Moses “wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD.” This itinerary is no accident; God commanded it to be recorded. And in that lies a truth of profound comfort: every single stage of the journey, every campsite, every weary mile, was known to God and noted by him.

Think of what these names contain. Some recall great deliverances; some recall bitter failures — Taberah where the fire fell, Kibroth-hattaavah where the cravers were buried, Kadesh where the spies brought their faithless report. The whole forty years, the triumphs and the tragedies, are gathered up in this list. Ferguson notes that God keeps the record of his people's pilgrimage; not one stage is lost or forgotten. The God who led them by cloud and fire also remembered every place they stopped. Their entire history is held in his hand.

And here is the application that should send warmth through the heart: your life is such an itinerary. Every stage of your pilgrimage — the green pastures and the dark valleys, the mountaintops and the wilderness wanderings, the places of joy and the places of failure — is known to God, written in his book, held in his care. Keller often drew comfort from this: the God who recorded every campsite of Israel records every step of your journey, and he is leading you, stage by stage, to the inheritance. “You keep track of all my sorrows. You have collected all my tears in your bottle” (Ps 56:8). Not one mile of your wilderness is wasted or forgotten. The same faithful God who brought Israel from Egypt to the edge of Canaan is bringing you home, and he knows the way you take.
33.theology:
Every stage known to God. God commanded the itinerary recorded, for every campsite of the journey was known and noted by him. Not one mile of the pilgrimage is lost or forgotten.

The redeemed are pilgrims. The rhythm of setting out and camping marks a people always on the move toward the promise, led by God from redemption to inheritance.

Wholehearted obedience. The idols not removed become thorns; sin tolerated becomes a snare. God's people are called to put to death the sins they are tempted to spare.
33.examples:
Then: God commanded Moses to record every stage of Israel's journey, from the deliverance in Egypt to the plains of Moab, every campsite known and noted by the Lord.

Now: Your life is such an itinerary. Every stage of your pilgrimage — the green pastures and the dark valleys, the joys and the failures — is known to God and held in his care. He has collected all your tears, and he is leading you, stage by stage, home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–49 — The Stages of the Journey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses writes down the whole itinerary of the wilderness years, camp by camp, from Rameses in Egypt to the plains of Moab — forty-two stages in all. It reads like a dry list of place-names, but it is something far richer: a record of every step of the way God led his people. He kept the log himself, through Moses’ pen, because not one stage of the journey was forgotten by God, and not one was outside his leading.
verseByVerse.theology: The recorded itinerary (vv.1-49) is a memorial of God’s faithful leading through every stage of the journey, the good camps and the bitter ones alike. That God had Moses write it all down testifies that he remembers the whole pilgrimage of his people — every step, every camp, every hardship (cf. Deut 8:2, “remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you”). None of it was aimless; the God who led by cloud and fire (9:15-23) was writing a purposeful story, stage by stage, all the way home.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: forty years of wandering were recorded camp by camp — every stage of the hard road kept in God’s remembrance.

Now: God remembers every stage of your journey too — the green pastures and the bitter waters alike. Look back and “remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you” (Deut 8:2); none of it was wasted or forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the stages of the people of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their companies under the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD, and these are their stages according to their starting places. They set out from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the day after the Passover, the people of Israel went out triumphantly in the sight of all the Egyptians, while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck down among them. On their gods also the LORD executed judgments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD. Before a single place-name, the chapter tells us who commissioned the list. This is not a travel diary Moses kept for himself. God told him to write it down.

That is the reason to read a chapter of forty-two campsites. Somewhere on the plains of Moab an old man sat with a record of every place his people had ever pitched a tent — including the places he would rather have forgotten, the ones named after failures, the stretches where nothing happened for years — and God said: put it all in. Nothing was too tedious and nothing too shameful to keep.

And notice where the record starts. Not with the wilderness but with a funeral in Egypt: the people of Israel went out triumphantly in the sight of all the Egyptians, while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn. The first line of the itinerary is redemption by the blood of a lamb, the night after Passover, with an empire in mourning behind them and its gods judged. Every stage that follows is the journey of a people who were bought out. So is every stage of yours. Whatever else is written on the list, the first entry is the same for all of them.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people of Israel set out from Rameses and camped at Succoth. And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, which is on the edge of the wilderness. And they set out from Etham and turned back to Pi-hahiroth, which is east of Baal-zephon, and they camped before Migdol. And they set out from before Hahiroth and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, and they went a three days' journey in the wilderness of Etham and camped at Marah. And they set out from Marah and came to Elim; at Elim there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there. And they set out from Elim and camped by the Red Sea. And they set out from the Red Sea and camped in the wilderness of Sin. And they set out from the wilderness of Sin and camped at Dophkah. And they set out from Dophkah and camped at Alush. And they set out from Alush and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. And they set out from Rephidim and camped in the wilderness of Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The early stages come fast — Succoth, Etham, Pi-hahiroth, and then, in eleven words, they set out from before Hahiroth and passed through the midst of the sea. The greatest miracle of the Old Testament is entered in the register between two campsites, in the same tone as everything else, as though it were a Tuesday.

Then Marah, where the water was bitter; then Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. That is the only descriptive detail in the whole chapter, and it is a green one. A man writing an itinerary forty years later still remembered the shade at Elim and how many springs there were, and thought it worth the ink.

Read the two together, because they came one after the other and always do. Bitter water, and then twelve springs. God does not run his people through Marah because he has nothing better, and he does not park them at Elim because the journey is over. Israel camped at both and set out from both, and the line under each entry is identical: and they set out. Nobody stays at Elim. Nobody stays at Marah either.

verseByVerse.quote: And they set out from the wilderness of Sinai and camped at Kibroth-hattaavah. And they set out from Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth. And they set out from Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah. And they set out from Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-perez. And they set out from Rimmon-perez and camped at Libnah. And they set out from Libnah and camped at Rissah. And they set out from Rissah and camped at Kehelathah. And they set out from Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher. And they set out from Mount Shepher and camped at Haradah. And they set out from Haradah and camped at Makheloth. And they set out from Makheloth and camped at Tahath. And they set out from Tahath and camped at Terah. And they set out from Terah and camped at Mithkah. And they set out from Mithkah and camped at Hashmonah. And they set out from Hashmonah and camped at Moseroth. And they set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan. And they set out from Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-haggidgad. And they set out from Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah. And they set out from Jotbathah and camped at Abronah. And they set out from Abronah and camped at Ezion-geber. And they set out from Ezion-geber and camped in the wilderness of Zin (that is, Kadesh). And they set out from Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor, on the edge of the land of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-two verses now pass in which almost nothing is said. And they set out from Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth. And they set out from Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah… Name after name, most of them mentioned nowhere else in the Bible and located nowhere on any map we possess. This is the wilderness generation, and this is what those thirty-eight years actually consisted of.

A few of the names still carry their stories. Kibroth-hattaavah means the graves of craving — where the people demanded meat and were buried in it (11:34). Hazeroth is where Miriam and Aaron turned on Moses (12:1). And verse 36 arrives at the wilderness of Zin (that is, Kadesh), which is where the whole thing went wrong and where, decades later, they were still standing.

But most of the list is unremarkable, and that is its value. Between the disasters and the deliverances lay years of ordinary marching that produced no story at all — and God had every one of those camps written into his book. There is a strange comfort in a page of forgotten place-names. It says that the stretches of a life in which nothing happens are not gaps in the record. They are the record. He was there at Rithmah too.

verseByVerse.quote: And Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the command of the LORD and died there, in the fortieth year after the people of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, on the first day of the fifth month. And Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor. And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb in the land of Canaan, heard of the coming of the people of Israel. And they set out from Mount Hor and camped at Zalmonah. And they set out from Zalmonah and camped at Punon. And they set out from Punon and camped at Oboth. And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the territory of Moab. And they set out from Iyim and camped at Dibon-gad. And they set out from Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim. And they set out from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo. And they set out from the mountains of Abarim and camped in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho; they camped by the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only once does the list stop for an event, and it stops here. And Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the command of the LORD and died there, in the fortieth year… on the first day of the fifth month. And Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor. The year, the month, the day, the age. An itinerary of a whole nation halts to date the death of one man to the afternoon. God counts the stages, and he also counts the men who do not finish them.

From Mount Hor the road turns at last toward the river: Zalmonah, Punon, Oboth, and on up the eastern side to the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. The list ends exactly where the reader is standing. Every name in the chapter has been leading here.

And it ends on the wrong side of the water. Forty-two stages, forty years, and the final entry is a camp within sight of the land and not in it. The itinerary of Israel closes at a riverbank, which is precisely where the book of Numbers closes, and where Moses will die.

Hebrews reads the whole Old Testament this way and does not pretend otherwise: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb. 11:13). Every believer’s list ends at a riverbank of some sort. The question the chapter puts is not whether you will get all the way in during this life, but whether the record God is keeping of your stages is the record of somebody who went out from Egypt and kept setting out.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Israel prepares to enter Canaan, God commands them to drive out its inhabitants and destroy their idols, and to divide the land by lot. The warning is stark: if they leave the peoples in the land, those they spare will become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides.” Compromise with the idolatry of the land will not be harmless; it will be a lasting wound.
verseByVerse.theology: The command to dispossess the Canaanites and destroy their idols (vv.51-53) guards Israel from the idolatry that would later ruin them. The warning that spared enemies become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” (v.55) proved tragically true in Judges. It teaches the abiding principle that tolerated sin does not stay contained but festers and wounds — a lesson the New Testament applies to the sin we must put to death in ourselves (Col 3:5; Rom 8:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel was warned that the idolatry they tolerated would become thorns in their sides — and in Judges it happened exactly so.

Now: the sin we spare in ourselves does not stay quiet; it becomes a thorn and a snare. “Put to death... what is earthly in you” (Col 3:5) — tolerated sin always wounds in the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Canaan, then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you and destroy all their figured stones and destroy all their metal images and demolish all their high places. And you shall take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given the land to you to possess it. You shall inherit the land by lot according to your clans. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance. Wherever the lot falls for anyone, that shall be his. According to the tribes of your fathers you shall inherit. But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those of them whom you let remain shall be as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land where you dwell. And I will do to you as I thought to do to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns from history to command, and the command is total: you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you and destroy all their figured stones and destroy all their metal images and demolish all their high places. Not tolerate, not regulate, not co-exist with — destroy. Israel had just watched twenty-four thousand of her own people die because a few Moabite women invited them to dinner. God is not going to leave the shrines standing.

Then the warning, and it is the sentence Israel’s entire subsequent history is written to illustrate: But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those of them whom you let remain shall be as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land where you dwell.

Look at the two images, because they are not chosen carelessly. A barb in the eye: something small, permanently painful, that ruins your sight. A thorn in the side: something you cannot reach, that catches every time you move. Neither is fatal. Both are unbearable, and neither goes away on its own. That is exactly what a tolerated sin does to a believer — it is never the thing that kills him, and it is always the thing that stops him seeing straight and makes every step hurt. Judges 1 and 2 are the record of Israel doing precisely what she was warned about here, and Judges 2:3 quotes this verse back at her.

The last line is the most sobering in the chapter: And I will do to you as I thought to do to them. Israel had no immunity. If she took up the sins the Canaanites were being judged for, she would be judged for the same sins, by the same God, and the exile proved it. Being on the right side of the covenant was never a licence; it was a calling. Which is why Paul, writing to Christians, takes the very same tone: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you (Col. 3:5). Not manage it. Not fence it. Put it to death — because the alternative is not neutrality, it is a barb in the eye for the rest of your life.

34.title: The Boundaries of Canaan: The Specificity of God's Promise
34.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel, and say to them, When you enter the land of Canaan (this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders),<sup>3</sup>your south side shall be from the wilderness of Zin alongside Edom, and your southern border shall run from the end of the Salt Sea on the east.<sup>4</sup>And your border shall turn south of the ascent of Akrabbim, and cross to Zin, and its limit shall be south of Kadesh-barnea. Then it shall go on to Hazar-addar, and pass along to Azmon.<sup>5</sup>And the border shall turn from Azmon to the Brook of Egypt, and its limit shall be at the sea.<sup>6</sup>"For the western border, you shall have the Great Sea and its coast. This shall be your western border.<sup>7</sup>"This shall be your northern border: from the Great Sea you shall draw a line to Mount Hor.<sup>8</sup>From Mount Hor you shall draw a line to Lebo-hamath, and the limit of the border shall be at Zedad.<sup>9</sup>Then the border shall extend to Ziphron, and its limit shall be at Hazar-enan. This shall be your northern border.<sup>10</sup>"You shall draw a line for your eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham.<sup>11</sup>And the border shall go down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain. And the border shall go down and reach to the shoulder of the Sea of Chinnereth on the east.<sup>12</sup>And the border shall go down to the Jordan, and its limit shall be at the Salt Sea. This shall be your land as defined by its borders all around."<sup>13</sup>Moses commanded the people of Israel, saying, "This is the land that you shall inherit by lot, which the LORD has commanded to give to the nine tribes and to the half-tribe.<sup>14</sup>For the tribe of the people of Reuben by fathers' houses and the tribe of the people of Gad by their fathers' houses have received their inheritance, and also the half-tribe of Manasseh.<sup>15</sup>The two tribes and the half-tribe have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, toward the sunrise."<sup>16</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"These are the names of the men who shall divide the land to you for inheritance: Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>18</sup>You shall take one chief from every tribe to divide the land for inheritance.<sup>19</sup>These are the names of the men: Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh.<sup>20</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud.<sup>21</sup>Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon.<sup>22</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Dan a chief, Bukki the son of Jogli.<sup>23</sup>Of the people of Joseph: of the tribe of the people of Manasseh a chief, Hanniel the son of Ephod.<sup>24</sup>And of the tribe of the people of Ephraim a chief, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan.<sup>25</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Zebulun a chief, Elizaphan the son of Parnach.<sup>26</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Issachar a chief, Paltiel the son of Azzan.<sup>27</sup>And of the tribe of the people of Asher a chief, Ahihud the son of Shelomi.<sup>28</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Naphtali a chief, Pedahel the son of Ammihud."<sup>29</sup>These are the men whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance for the people of Israel in the land of Canaan.
34.overview:
Before Israel has set a single foot in the land, God draws its borders. Chapter 34 maps out the boundaries of Canaan — the southern border, the western, the northern, the eastern — and names the leaders who will oversee the division of the inheritance among the tribes. There is something quietly glorious in this. God does not promise his people a vague, indefinite blessing; he defines the inheritance with precision, border by border, as a man marks out the deed to a property he is about to give.

The specificity is the point. Wenham notes that the careful delineation of borders reflects the concreteness and certainty of God's promise. This is not wishful thinking or a hazy ideal; it is a defined, surveyed, deeded inheritance. God speaks of it as already settled: “this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance.” The borders are drawn in advance because the gift is sure. The God who promises does not deal in vagueness; his promises have edges, dimensions, reality.

This is enormously comforting for the people of God in every age. The inheritance Christ has secured for us is not a vague hope but a definite reality, as concrete as a surveyed land with marked borders. Peter speaks of “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet 1:4) — reserved, defined, certain. Keller often pressed this: Christian hope is not generalized optimism but confidence in a specific, promised future secured by God. Just as God drew the borders of Canaan before Israel entered, so he has prepared and defined the place he is giving his people. Jesus said, “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2) — a real place, a definite inheritance. The God who maps the borders before the conquest is the God who has secured every detail of the inheritance that awaits all who are in Christ. The promise has edges, and they are drawn by his own faithful hand.
34.theology:
The specificity of God's promise. God draws the borders before Israel enters. His promises are not vague but definite, with edges and dimensions, as sure as a surveyed and deeded inheritance.

A reserved inheritance. The defined land prefigures the inheritance imperishable and undefiled, kept in heaven for God's people (1 Pet 1:4). Christ goes to prepare a real and definite place.

Divine apportioning. The land is divided by lot and by appointed leaders. God sovereignly assigns each his portion, ordering the inheritance by his own faithful hand.
34.examples:
Then: Before Israel entered, God drew the borders of Canaan and appointed leaders to divide the inheritance, defining the promised land with precision.

Now: Your inheritance in Christ is not a vague hope but a definite reality, with borders drawn by God's own hand. He has gone to prepare a real place for you, an inheritance kept in heaven, certain and secure. The promise has edges, and they are drawn by his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Boundaries of the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God traces the borders of the inheritance — south, west, north, and east — the land he is giving his people. He names its edges precisely, because this is no vague promise but a real, bounded gift, already mapped in the mind of God before Israel has set foot in it. The inheritance is definite, described, and secured by the word of the God who gives it.
verseByVerse.theology: God defines the land’s boundaries in detail (vv.1-12) — the inheritance is concrete and certain, “the land... that shall fall to you for an inheritance” (v.2). What God promises he specifies; his gifts are not vague sentiments but definite realities. The earthly inheritance, carefully bounded, points to the sure and “imperishable” inheritance God has mapped out for his people in Christ (1 Pet 1:4; John 14:2, “I go to prepare a place for you”).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: before Israel crossed over, God had already drawn the borders of their home — a definite, promised place waiting for them.

Now: our inheritance is just as certain and just as prepared: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2). God’s promises have addresses, not just sentiments.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel, and say to them, When you enter the land of Canaan (this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders), your south side shall be from the wilderness of Zin alongside Edom, and your southern border shall run from the end of the Salt Sea on the east. And your border shall turn south of the ascent of Akrabbim, and cross to Zin, and its limit shall be south of Kadesh-barnea. Then it shall go on to Hazar-addar, and pass along to Azmon. And the border shall turn from Azmon to the Brook of Egypt, and its limit shall be at the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders. Then a survey: from the wilderness of Zin along the edge of Edom, past the ascent of Akrabbim and south of Kadesh-barnea, on to Hazar-addar and Azmon and the Brook of Egypt, and out to the sea.

Two things about that are remarkable, and neither is the geography. The first is the tense. Israel does not own a square foot of this. There is a river in front of them and walled cities beyond it and not one Israelite has crossed. And God speaks of it as settled — the land that shall fall to you — and then does what a man does when a property is already his: he walks the boundary and names the corners.

The second is the precision. God does not promise his people a land. He gives them a surveyed one, with a southern border defined to the wadi, a coastline, and named turning points. Vagueness is a mark of promises nobody intends to keep. A man who is actually going to hand over a field tells you where the fence runs.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the western border, you shall have the Great Sea and its coast. This shall be your western border. "This shall be your northern border: from the Great Sea you shall draw a line to Mount Hor. From Mount Hor you shall draw a line to Lebo-hamath, and the limit of the border shall be at Zedad. Then the border shall extend to Ziphron, and its limit shall be at Hazar-enan. This shall be your northern border. "You shall draw a line for your eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham. And the border shall go down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain. And the border shall go down and reach to the shoulder of the Sea of Chinnereth on the east. And the border shall go down to the Jordan, and its limit shall be at the Salt Sea. This shall be your land as defined by its borders all around."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the survey: the Great Sea for the western border, a northern line running from the coast through Lebo-hamath to Hazar-enan, and an eastern border coming down past the Sea of Chinnereth — the lake we call Galilee — along the Jordan to the Salt Sea. This shall be your land as defined by its borders all around.

Most of these places cannot now be located with confidence, and that does not matter in the slightest for the point being made. What matters is that they could be located then. This is a legal description of a real estate, drawn before possession, and the whole thing is closed — all around. There is no open side.

Which is exactly the language the New Testament uses about the inheritance of a Christian, and it uses it deliberately. Peter, writing to people who owned very little and were about to lose that, describes what is waiting for them as an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Pet. 1:4). Kept. Reserved. Already under somebody’s guard. Heaven is not a mood or a vagueness; it is as definite as a surveyed coastline, and a great deal of the comfort of it lies in the fact that God speaks about it the way a man speaks about a deed he has already signed.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses commanded the people of Israel, saying, "This is the land that you shall inherit by lot, which the LORD has commanded to give to the nine tribes and to the half-tribe. For the tribe of the people of Reuben by fathers' houses and the tribe of the people of Gad by their fathers' houses have received their inheritance, and also the half-tribe of Manasseh. The two tribes and the half-tribe have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, toward the sunrise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses adds a note of accounting: this survey is for the nine tribes and… the half-tribe, because Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, toward the sunrise.

The eastern tribes are not written out of Israel; their portion is simply recorded as already settled, and the map that follows is drawn for everybody else. Two chapters ago they made a bargain, and here it is in the title deeds. God keeps the arrangements his people make before him.

But there is a wistful note in the phrasing that a careful reader will catch. The land being surveyed in this chapter is called the land of Canaan — the promise proper — and the eastern portion sits outside the survey, described by where it is in relation to somewhere else: beyond the Jordan, toward the sunrise. They have a real inheritance, granted by God and honoured by Moses. It is simply not inside the borders being drawn here. Scripture does not moralise about it, and neither should we. It merely draws the line where the line goes, and leaves two and a half tribes on the far side of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–29 — The Leaders Who Will Divide the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names the men who will oversee the dividing of the land — Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and a chief from each tribe. The distribution of the inheritance is entrusted to appointed, accountable leaders, so that it may be done rightly and fairly. Even the joyful task of parceling out the promise is done under God’s order, by men he has chosen.
verseByVerse.theology: God appoints named, accountable leaders — a priest, a commander, and a representative from each tribe — to divide the inheritance (vv.17-29). The orderly distribution under appointed authority reflects God’s character as a God “of peace” and order (1 Cor 14:33), not confusion. Even the good work of sharing out the promise is done through God-ordained structures, that all may be done “decently and in order” (1 Cor 14:40).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the land was divided not by a free-for-all but by appointed leaders, so that every tribe received its due fairly.

Now: God still works through appointed, accountable leadership, and loves order over chaos. His good gifts are distributed rightly, “decently and in order” (1 Cor 14:40).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "These are the names of the men who shall divide the land to you for inheritance: Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun. You shall take one chief from every tribe to divide the land for inheritance. These are the names of the men: Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Of the tribe of the people of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud. Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon. Of the tribe of the people of Dan a chief, Bukki the son of Jogli. Of the people of Joseph: of the tribe of the people of Manasseh a chief, Hanniel the son of Ephod. And of the tribe of the people of Ephraim a chief, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan. Of the tribe of the people of Zebulun a chief, Elizaphan the son of Parnach. Of the tribe of the people of Issachar a chief, Paltiel the son of Azzan. And of the tribe of the people of Asher a chief, Ahihud the son of Shelomi. Of the tribe of the people of Naphtali a chief, Pedahel the son of Ammihud." These are the men whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance for the people of Israel in the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a list of men: Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun, and one chief from each of the ten tribes who still need land, named individually, tribe by tribe, with their fathers’ names — Caleb the son of Jephunneh for Judah, Shemuel for Simeon, Elidad for Benjamin, and the rest.

God will not have the inheritance divided by an anonymous committee. Every man who will hold a measuring line over somebody else’s future is named in Scripture before he does it, along with the tribe he answers to. There is no way for one of these men to take a bribe or favour his own clan without the whole nation knowing exactly who did it. Accountability in God’s work is not a modern administrative virtue; it is here, in the last chapters of the Pentateuch, written into the arrangements from the start.

And stop on one of the names. Of the tribe of the people of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Forty-five years earlier this man walked into that same land as a spy, came back, and told a terrified nation let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it (13:30), and they picked up stones to kill him for it. He watched every man who disagreed with him die in the desert, one funeral at a time, for thirty-eight years. Now he is eighty and he is on the commission that will hand out the fields.

God had made him a promise about this land when nobody else believed a word of it (14:24), and here is the promise beginning to be paid, in a list of surveyors at the end of a chapter about borders. He is faithful to nations and to maps and to old men who were right and had to wait four decades to be shown it.

35.title: Cities of Refuge: A Place to Flee, a Death That Frees
35.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel to give to the Levites some of the inheritance of their possession as cities for them to dwell in. And you shall give to the Levites pasturelands around the cities.<sup>3</sup>The cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and their pasturelands shall be for their cattle and for their livestock and for all their beasts.<sup>4</sup>The pasturelands of the cities, which you shall give to the Levites, shall reach from the wall of the city outward a thousand cubits all around.<sup>5</sup>And you shall measure, outside the city, on the east side two thousand cubits, and on the south side two thousand cubits, and on the west side two thousand cubits, and on the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle.
