This shall belong to them as pastureland for their cities.<sup>6</sup>"The cities that you give to the Levites shall be the six cities of refuge, where you shall permit the manslayer to flee, and in addition to them you shall give forty-two cities.<sup>7</sup>All the cities that you give to the Levites shall be forty-eight, with their pasturelands.<sup>8</sup>And as for the cities that you shall give from the possession of the people of Israel, from the larger tribes you shall take many, and from the smaller tribes you shall take few; each, in proportion to the inheritance that it inherits, shall give of its cities to the Levites."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan,<sup>11</sup>then you shall select cities to be cities of refuge for you, that the manslayer who kills any person without intent may flee there.<sup>12</sup>The cities shall be for you a refuge from the avenger, that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment.<sup>13</sup>And the cities that you give shall be your six cities of refuge.<sup>14</sup>You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan, to be cities of refuge.<sup>15</sup>These six cities shall be for refuge for the people of Israel, and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them, that anyone who kills any person without intent may flee there.<sup>16</sup>"But if he struck him down with an iron object, so that he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>And if he struck him down with a stone tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>18</sup>Or if he struck him down with a wooden tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>19</sup>The avenger of blood shall himself put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death.<sup>20</sup>And if he pushed him out of hatred or hurled something at him, lying in wait, so that he died,<sup>21</sup>or in enmity struck him down with his hand, so that he died, then he who struck the blow shall be put to death. He is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall put the murderer to death when he meets him.<sup>22</sup>"But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled anything on him without lying in wait<sup>23</sup>or used a stone that could cause death, and without seeing him dropped it on him, so that he died, though he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm,<sup>24</sup>then the congregation shall judge between the manslayer and the avenger of blood, in accordance with these rules.<sup>25</sup>And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge to which he had fled, and he shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil.<sup>26</sup>But if the manslayer shall at any time go beyond the boundaries of his city of refuge to which he fled,<sup>27</sup>and the avenger of blood finds him outside the boundaries of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer, he shall not be guilty of blood.<sup>28</sup>For he must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest, but after the death of the high priest the manslayer may return to the land of his possession.<sup>29</sup>And these things shall be for a statute and rule for you throughout your generations in all your dwelling places.<sup>30</sup>"If anyone kills a person, the murderer shall be put to death on the evidence of witnesses. But no person shall be put to death on the testimony of one witness.<sup>31</sup>Moreover, you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death.<sup>32</sup>And you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge, that he may return to dwell in the land before the death of the high priest.<sup>33</sup>You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it.<sup>34</sup>You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel."
35.overview:
Chapter 35 establishes the Levitical cities, and within them, six cities of refuge — a provision so rich with gospel meaning that it has stirred the hearts of God's people for ages. In a society without police or prisons, where the blood of a slain man was avenged by his nearest kinsman, the cities of refuge offered protection for the manslayer who had killed unintentionally. He could flee to the nearest refuge city and be safe from the avenger of blood until his case was judged. Here, in the structure of Israel's justice, mercy and justice meet.

The provision is exquisitely balanced. The deliberate murderer found no refuge; justice demanded his life. But the one who killed by accident, without malice, could flee to the city and live. The roads to these cities, the rabbis tell us, were kept clear and marked, that the fleeing man might run without stumbling and reach safety in time. The whole arrangement preaches that God is both just — he does not let murder go unpunished — and merciful, providing a place of safety for the one overtaken by tragedy. Sproul noted that the cities of refuge display the very character of God, who is both righteous and gracious, and who provides a way for guilt to be sheltered without justice being denied.

But the deepest wonder is in verse 25: the manslayer must remain in the city of refuge “until the death of the high priest.” When the high priest died, the refugee was free to return home, fully released. His freedom was secured by a death — the death of the high priest. The New Testament gathers up this stunning picture. Hebrews speaks of those “who have fled for refuge” to “lay hold of the hope set before us” (Heb 6:18). Christ is our city of refuge, to whom we flee from the avenging justice of the law. And it is precisely the death of our great High Priest that sets us free — not someone else's death, but his own. Ferguson marveled at the fusion: in the cities of refuge, the refugee was freed by the high priest's death, and Christ is both our refuge and our High Priest, whose death secures our everlasting release. We have fled to him, and because he has died, we are free.
35.theology:
Justice and mercy meet. The cities of refuge shelter the unintentional manslayer without sparing the murderer. God is both righteous and gracious, providing safety without denying justice.

Christ our refuge. We have fled for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before us (Heb 6:18). Christ is the city to whom the guilt-stricken flee from the avenging justice of the law.

Freed by the high priest's death. The refugee's release came through the death of the high priest. Christ is both our refuge and our High Priest, whose own death secures our everlasting freedom.
35.examples:
Then: God appointed cities of refuge where the unintentional manslayer could flee from the avenger of blood and remain safe until the death of the high priest released him.

Now: Flee to Christ, your city of refuge, from the avenging justice of the law. He is both your refuge and your great High Priest, and because he has died, you are set free forever. You have run to him, and the door of mercy stands open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites receive no territory of their own, for the LORD is their inheritance — but they must live somewhere. So God commands that the other tribes give them forty-eight cities, scattered throughout the land, with pastureland around them. The tribe devoted to God’s service is spread among all the tribes, so that worship, teaching, and the knowledge of God are never far from anyone in Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: The Levites, having no land-inheritance because “the LORD is their portion” (18:20), are given forty-eight cities distributed among all the tribes (vv.7-8). The scattering was strategic: those set apart for God’s service lived within reach of every Israelite, so that instruction in God’s law and the ministry of worship permeated the whole nation. It pictures how God means the knowledge of himself to saturate the life of his people, never confined to one corner (cf. Mal 2:7, the priest’s lips guarding knowledge).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the tribe devoted to God was spread through all the others, so no Israelite lived far from the ministry of the Word.

Now: God still means the knowledge of himself to permeate all of life, not stay walled off in one place. His servants are scattered as salt and light throughout the world (Matt 5:13-14).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Command the people of Israel to give to the Levites some of the inheritance of their possession as cities for them to dwell in. And you shall give to the Levites pasturelands around the cities. The cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and their pasturelands shall be for their cattle and for their livestock and for all their beasts. The pasturelands of the cities, which you shall give to the Levites, shall reach from the wall of the city outward a thousand cubits all around. And you shall measure, outside the city, on the east side two thousand cubits, and on the south side two thousand cubits, and on the west side two thousand cubits, and on the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle. This shall belong to them as pastureland for their cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites get no territory, and God will not therefore leave them homeless. Command the people of Israel to give to the Levites some of the inheritance of their possession as cities for them to dwell in. Not a region of their own; towns inside everyone else’s region, with pastureland measured out around each one.

A reader who checks the figures will find an apparent conflict — verse 4 gives a thousand cubits and verse 5 says two thousand on each side. The usual explanation is the simple one: verse 4 measures outward from the wall, and verse 5 gives the length of each side of the resulting square, which is the town in the middle plus a thousand cubits at either end. It is a surveyor’s description, and it is exact.

But look at what the arrangement does. Levi is not settled in a block; Levi is distributed. Forty-eight towns scattered through every tribe in Israel, so that no family in the nation lived more than a short walk from someone whose whole life was the law of God. And Jacob had said something over this tribe on his deathbed that sounded like a curse: of Simeon and Levi, I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Gen. 49:7). The scattering came. And in God’s hands the punishment turned into the mechanism by which a whole nation was taught. He does not always remove what he has pronounced. Sometimes he keeps it, and turns it round, and uses the very thing to do good that was first spoken as a judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "The cities that you give to the Levites shall be the six cities of refuge, where you shall permit the manslayer to flee, and in addition to them you shall give forty-two cities. All the cities that you give to the Levites shall be forty-eight, with their pasturelands. And as for the cities that you shall give from the possession of the people of Israel, from the larger tribes you shall take many, and from the smaller tribes you shall take few; each, in proportion to the inheritance that it inherits, shall give of its cities to the Levites."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cities that you give to the Levites shall be the six cities of refuge… and in addition to them you shall give forty-two cities. Six out of forty-eight, and the six are named first.

Consider the design. The cities where a man could run for his life were priests’ towns. The frightened fugitive did not arrive at a garrison or a magistrate’s house; he arrived somewhere full of men whose business was the mercy and holiness of God. Sanctuary and instruction were put in the same place on purpose. A man running for his life was going to end up living among the people best equipped to tell him why he was still alive.

And the cost of it is spread by a rule that runs all through Scripture: from the larger tribes you shall take many, and from the smaller tribes you shall take few; each, in proportion to the inheritance that it inherits. Nobody gives the same; everybody gives proportionally. That is the standard the New Testament applies to Christian giving without alteration — if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (2 Cor. 8:12) — and it is the reason a widow’s two coins outweighed a rich man’s heap.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six of the Levite cities are set apart as cities of refuge. If a person kills someone accidentally, he may flee to one of these cities and be safe from the avenger of blood until his case is judged. If he is found guilty of murder, he is handed over; but if the killing was unintentional, he stays safe in the city of refuge — until the death of the high priest, after which he may return home free. And running through it all is a solemn truth: bloodshed pollutes the land, and life is sacred to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The cities of refuge picture the gospel: a God-appointed place to flee where the guilty-yet-not-condemned are safe from the avenger — “we who have fled for refuge” (Heb 6:18). Most strikingly, the manslayer is freed to return home only at “the death of the high priest” (vv.25, 28): the high priest’s death releases him. So the death of our great High Priest sets us free (Heb 9:15). And the insistence that innocent blood “pollutes the land” which can be cleansed only by the blood of the one who shed it (vv.33-34) upholds the sanctity of life and the justice of God — justice fully satisfied at the cross, where the High Priest was himself the sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the manslayer lived safe inside the city of refuge, and was set free to go home only when the high priest died.

Now: we have “fled for refuge” to Christ (Heb 6:18), and the death of our High Priest is the very thing that sets us free (Heb 9:15). Run to him, and no accuser can reach you.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan, then you shall select cities to be cities of refuge for you, that the manslayer who kills any person without intent may flee there. The cities shall be for you a refuge from the avenger, that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the institution itself, and it needs the background before it can be felt. In a society with no police force and no public prosecutor, the pursuit of a killer fell to the dead man’s nearest relative — the avenger of blood, the goel haddam, the kinsman whose duty it was to see that a life taken was answered for. That was not lawlessness. It was the only enforcement mechanism the ancient world had, and without it a man could be killed and nothing would happen at all.

But it had an obvious and terrible weakness. A grieving brother, riding out on the day of the funeral, is in no condition to distinguish a murder from an accident, and he is not going to stop and ask. Between the death and the vengeance there was nothing at all: no hearing, no evidence, no delay.

So God puts something in the gap. The cities shall be for you a refuge from the avenger, that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment. Read that clause again and take in what it is. In the Bronze Age, God legislated a right to a hearing before execution. The entire purpose of the institution is to slow a killing down long enough for the facts to be established. That is what the justice of God looks like when it is written into a statute: not indifference to blood — the next paragraphs are ferocious about blood — but an absolute refusal to let a man die before anybody has found out what he did.

verseByVerse.quote: And the cities that you give shall be your six cities of refuge. You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan, to be cities of refuge. These six cities shall be for refuge for the people of Israel, and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them, that anyone who kills any person without intent may flee there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan. Six in all, spread so that no one in Israel was more than a day’s hard run from one of them. The whole system is useless if a man cannot reach it in time, so God arranged the map around the speed of a frightened human being.

Then a clause that keeps appearing in this book and should never stop surprising us: These six cities shall be for refuge for the people of Israel, and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them. The foreigner gets the same protection as the citizen. Not a lesser version, not a supervised version — the same six cities, on the same terms.

Numbers has now said this three times. The water of cleansing was for Israel and for the stranger who sojourns among them (19:10). The law of the offerings was one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you (15:16). And now the refuge. Long before any Gentile had heard of the God of Israel, the God of Israel had written the outsider into the emergency provisions of his law. He is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Eph. 2:14) was not a change of mind. It was the finishing of something begun here.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he struck him down with an iron object, so that he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. And if he struck him down with a stone tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. Or if he struck him down with a wooden tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. The avenger of blood shall himself put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death. And if he pushed him out of hatred or hurled something at him, lying in wait, so that he died, or in enmity struck him down with his hand, so that he died, then he who struck the blow shall be put to death. He is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall put the murderer to death when he meets him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before mercy is extended to anybody, murder is defined with great care, and the definition runs on two tracks.

The first is the instrument. If he struck him down with an iron object… with a stone tool that could cause death… with a wooden tool that could cause death — the law asks what was in the man’s hand and whether it was capable of killing. A man who swings an iron bar at somebody’s head has told you what he intended, whatever he says afterwards.

The second is the heart, and it is stated four different ways in two verses: if he pushed him out of hatred or hurled something at him, lying in wait… or in enmity struck him down with his hand. Hatred. Lying in wait. Enmity. God’s law is not content to establish that a death occurred; it goes after what the man wanted and how long he had wanted it.

That distinction is so familiar to us that it is easy to miss how remarkable it is. The difference between murder and manslaughter, which every legal system in the West still turns on, is not an obvious idea and many ancient codes did not make it. It is here, in the fifth book of the Bible, because the God who gave the law is a God who reads motives. And the same God who insists on that distinction in a courtroom takes it further still, into a place no court can reach: everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). The law of Moses could only reach the hand. The Lord Jesus went for the enmity that puts the weapon in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled anything on him without lying in wait or used a stone that could cause death, and without seeing him dropped it on him, so that he died, though he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm, then the congregation shall judge between the manslayer and the avenger of blood, in accordance with these rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the other case, and the writing is unusually tender. But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled anything on him without lying in wait, or used a stone that could cause death, and without seeing him dropped it on him, so that he died, though he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm…

Three separate tests, and each of them looks inside the man rather than at the corpse. No enmity. No lying in wait. No desire for his harm. And the picture in the middle is the most ordinary thing imaginable: a man working on a wall or a roof, a stone in his hands, somebody below he never saw. It took a second and there is nothing to be done and a man is dead.

This is the passage for anyone who has caused a death. The driver at the junction. The doctor who missed it. The parent who looked away for the length of a phone call. People carry these for decades, and the accusation they live under is always the same: you are a killer. God’s law had a different category for them three and a half thousand years ago. It did not pretend nothing had happened — a life was gone, a family was destroyed, and the man went into exile for years. But it looked at him and said: this is not murder, and you are not a murderer, and there is a place for you to go where the accuser cannot reach you.

And who decides? Then the congregation shall judge between the manslayer and the avenger of blood. Not the frightened man, who would always plead accident, and not the grieving man, who would always call it murder. The assembly of God’s people, hearing both, at a distance from the grave. Mercy in Scripture is never a failure to look at the facts. It is what the facts turn out to allow, once somebody has finally sat down and heard them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge to which he had fled, and he shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil. But if the manslayer shall at any time go beyond the boundaries of his city of refuge to which he fled, and the avenger of blood finds him outside the boundaries of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer, he shall not be guilty of blood. For he must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest, but after the death of the high priest the manslayer may return to the land of his possession.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sentence, and it is like nothing else in the law. The man is not fined. He does not serve a fixed term. He is not put to work. He shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil.

His freedom hangs on one man’s life ending. It could be forty years or it could be next week; nothing the manslayer does affects it in the slightest, and nothing anybody else does either. And the reason is not arbitrary. The high priest was the man who stood for the whole nation before God, who carried the twelve tribal names over his heart into the Most Holy Place and made atonement for the people. When he died, an era closed and, in a sense the law itself implies, the outstanding blood-guilt of the land died with him. It took a death to release the man — not his own, and not the victim’s, but the priest’s.

There is no mistaking what that is a picture of. We who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us (Heb. 6:18) is written about Christians, in the language of this chapter, by a man whose whole letter is about a High Priest. Our High Priest has died. Every soul who has run to him for shelter is free, not by serving out a term or by improving, but because the Priest is dead and the sentence went into the ground with him. And here the picture breaks in the direction of glory: the manslayer’s release came by an accident of timing, from a priest who never knew his name and did not die for him. Ours died on purpose, knowing exactly who we were and what we had done, and calling it love.

Read the warning attached, though, because it is severe. If the manslayer shall at any time go beyond the boundaries of his city of refuge… and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer, he shall not be guilty of blood. The safety was real and it was local. Inside the wall, untouchable; one step outside, and the law itself declared his killer innocent. That is the exact shape of the gospel’s comfort and the gospel’s seriousness together. There is complete safety in Christ and there is no safety anywhere else, and the man who wanders out to see whether the old country is still there has left the only place where he cannot be reached. Abide in me, and I in you (John 15:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And these things shall be for a statute and rule for you throughout your generations in all your dwelling places. "If anyone kills a person, the murderer shall be put to death on the evidence of witnesses. But no person shall be put to death on the testimony of one witness. Moreover, you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death. And you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge, that he may return to dwell in the land before the death of the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two prohibitions close the legal section, and both are about money.

The first: you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death. In every surrounding culture a killing could be settled by payment — a price list existed, and a rich man could afford a death. Israel alone forbade it outright. A human life cannot be converted into silver, because of what a human being is: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image (Gen. 9:6). To let a murderer buy his way out is to put a price on the image of God, and the law will not permit the transaction at any figure.

The second closes the other door: you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge, that he may return… before the death of the high priest. The manslayer cannot buy his way out early either. The system cannot be bought at either end, by the guilty or by the unfortunate.

Hold those two verses in your hand and then read this. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). God had declared, in his own law, that for a life like ours no ransom whatever would be accepted. And then the only ransom he would ever take, he provided himself, out of his own house, at the price of his own Son. You were ransomed… not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18–19). No amount of money could have bought a single one of us out. It was never going to be money.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it. You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends by telling us why any of this mattered so much. You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it. You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel.

Blood soaks into ground and stays there. That is the picture — not a legal fiction but a stain, and one that cannot be washed out by ceremony, by payment, or by the passage of time. Scripture has said so since the first murder, when God told Cain, the voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground (Gen. 4:10). Shed blood has a voice, and it does not stop.

And the reason the land must be kept clean is given in the last clause, and it is the reason for everything else in the book: I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel. Not visits. Dwells. The whole apparatus of Numbers — the camp arranged around a tent, the Levites ringing it, the cleansing of the death-defiled, the refuge cities, the boundaries — exists for the sake of that one clause. He is not visiting. He lives there, and a God who lives among people has views about the ground they live on.

So the book that opened by arranging a camp around the dwelling place of God closes its law with blood crying out of the ground and no way to silence it. And there is one place in all of Scripture where that voice is answered. The church has come, Hebrews says, to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Heb. 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for justice from the soil and could not be quieted. Christ’s blood was poured out on the same cursed ground and cries louder, and what it says is not avenge but forgive. The avenger has been met. The Priest has died. The refuge is open, and the door of it is a Person.

36.title: The Inheritance Preserved: God's Faithfulness to the Last Detail
36.text: <sup>1</sup>The heads of the fathers' houses of the clan of the people of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of the people of Joseph, came near and spoke before Moses and before the chiefs, the heads of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>They said, "The LORD commanded my lord to give the land for inheritance by lot to the people of Israel, and my lord was commanded by the LORD to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother to his daughters.<sup>3</sup>But if they are married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the people of Israel, then their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of our fathers and added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. So it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance.<sup>4</sup>And when the jubilee of the people of Israel comes, then their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry, and their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers."<sup>5</sup>And Moses commanded the people of Israel according to the word of the LORD, saying, "The tribe of the people of Joseph is right.<sup>6</sup>This is what the LORD commands concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: 'Let them marry whom they think best, only they shall marry within the clan of the tribe of their father.<sup>7</sup>The inheritance of the people of Israel shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, for every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.<sup>8</sup>And every daughter who possesses an inheritance in any tribe of the people of Israel shall be wife to one of the clan of the tribe of her father, so that every one of the people of Israel may possess the inheritance of his fathers.<sup>9</sup>So no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another, for each of the tribes of the people of Israel shall hold on to its own inheritance.'"<sup>10</sup>The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded Moses,<sup>11</sup>for Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to sons of their father's brothers.<sup>12</sup>They were married into the clans of the people of Manasseh the son of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father's clan.<sup>13</sup>These are the commandments and the rules that the LORD commanded through Moses to the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
36.overview:
The book of Numbers ends not with a thunderclap but with a quiet matter of inheritance law — and that quietness is itself a kind of glory. Back in chapter 27, the daughters of Zelophehad had won the right to inherit their father's land because he had no sons. Now a question arises: if these daughters marry into another tribe, their inherited land will pass to that tribe, and the careful allotment of the inheritance will be disturbed. So God provides that they marry within their own tribe, that the inheritance of each tribe may be preserved intact.

It seems a small thing on which to end a great book. But consider what it reveals. The God who split the sea, who fed millions with manna, who spoke from Sinai and led by cloud and fire, is also the God who cares about the precise preservation of a single family's inheritance within a single tribe. No detail of the promise is too small for his attention. Wenham notes the fitting conclusion: the book that began with the ordering of the people ends with the securing of their inheritance down to the last allotment. God is faithful in the smallest particulars.

And here is the abiding comfort. The God of Numbers is faithful to his promises down to the last detail. He does not lose interest after the grand acts of redemption; he attends to the full and final preservation of the inheritance he has promised. Ferguson notes that the meticulous care of these closing verses preaches the meticulous faithfulness of God. Not one of his promises will fail; not one portion of the inheritance will be lost. Peter speaks of an inheritance “kept in heaven for you,” for those “who by God's power are being guarded through faith” (1 Pet 1:4–5). The same God who ensured that no tribe lost its allotment guards the inheritance of every believer with infinite care. The book that journeyed through grumbling, rebellion, and judgment ends on the bedrock of God's unwavering faithfulness: the inheritance is preserved, the promise stands, and the God who keeps his word will surely bring his pilgrim people home, not losing one of them, not forfeiting one portion, all the way to the end.
36.theology:
God's faithfulness in the smallest detail. The God who split the sea attends to the preservation of a single family's portion. No detail of his promise is too small for his meticulous care.

The inheritance preserved. God secures the allotment so that not one portion is lost, prefiguring the inheritance kept in heaven for those guarded by his power through faith (1 Pet 1:4–5).

Faithful obedience. The daughters obey God's word, and the book ends on trust and submission to the Lord's commandments, the people ordering their lives by his word.
36.examples:
Then: God secured the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters within their own tribe, and the book ended with their faithful obedience on the plains of Moab.

Now: The God who ensured no tribe lost its portion guards your inheritance in Christ with infinite care, down to the last detail. Not one of his promises will fail. He will bring his pilgrim people home, losing none, all the way to the end. The promise stands, for the God who keeps it cannot fail.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Keeping the Inheritance in the Tribe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book of Numbers ends where it has often lingered — on the inheritance. A concern is raised about the daughters of Zelophehad: if they marry into another tribe, their father’s land will pass to that tribe, and the tribal inheritance will be diminished. God’s solution honors both the daughters’ rights and the tribes’ integrity: they may marry whomever they wish, only within their own tribe, so that no inheritance passes from tribe to tribe. The book closes with the promised land carefully guarded, ready to be received.
verseByVerse.theology: The final chapter guards the inheritance so that “no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another” (v.9) — God’s gifts are to be kept, not squandered or lost. That Numbers, a book of wandering and failure, ends fixed on the secure inheritance testifies to God’s unwavering faithfulness: despite forty years of rebellion, the promise stands, mapped, apportioned, and protected, waiting for the new generation. It points to the inheritance “kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet 1:4) that can never be lost, because God himself guards it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the book of wandering ends not in the desert but with the inheritance secured — every tribe’s portion guarded, the promise intact.

Now: our inheritance is guarded by God himself, “kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet 1:4). Despite all our wandering, the promise stands, and the land is ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: The heads of the fathers' houses of the clan of the people of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of the people of Joseph, came near and spoke before Moses and before the chiefs, the heads of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel. They said, "The LORD commanded my lord to give the land for inheritance by lot to the people of Israel, and my lord was commanded by the LORD to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother to his daughters. But if they are married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the people of Israel, then their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of our fathers and added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. So it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance. And when the jubilee of the people of Israel comes, then their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry, and their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book closes with a legal query, and the men raising it are being scrupulously careful. The heads of the fathers’ houses of the clan of the people of Gilead… came near and spoke before Moses and before the chiefs. They do not go behind anybody’s back and they do not contest the earlier ruling; they begin by reciting it, correctly and in full, as the word of the LORD.

Their difficulty is real. Zelophehad’s daughters have been granted their father’s land (ch. 27). But if they marry outside the tribe, that land goes with them into their husbands’ families — and permanently, because when the jubilee of the people of Israel comes, the year when every field in Israel reverted to its original family, it will revert to the wrong family. The jubilee, designed to keep land in the clan for ever, would in this one case lock the loss in.

Two things stand out about how they raise it. They bring it to the leadership rather than to the women. And their objection is not that the daughters got too much; they accept the ruling entirely and ask only how to keep it from unravelling something else. That is what honest disagreement inside the people of God looks like — a question asked in the open, to the right people, about the consequences of a decision rather than about the decision itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses commanded the people of Israel according to the word of the LORD, saying, "The tribe of the people of Joseph is right. This is what the LORD commands concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: 'Let them marry whom they think best, only they shall marry within the clan of the tribe of their father. The inheritance of the people of Israel shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, for every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers. And every daughter who possesses an inheritance in any tribe of the people of Israel shall be wife to one of the clan of the tribe of her father, so that every one of the people of Israel may possess the inheritance of his fathers. So no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another, for each of the tribes of the people of Israel shall hold on to its own inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribe of the people of Joseph is right.

Those are almost exactly the words God used nine chapters earlier about the daughters themselves: The daughters of Zelophehad are right (27:7). The same verdict, given to the other side. God had not made a mistake in chapter 27 that needed correcting in chapter 36; he had made a ruling that raised a second question, and now he answers that one too. Both parties were right, and it took two decisions to say so.

And the answer costs neither of them anything. Let them marry whom they think best, only they shall marry within the clan of the tribe of their father. Read the order of that sentence. The freedom comes first and the limit second — whom they think best, which was more choice than most women in the ancient world had, and then one boundary drawn around it. The daughters keep the land and keep the choice. Manasseh keeps its allotment. The whole tribal map of Israel stays intact.

God is not obliged to settle every dispute by finding one party at fault. Sometimes two legitimate claims collide because the world is complicated, and the answer is not a compromise in which everyone loses a little but a provision neither side had thought of. It is a small domestic case in an obscure chapter, and it shows something about how God governs: he can uphold the rights of five orphaned women and the integrity of a tribe’s inheritance at the same time, without shaving anything off either.

verseByVerse.quote: The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded Moses, for Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to sons of their father's brothers. They were married into the clans of the people of Manasseh the son of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father's clan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded Moses… and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father’s clan.

They are named one final time — Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah and Noah — and the last thing Scripture records about them is obedience. The women who walked to the front of a national assembly and pressed a claim nobody had ever granted now accept a restriction on whom they may marry, and do it without a word of protest.

Both halves belong to the same character. It takes courage to stand in front of Moses and the chiefs of Israel and say that the law as it stands is not right, and it takes something just as rare to hear God narrow your options afterwards and simply comply. Faith that will contend for what God has promised and then bow to how God orders it is a whole thing. A person who can only do the first is not brave, only wilful; a person who can only do the second is not humble, only passive.

And notice what they got. Not less than they asked for — the land is theirs, and the last clause says so: their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father’s clan. Their father’s name was not blotted out of Israel. Five women had gone to the trouble of asking, and because they asked, a dead man in an unmarked grave in the wilderness still had a place among the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the commandments and the rules that the LORD commanded through Moses to the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the commandments and the rules that the LORD commanded through Moses to the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.

That is the last verse of Numbers, and there is no fanfare in it. No summary of the forty years, no oration, no crossing. Just a note of where the laws were given, and the note is a map reference: by the Jordan at Jericho. On the wrong bank, in sight of the walls.

Consider how the book began. A census at Sinai, a nation drawn up in perfect order around the tent of God, banners and divisions and everybody in their place, about to march eleven days to the promise. And consider what happened: the quail and the graves of craving, Miriam’s leprosy, ten spies and a night of weeping, forty years, Korah swallowed alive, the rock struck twice, the serpents, Peor and twenty-four thousand dead, Miriam buried at Kadesh, Aaron stripped on a mountain, Moses told he may look and not enter. Numbers is the record of a generation that could not be got into a land eleven days away, and it ends with them camped outside it.

And yet look at what is standing on that riverbank. A nation as large as the one that left Sinai, counted man for man. A high priest in office and a commissioned leader with the Spirit in him. A calendar of worship, a law of refuge, a map with borders drawn, and five women whose title deeds are in order. Everything Israel deserved was a wilderness. Everything Israel has is a gift.

The book that carries the most human failure of any in the Pentateuch ends with not one promise of God unfulfilled and not one of them cancelled by the failure. If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13). The last words place the reader on the near bank of a river with the land in view, which is exactly where every believer stands, and the book’s whole argument is about the character of the God who brought them that far. He did not bring them through the wilderness to leave them at the water. Behind them the graves; in front of them the Jordan; and over them the same pillar of cloud that had never once failed to move on ahead.
